items.gloss_md: Gene encoding PD-1, the inhibitory immune-checkpoint receptor on activated and exhausted T cells.
items.body_md:
Programmed cell death 1. Previous name/alias PD1, CD279. Located on 2q37.3.

Encodes the receptor PD-1 (CD279), a CD28-family member expressed on activated T cells, B cells, NK cells and, persistently and at high levels, on exhausted T cells in chronic infection and cancer. Ligation by PD-L1 or PD-L2 dampens T-cell receptor and CD28 signalling and maintains peripheral tolerance.

Discovered in 1992 by Tasuku Honjo's group (Ishida et al.) as a gene induced in a T-cell hybridoma undergoing cell death, hence the name, although PD-1 itself does not trigger apoptosis. Pdcd1 knockout mice develop late-onset autoimmunity (lupus-like disease, dilated cardiomyopathy depending on strain).

Clinical relevance: the target of anti-PD-1 antibodies (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, tislelizumab). In transplant recipients, checkpoint blockade carries a high risk of allograft rejection. High PDCD1 expression is a core gene in exhaustion signatures in scRNA-seq.

attrs.anecdote: Tasuku Honjo, who found PD-1 in 1992, shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with James Allison (CTLA-4) for cancer therapy by inhibition of negative immune regulation.

items.gloss_md: Inhibitory checkpoint receptor (CD279) on activated and exhausted T cells; blocking it with antibodies releases anti-tumour T-cell responses.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane receptor of the CD28 family with one IgV-like extracellular domain and a cytoplasmic tail carrying an ITIM and an ITSM motif. It is a monomer at the cell surface (unlike CD28 and CTLA-4).

Binding of PD-L1 or PD-L2 phosphorylates the ITSM, which recruits the phosphatase SHP-2; SHP-2 dephosphorylates CD28 and proximal TCR signalling molecules, reducing proliferation, cytokine production and glycolysis. Expression is induced by TCR activation and stays high under chronic antigen stimulation (exhaustion, together with TIM-3, LAG-3, TIGIT and TOX).

Encoded by *PDCD1*. Drugs: nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab and others. Immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis) follow from lost tolerance. In HCC anti-PD-1/PD-L1 combinations are first-line; in PDAC checkpoint blockade works essentially only in the rare MSI-high/dMMR tumours.

attrs.mnemonic: PD-1 is the brake on the T cell, PD-L1 is the foot (the Ligand) pressing it; anti-PD-1 lifts the foot off the brake.
attrs.anecdote: Its name is a historical accident: PD-1 was cloned from dying T cells and named 'programmed death', but it does not cause cell death – it is an off switch.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding PD-L1, the main ligand of PD-1, expressed by tumour, myeloid and inflamed tissue cells.
items.body_md:
CD274 molecule. Aliases B7-H1, PDCD1L1, PD-L1. Located on 9p24.1, next to *PDCD1LG2* (PD-L2) and close to *JAK2*.

Encodes PD-L1, a B7-family ligand expressed constitutively at low levels on antigen-presenting cells and induced on many cell types by interferon-γ (via JAK–STAT1–IRF1), a process called adaptive immune resistance.

Cancer relevance: 9p24.1 amplification (PD-L1/PD-L2/JAK2) is a hallmark of classical Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma and explains their high response to PD-1 blockade. Structural variants disrupting the CD274 3' UTR stabilise the transcript in some tumours. Oncogenic signalling (e.g. MYC, EGFR) can raise expression.

Clinical relevance: the PD-L1 IHC level (TPS, CPS, IC score) is a companion or complementary diagnostic for anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy in many tumour types.

attrs.mnemonic: 9p24.1 is the 'checkpoint street': PD-L1, PD-L2 and JAK2 live next door, so one amplification in Hodgkin lymphoma hits all three.

items.gloss_md: Ligand of PD-1 (B7-H1, CD274) that switches off T cells; its expression measured by IHC guides checkpoint immunotherapy.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane B7-family protein with an IgV and an IgC domain. Binds PD-1 on T cells and, in cis on the same antigen-presenting cell, CD80, which blocks CD80–CTLA-4 interaction.

Expressed on tumour cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, endothelium and hepatocytes / Kupffer cells after interferon-γ exposure; in the liver it contributes to the organ's tolerogenic environment. A soluble form and exosomal PD-L1 also exist.

IHC scoring: tumour proportion score (TPS, % PD-L1+ tumour cells), combined positive score (CPS, PD-L1+ tumour and immune cells per 100 tumour cells) and immune-cell score; assays use clones 22C3, 28-8, SP263 and SP142, which are not fully interchangeable.

Encoded by *CD274*. Drugs: atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab. In unresectable HCC, atezolizumab + bevacizumab (IMbrave150) and durvalumab + tremelimumab (HIMALAYA) are standard first-line options.

attrs.mnemonic: TPS counts Tumour cells only, CPS Counts Plus immune cells.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding PD-L2, the second PD-1 ligand, mainly expressed on dendritic cells and macrophages.
items.body_md:
Programmed cell death 1 ligand 2. Aliases B7-DC, CD273, PD-L2. Located on 9p24.1, adjacent to *CD274*.

Encodes PD-L2, whose expression is more restricted than PD-L1: mainly dendritic cells, macrophages and some B-cell subsets, induced by IL-4 and interferons. It binds PD-1 with higher affinity than PD-L1 and also binds RGMb.

Cancer relevance: co-amplified with *CD274* and *JAK2* in the 9p24.1 amplicon of classical Hodgkin lymphoma and primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma. Anti-PD-1 antibodies block both ligands, whereas anti-PD-L1 antibodies leave PD-L2–PD-1 signalling intact, a frequently discussed theoretical difference between the two drug classes.

items.gloss_md: Second ligand of PD-1 (B7-DC, CD273), mainly on dendritic cells and macrophages.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane B7-family protein (IgV + IgC domains) that binds PD-1 with roughly two- to six-fold higher affinity than PD-L1, and additionally binds repulsive guidance molecule b (RGMb), which is relevant in lung tolerance.

Expressed on dendritic cells, macrophages (induced by IL-4 in alternatively activated macrophages), mast cells and some B cells; tumour expression occurs particularly in lymphomas with 9p24.1 amplification.

Encoded by *PDCD1LG2*. Not targeted specifically by an approved drug, but anti-PD-1 antibodies block its interaction with PD-1. When interpreting checkpoint biomarkers, PD-L2 expression can explain responses in PD-L1-negative tumours.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CTLA-4, the inhibitory receptor that competes with CD28 for CD80/CD86.
items.body_md:
Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4. Alias CD152. Located on 2q33.2 in a cluster with *CD28* and *ICOS*.

Encodes CTLA-4, a high-affinity receptor for CD80 and CD86, expressed constitutively by Tregs and induced in activated conventional T cells. It is a key regulator of the priming phase of T-cell responses.

First cloned in 1987 by Brunet et al. (Golstein lab) from cytotoxic T cells. Ctla4 knockout mice die within weeks from massive lymphoproliferation. In humans, heterozygous germline loss-of-function (CTLA-4 haploinsufficiency) causes an immune dysregulation syndrome with autoimmunity, enteropathy and lymphocytic infiltration; common CTLA4 polymorphisms associate with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease.

Clinical relevance: blocked by ipilimumab and tremelimumab (cancer); its extracellular domain fused to IgG Fc gives abatacept (rheumatoid arthritis) and belatacept (kidney transplant immunosuppression).

attrs.anecdote: James Allison's group showed in 1996 that blocking CTLA-4 makes mice reject tumours; ipilimumab became the first checkpoint inhibitor approved (melanoma, 2011) and Allison shared the 2018 Nobel Prize with Honjo.

items.gloss_md: Inhibitory receptor (CD152) on Tregs and activated T cells that outcompetes CD28 for CD80/CD86 and thereby limits T-cell priming.
items.body_md:
Covalent homodimeric type I transmembrane protein of the CD28 family; the MYPPPY motif binds CD80/CD86 with much higher affinity than CD28. Most CTLA-4 sits in intracellular vesicles and is recruited to the immune synapse after activation.

Mechanisms: competition with CD28 for ligands, removal of CD80/CD86 from antigen-presenting cells by trans-endocytosis (especially by Tregs), and inhibitory signalling. It acts mainly in lymph nodes during priming, whereas PD-1 acts mainly in peripheral tissues.

Encoded by *CTLA4*. Antagonists: ipilimumab, tremelimumab (combined with nivolumab or durvalumab, e.g. HIMALAYA in HCC); toxicity (colitis, hepatitis, hypophysitis) is higher than with PD-1 blockade. Agonistic fusion proteins: abatacept and belatacept (CTLA4-Ig), which block costimulation; belatacept is a calcineurin-inhibitor-free maintenance option in kidney transplantation.

attrs.mnemonic: CTLA-4 acts in the lymph node (priming), PD-1 in the tissue (effector phase): 'CTLA-4 early and central, PD-1 late and peripheral'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD28, the main costimulatory receptor providing 'signal 2' to naive T cells.
items.body_md:
CD28 molecule, located on 2q33.2 next to *CTLA4* and *ICOS*.

Encodes CD28, constitutively expressed on most human CD4+ and about half of CD8+ T cells; loss of CD28 marks terminally differentiated (CD28null) T cells that accumulate with age and chronic CMV infection.

Function: binding to CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells provides the costimulatory second signal required with TCR engagement (signal 1) for IL-2 production, proliferation, survival and metabolic reprogramming; TCR signalling without CD28 leads to anergy.

Clinical relevance: CD28 costimulation is blocked by belatacept and abatacept (via the ligands); CD28 signalling domains are part of second-generation CAR constructs (e.g. axicabtagene ciloleucel). PD-1 inhibition acts largely by dephosphorylating CD28.

attrs.mnemonic: Three signals: 1 = TCR sees peptide–MHC, 2 = CD28 sees B7 (CD80/CD86), 3 = cytokines. Signal 1 without signal 2 = anergy.

items.gloss_md: Costimulatory receptor on T cells that binds CD80/CD86 and provides the second signal for full activation.
items.body_md:
Disulfide-linked homodimeric type I transmembrane protein with one IgV domain (MYPPPY ligand motif) and a cytoplasmic tail with YMNM and PxxP motifs that recruit PI3K, GRB2 and LCK, enhancing AKT–mTOR, NF-κB and NFAT/AP-1 activity, IL-2 transcription and glycolysis.

Binds CD80 and CD86 with lower affinity than CTLA-4, so CTLA-4 outcompetes it once induced. PD-1-recruited SHP-2 preferentially dephosphorylates CD28.

Encoded by *CD28*. Used as a costimulatory domain in CAR T cells; blocked indirectly by CTLA4-Ig fusion proteins (belatacept, abatacept).

With ageing and chronic CMV infection, CD28-negative CD8+ (and some CD4+) T cells accumulate; they are cytotoxic, independent of CD28 costimulation and have been linked to belatacept-resistant rejection.

attrs.anecdote: In 2006 the CD28 superagonist antibody TGN1412 caused a life-threatening cytokine storm in all six healthy volunteers of a first-in-human trial in London (Northwick Park), a landmark case for trial safety rules.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD80 (B7-1), a costimulatory ligand on antigen-presenting cells.
items.body_md:
CD80 molecule, alias B7-1, B7. Located on 3q13.33, near *CD86*.

Encodes CD80, expressed on activated dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, and upregulated later than CD86 after activation. Binds CD28 (activation), CTLA-4 (inhibition) and, in cis, PD-L1.

Clinical relevance: target of the CTLA4-Ig fusion proteins abatacept and belatacept, which block CD80/CD86 and thereby costimulation. Used as an activation marker of dendritic cells and of 'M1-like' macrophages in flow cytometry.

Expression is induced by TLR ligands, CD40 ligation and interferons. CD80 and CD86 together form the 'B7' costimulatory ligands, and their joint blockade is the principle of costimulation-blockade immunosuppression.

items.gloss_md: Costimulatory B7 ligand on activated antigen-presenting cells that binds CD28, CTLA-4 and PD-L1.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane IgV/IgC protein forming homodimers. It binds CTLA-4 with higher avidity than CD28, making it a preferred CTLA-4 ligand; its cis interaction with PD-L1 on the same cell blocks PD-L1–PD-1 binding and CD80–CTLA-4 binding.

Expression is low on resting antigen-presenting cells and induced by TLR ligands, CD40 signalling and interferons, typically later than CD86. Used as a maturation marker of dendritic cells.

Encoded by *CD80*. Blocked by abatacept and belatacept (via CTLA-4 extracellular domain fusion).

Structurally, CD80 and CTLA-4 homodimers can form a zipper-like lattice at the immune synapse, which contributes to the very high avidity of this inhibitory interaction.

attrs.mnemonic: B7-1 comes first by name but second in time: CD86 (B7-2) is upregulated faster than CD80 (B7-1).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD86 (B7-2), the main early costimulatory ligand on antigen-presenting cells.
items.body_md:
CD86 molecule, alias B7-2, B70. Located on 3q13.33, near *CD80*.

Encodes CD86, constitutively expressed at low levels on monocytes and dendritic cells and rapidly upregulated after activation, so it is considered the dominant ligand for initiating CD28 costimulation.

Clinical relevance: blocked together with CD80 by abatacept and belatacept; belatacept has higher affinity for CD86 than abatacept, which was the reason for its development for transplantation. Used as an activation marker of antigen-presenting cells and B cells in flow cytometry.

In research, CD86 together with CD80, CD40 and HLA-DR defines the maturation state of dendritic cells and the activation state of B cells.

items.gloss_md: Costimulatory B7 ligand on antigen-presenting cells that binds CD28 and CTLA-4 and is upregulated early after activation.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane protein with IgV and IgC domains, mostly monomeric, which favours binding to CD28 relative to CTLA-4 compared with CD80.

Present at low levels on resting monocytes and dendritic cells and rapidly induced by TLR ligands and CD40 signalling, so it delivers the first costimulatory signal to naive T cells. CTLA-4 on Tregs removes CD86 from antigen-presenting cells by trans-endocytosis.

Encoded by *CD86*. Target of belatacept (two amino-acid substitutions in the CTLA-4 part increase avidity for CD86 roughly fourfold over abatacept) and abatacept.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding LAG-3, an inhibitory checkpoint receptor related to CD4 and binding MHC class II.
items.body_md:
Lymphocyte activating 3. Alias CD223. Located on 12p13.31, close to *CD4*, with which it shares structural homology (four extracellular Ig-like domains).

Encodes LAG-3, expressed on activated and exhausted T cells, Tregs, NK cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells. Described in 1990 by Triebel and colleagues.

Clinical relevance: the third checkpoint with an approved antagonist, relatlimab, given as a fixed-dose combination with nivolumab (Opdualag) for advanced melanoma (FDA 2022). Co-expression of LAG3 with PDCD1, HAVCR2 and TIGIT is part of exhaustion signatures in scRNA-seq.

items.gloss_md: Inhibitory checkpoint receptor (CD223) on exhausted T cells and Tregs that binds MHC class II; targeted by relatlimab.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane protein with four extracellular Ig-like domains, structurally related to CD4 but binding MHC class II with higher affinity. Further ligands include FGL1 (fibrinogen-like protein 1, hepatocyte- and tumour-derived), galectin-3 and LSECtin (expressed in liver). The cytoplasmic KIEELE motif is required for its inhibitory function.

Expressed on activated and exhausted CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, Tregs and NK cells; it synergises with PD-1 in maintaining exhaustion. A soluble form is shed by ADAM10/17.

Encoded by *LAG3*. Antagonist relatlimab (with nivolumab, melanoma); eftilagimod alpha is a soluble LAG-3–Ig fusion acting as an antigen-presenting cell activator.

attrs.mnemonic: LAG-3 is a CD4 look-alike: both bind MHC class II, and their genes are neighbours on 12p13.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding TIM-3, an inhibitory receptor on exhausted T cells, Tregs and myeloid cells.
items.body_md:
Hepatitis A virus cellular receptor 2. Aliases TIM-3, TIM3, CD366. Located on 5q33.3 in the TIM gene cluster. The name comes from the family member TIM-1 (HAVCR1), identified as a hepatitis A virus receptor.

Encodes TIM-3, first described on IFN-γ-producing Th1 and CD8+ T cells; now known as a marker of terminally exhausted T cells and expressed on dendritic cells, macrophages and NK cells.

Disease relevance: germline biallelic loss-of-function variants (e.g. Y82C, I97M) cause subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma, often with haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Several anti-TIM-3 antibodies (e.g. sabatolimab, cobolimab) reached clinical trials, but none is approved so far.

items.gloss_md: Inhibitory receptor (CD366) marking terminally exhausted T cells; ligands include galectin-9, phosphatidylserine and CEACAM1.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane protein with an IgV domain and a mucin domain (T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain 3). The cytoplasmic tail lacks classic ITIMs; in the resting state BAT3 binds it, and ligand binding releases BAT3 and promotes inhibitory signalling.

Ligands: galectin-9, phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells, HMGB1 and CEACAM1. Co-expression of PD-1 and TIM-3 identifies terminally exhausted CD8+ T cells, whereas PD-1+TIM-3− TCF-1+ cells are the progenitor-exhausted cells that respond to PD-1 blockade. In dendritic cells TIM-3 regulates inflammasome activation and nucleic acid sensing.

Encoded by *HAVCR2*. Investigational target of several antibodies in combination with PD-1 blockade.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding TIGIT, an inhibitory receptor on T and NK cells that competes with DNAM-1 for CD155.
items.body_md:
T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains. Aliases VSIG9, VSTM3, WUCAM. Located on 3q13.31. Described in 2009 as a Treg/T follicular helper and NK-cell receptor.

Encodes TIGIT, expressed on Tregs, memory and exhausted T cells and NK cells. Its pathway parallels the B7–CD28 system: CD155 (PVR) and CD112 are shared with the activating receptor DNAM-1 (CD226), and TIGIT binds CD155 with higher affinity.

Clinical relevance: anti-TIGIT antibodies (tiragolumab, vibostolimab, domvanalimab) were combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in large trials; several phase 3 trials failed to show benefit, and no anti-TIGIT drug is approved so far.

attrs.full_name: T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains

items.gloss_md: Inhibitory receptor on T cells, Tregs and NK cells that binds CD155 (PVR) and counteracts the activating receptor DNAM-1.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane protein with one IgV domain and cytoplasmic ITT-like and ITIM motifs. Binds CD155 (PVR, poliovirus receptor) with high affinity and CD112 (nectin-2) more weakly, outcompeting DNAM-1 (CD226) and also disrupting DNAM-1 homodimerisation in cis.

Effects: direct inhibition of T- and NK-cell signalling, induction of IL-10 in dendritic cells via CD155, and enhanced Treg suppressive function. CD155 is overexpressed in many tumours, including PDAC and HCC.

Encoded by *TIGIT*. Investigational target (tiragolumab and others); clinical benefit has not been confirmed in phase 3 so far.

aliases: T-cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains
attrs.mnemonic: TIGIT vs DNAM-1 mirrors CTLA-4 vs CD28: an inhibitory receptor stealing the ligand of an activating twin.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD3ε, the invariant signalling chain of the T-cell receptor complex and pan-T-cell marker.
items.body_md:
CD3 epsilon subunit of T-cell receptor complex. Located on 11q23.3 together with *CD3D* and *CD3G*; CD3ζ is encoded by *CD247* on chromosome 1.

Encodes CD3ε, which pairs with CD3γ or CD3δ; together with the ζζ homodimer these chains transmit signals from the antigen-binding TCR αβ or γδ chains via ITAMs.

Disease relevance: biallelic loss-of-function mutations in CD3 genes cause severe combined immunodeficiency (T−B+NK+ SCID).

Clinical relevance: CD3 is the pan-T-cell marker in IHC and flow cytometry, and the T-cell-engaging arm of bispecific antibodies (blinatumomab: CD19×CD3; teclistamab, tebentafusp, tarlatamab and others). Anti-CD3 antibodies: muromonab-CD3 (OKT3, transplant rejection) and teplizumab (delays type 1 diabetes onset, FDA 2022).

attrs.full_name: CD3 epsilon subunit of T-cell receptor complex
attrs.anecdote: The first therapeutic monoclonal antibody, OKT3 (muromonab-CD3, approved 1986 for kidney transplant rejection), was named after Ortho Pharmaceuticals and Patrick Kung's T-cell antibody series.

items.gloss_md: Invariant signalling complex (CD3γ, δ, ε, ζ) associated with the T-cell receptor; the defining pan-T-cell marker.
items.body_md:
Each TCR (αβ or γδ) associates with CD3εγ, CD3εδ and a CD3ζζ homodimer; together they carry ten ITAMs that are phosphorylated by LCK after antigen recognition, recruiting ZAP-70 and launching TCR signalling (LAT, PLCγ1, Ca²⁺–calcineurin–NFAT, RAS–MAPK, NF-κB).

Use: CD3 identifies T cells in IHC (cytoplasmic and membranous staining), flow cytometry (CD3+ lymphocytes; CD3−CD56+ are NK cells) and multiplex imaging. NKT cells are CD3+CD56+.

Encoded by *CD3E*, *CD3D*, *CD3G* and *CD247* (ζ). Therapeutic target: anti-CD3 mAbs (muromonab, teplizumab) and the CD3 arm of T-cell-engaging bispecifics, whose typical toxicity is cytokine release syndrome.

attrs.anecdote: Muromonab-CD3 (OKT3), approved in 1986 to treat acute kidney transplant rejection, was the first monoclonal antibody approved for human therapy.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD4, the MHC class II co-receptor defining helper T cells and the main HIV receptor.
items.body_md:
CD4 molecule, located on 12p13.31 (near *LAG3*).

Encodes CD4, a co-receptor that binds the β2 domain of MHC class II and brings the kinase LCK to the TCR complex. Expressed on helper T cells (Th1, Th2, Th17, Tfh) and Tregs, at low levels on monocytes, macrophages and some dendritic cells.

Disease relevance: CD4 is the primary receptor for HIV gp120 (with CCR5 or CXCR4 as co-receptor); the CD4+ T-cell count stages HIV infection and guides prophylaxis. During thymic development, double-positive (CD4+CD8+) thymocytes become CD4 or CD8 single positive depending on MHC class II or I recognition.

Clinical relevance: CD4/CD8 ratio is a routine immune-monitoring parameter (normal ~1–2.5, inverted in HIV, CMV and ageing); IHC marker for T-cell lymphoma classification.

attrs.anecdote: In 1984 the groups of Robin Weiss/Angus Dalgleish and Luc Montagnier/David Klatzmann showed independently that HIV uses CD4 to enter cells – explaining the loss of CD4+ T cells in AIDS.

items.gloss_md: Co-receptor on helper T cells that binds MHC class II and recruits LCK; also the receptor for HIV.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane glycoprotein with four extracellular Ig-like domains (D1–D4); D1 binds the β2 domain of MHC class II and HIV gp120. The cytoplasmic tail binds LCK via a zinc clasp, delivering the kinase to the TCR–CD3 complex.

Marks helper T cells and Tregs (CD4+CD25highCD127low FOXP3+); low expression on monocytes/macrophages. Normal adult blood CD4+ count is roughly 500–1500 cells/µL; below 200/µL defines AIDS.

Encoded by *CD4*. Used in flow cytometry and IHC; the CD4/CD8 ratio is a standard immune-monitoring parameter, also after transplantation and in chronic infections.

attrs.mnemonic: Rule of eight: CD4 × MHC II = 8 and CD8 × MHC I = 8. CD4 helpers see class II, CD8 killers see class I.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the CD8α chain, the MHC class I co-receptor of cytotoxic T cells.
items.body_md:
CD8 subunit alpha, located on 2p11.2 next to *CD8B*.

Encodes CD8α, which forms CD8αβ heterodimers on conventional cytotoxic T cells and CD8αα homodimers on NK cells, some γδ T cells, intraepithelial lymphocytes and some dendritic-cell subsets (in mice).

Function: CD8 binds the α3 domain of MHC class I and recruits LCK, increasing TCR sensitivity of cytotoxic T cells, which kill infected or malignant cells with perforin and granzymes.

Clinical relevance: CD8+ tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte density is prognostic in many cancers (e.g. Immunoscore in colorectal cancer). CD8A expression is the standard marker for cytotoxic T cells in scRNA-seq and deconvolution. Rare CD8A loss-of-function causes CD8 deficiency.

attrs.mnemonic: Rule of eight: CD8 × MHC class I = 8, CD4 × MHC class II = 8.

items.gloss_md: Co-receptor on cytotoxic T cells that binds MHC class I; marks the killer T-cell population.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane dimer (CD8αβ on conventional cytotoxic T cells, CD8αα on NK cells, some γδ and intraepithelial T cells). Each chain has an IgV-like domain and a long stalk; the α chain carries the LCK-binding motif.

CD8 binds a conserved site on the α3 domain of MHC class I, stabilising TCR–peptide–MHC interaction and bringing LCK to CD3. CD8+ T cells differentiate into effector, memory (central, effector, tissue-resident) and, under chronic stimulation, exhausted states (PD-1, TIM-3, TOX).

Encoded by *CD8A* and *CD8B*. Used in IHC, flow cytometry and multiplex imaging to quantify cytotoxic infiltrates; in transplant biopsies CD8+ cells participate in T-cell-mediated rejection.

attrs.mnemonic: Rule of eight: CD8 × MHC class I = 8 – CD8 killers inspect class I, which every nucleated cell displays.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD45, the leukocyte common antigen tyrosine phosphatase present on all nucleated haematopoietic cells.
items.body_md:
Protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type C. Aliases CD45, LCA (leukocyte common antigen), T200. Located on 1q31.3.

Encodes CD45, whose isoforms arise by alternative splicing of exons 4, 5 and 6 (A, B, C): CD45RA (contains exon A) on naive T cells and CD45RO (no variable exons) on memory and activated T cells; B cells express CD45RB/B220.

Function: dephosphorylates the inhibitory C-terminal tyrosine of LCK and FYN, which is required for TCR and BCR signalling.

Disease relevance: CD45 deficiency causes SCID. Clinically CD45 is used to confirm haematopoietic origin of an undifferentiated tumour (IHC), to gate leukocytes in flow cytometry (CD45 vs side scatter), and in scRNA-seq to split immune (PTPRC+) from epithelial, stromal and endothelial cells.

attrs.full_name: protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type C
attrs.mnemonic: CD45 = leukocyte common antigen: every white blood cell wears it, so in scRNA-seq 'PTPRC+' simply means 'immune cell'.

items.gloss_md: Receptor tyrosine phosphatase on all leukocytes (leukocyte common antigen) that activates Src-family kinases in TCR/BCR signalling.
items.body_md:
Large type I transmembrane protein with a heavily glycosylated, alternatively spliced extracellular domain and two cytoplasmic phosphatase domains (D1 active, D2 regulatory). It makes up a large fraction of the leukocyte surface.

Isoforms: CD45RA (naive T cells, also terminally differentiated TEMRA cells), CD45RO (memory/activated T cells), CD45RB, CD45R0 being the shortest. Naive T cells are typically CD45RA+CCR7+, central memory CD45RO+CCR7+, effector memory CD45RO+CCR7−.

Encoded by *PTPRC*. Clinical use: IHC 'leukocyte common antigen' to classify undifferentiated tumours (lymphoma vs carcinoma vs melanoma), flow-cytometric leukocyte gating, and CD34/CD45 stem-cell enumeration (ISHAGE protocol).

attrs.mnemonic: RA = 'Really Arrived' (naive, fresh), RO = 'Remembers Old' (memory).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding FOXP3, the master transcription factor of regulatory T cells.
items.body_md:
Forkhead box P3. Alias scurfin, JM2, IPEX. Located on Xp11.23.

Encodes FOXP3, a forkhead/winged-helix transcription factor required for development and suppressive function of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells. Stable thymic Treg identity depends on demethylation of the conserved non-coding region CNS2, the Treg-specific demethylated region (TSDR); TSDR methylation analysis is used to count Tregs from DNA.

Discovery: the gene defect of the scurfy mouse and of the human IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked) was identified in 2001; in 2003 three groups (Hori/Sakaguchi, Fontenot/Rudensky, Khattri/Ramsdell) showed that it programs Treg development.

Clinical relevance: Treg marker in IHC and flow cytometry; high FOXP3+ Treg infiltration is generally an adverse prognostic factor in solid tumours. Note: activated human conventional T cells transiently express FOXP3 too.

attrs.anecdote: The scurfy mouse, a spontaneous X-linked mutant from Oak Ridge National Laboratory with scaly skin and fatal autoimmunity, carries a Foxp3 frameshift; the same gene is mutated in boys with IPEX syndrome.

items.gloss_md: Forkhead transcription factor that defines regulatory T cells and programs their suppressive function.
items.body_md:
Nuclear transcription factor with an N-terminal repressor domain, zinc finger and leucine zipper (for homo-/heterodimerisation) and a C-terminal forkhead DNA-binding domain. It acts in large complexes with partners such as NFAT, RUNX1, EOS and AML1.

FOXP3 represses IL-2 and effector cytokine genes and induces CD25, CTLA-4 and GITR, making Tregs dependent on exogenous IL-2 and able to suppress via IL-2 consumption, CTLA-4-mediated depletion of CD80/CD86, IL-10, TGF-β and adenosine (CD39/CD73).

Encoded by *FOXP3*. Marker: nuclear IHC staining; flow phenotype CD4+CD25highCD127low FOXP3+. Treg expansion and adoptive Treg therapy are studied to induce transplant tolerance; reduced Treg number or function underlies several autoimmune diseases.

attrs.mnemonic: FOXP3 = 'Fox Protects': the fox guards the hen house from self-attack.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD25, the α chain of the high-affinity IL-2 receptor, a Treg and T-cell activation marker.
items.body_md:
Interleukin 2 receptor subunit alpha. Aliases CD25, TAC antigen, IL2R. Located on 10p15.1.

Encodes CD25, which with IL-2Rβ (CD122, *IL2RB*) and the common γ chain (CD132, *IL2RG*) forms the high-affinity IL-2 receptor. CD25 is constitutively high on Tregs and induced on activated T cells.

Disease relevance: biallelic loss causes an IPEX-like immune dysregulation; common variants are associated with type 1 diabetes and multiple sclerosis.

Clinical relevance: target of basiliximab (Simulect), an anti-CD25 monoclonal antibody used for induction immunosuppression in kidney transplantation. Soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R, sCD25) in serum is a marker of T-cell activation, used in sarcoidosis and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH-2004 criterion ≥2400 U/mL).

attrs.mnemonic: Treg phenotype: CD4+ CD25high CD127low FOXP3+ – Tregs crave IL-2 (CD25) but ignore IL-7 (CD127).

items.gloss_md: α chain of the high-affinity IL-2 receptor; high on regulatory T cells and on activated T cells, target of basiliximab.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane protein with two sushi domains and a short cytoplasmic tail without signalling capacity. It raises IL-2 affinity about 100-fold when combined with IL-2Rβ and γc, which signal through JAK1/JAK3–STAT5.

Expression: constitutive and high on FOXP3+ Tregs (CD25high), induced on conventional T cells after activation, also on activated B cells, some NK cells and malignant cells (adult T-cell leukaemia, hairy cell leukaemia). Shed by proteases to give soluble IL-2R.

Encoded by *IL2RA*. Drugs: basiliximab (induction therapy in kidney transplantation, reducing early acute rejection); daclizumab was withdrawn. Low-dose IL-2 therapy exploits the high CD25 density on Tregs to expand them selectively.

attrs.mnemonic: Basili-XI-mab: the -xi- marks a chimeric antibody; it blocks CD25 so effector T cells cannot hear IL-2.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding ICOS, an inducible CD28-family costimulator essential for T follicular helper cells.
items.body_md:
Inducible T cell costimulator. Alias CD278, AILIM. Located on 2q33.2 in the CD28–CTLA4–ICOS cluster.

Encodes ICOS, expressed on activated T cells, T follicular helper (Tfh) cells and effector Tregs; its ligand is ICOS-L (B7-H2, *ICOSLG*) on B cells, dendritic cells and some non-haematopoietic cells.

Disease relevance: biallelic ICOS deficiency causes a form of common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) with defective germinal centres and hypogammaglobulinaemia. ICOS+ cells expand after anti-CTLA-4 therapy, making ICOS a pharmacodynamic marker of ipilimumab activity.

ICOS+ effector Tregs are enriched in many tumours, and ICOS-L is also expressed on endothelial and epithelial cells, extending the pathway beyond professional antigen-presenting cells.

items.gloss_md: Inducible costimulatory receptor (CD278) on activated T cells and Tfh cells that binds ICOS-L and supports germinal-centre B-cell help.
items.body_md:
Disulfide-linked homodimeric CD28-family receptor with a FDPPPF motif (instead of MYPPPY), so it binds ICOS-L but not CD80/CD86. Its cytoplasmic YMFM motif recruits PI3K strongly, promoting AKT signalling, IL-4, IL-10 and IL-21 production.

Absent on naive T cells and induced within 24–48 h of activation; constitutively high on Tfh cells (CXCR5+PD-1+ICOS+BCL6+), where it drives germinal-centre formation and class-switched antibody production.

Encoded by *ICOS*. Agonist and antagonist antibodies have been tested in oncology and autoimmunity without approval so far. In transplantation, Tfh activity contributes to donor-specific antibody formation.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding granzyme B, the main pro-apoptotic serine protease of cytotoxic T and NK cells.
items.body_md:
Granzyme B, located on 14q12 in a cluster with *GZMH* and *CTSG*. Aliases CTLA1, CSPB.

Encodes granzyme B, stored in cytotoxic granules of CD8+ T cells and NK cells and also produced by plasmacytoid dendritic cells, some B cells, Tregs and mast cells.

Clinical relevance: GZMB, together with PRF1, GNLY and NKG7, is a core gene of cytotoxicity signatures in bulk and single-cell transcriptomics; granzyme B IHC identifies cytotoxic lymphocytes and cytotoxic lymphomas (e.g. extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma). In kidney transplant molecular diagnostics, cytotoxic transcripts are part of rejection-associated transcript sets. Granzyme B ELISpot measures antigen-specific cytotoxic responses.

items.gloss_md: Serine protease released by cytotoxic T and NK cells that enters target cells through perforin pores and triggers apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Chymotrypsin-fold serine protease with a rare preference for cleaving after aspartate residues, like caspases. Stored as active enzyme bound to serglycin in acidic cytotoxic granules; activated from its zymogen by cathepsin C (dipeptidyl peptidase I).

After granule exocytosis at the immune synapse, perforin lets granzyme B enter the target cytosol, where it cleaves BID (activating the mitochondrial pathway) and directly cleaves caspase-3 and caspase-7, killing within minutes. Serpin B9 (PI-9) is its endogenous inhibitor.

Encoded by *GZMB*. Used as an IHC and flow marker of cytotoxic activity; granzyme B PET tracers are explored to image response to immunotherapy.

attrs.mnemonic: Perforin punches the hole, granzyme B goes through it and 'B'uries the cell by cleaving after aspartate, like a caspase.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding perforin, the pore-forming protein of cytotoxic granules.
items.body_md:
Perforin 1, located on 10q22.1.

Encodes perforin, expressed by cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, NK cells and some γδ T cells, and indispensable for granule-mediated killing.

Disease relevance: biallelic loss-of-function mutations cause familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis type 2 (FHL2), a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome of infancy in which cytotoxic cells fail to clear activated antigen-presenting cells, leading to an IFN-γ-driven cytokine storm; treated with immunochemotherapy and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Hypomorphic variants (e.g. A91V) are associated with later-onset disease.

Perforin expression is part of cytotoxicity gene signatures (with GZMB, GNLY, NKG7).

items.gloss_md: Pore-forming protein of cytotoxic granules that allows granzymes to enter target cells.
items.body_md:
Calcium-dependent pore-forming protein of the MACPF/CDC superfamily, structurally related to the complement membrane-attack complex component C9. It has a MACPF domain that unfolds into transmembrane β-hairpins and a C2 domain that binds the target membrane in a Ca²⁺-dependent way.

Stored in acidic granules where low pH and calcium keep it inactive; after release into the synapse it oligomerises into pores of about 20 subunits, through which granzymes enter (or which trigger endocytic uptake).

Encoded by *PRF1*. Reduced perforin expression on NK cells by flow cytometry is a rapid screening test for FHL2.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD19, the pan-B-cell co-receptor and target of CAR T cells and blinatumomab.
items.body_md:
CD19 molecule, located on 16p11.2.

Encodes CD19, expressed from the pro-B-cell stage through mature and memory B cells to plasmablasts, but lost on most long-lived plasma cells; it is absent on other lineages, which makes it an ideal immunotherapy target.

Function: part of the B-cell co-receptor complex with CD21 (complement receptor 2) and CD81, lowering the BCR activation threshold for complement-coated (C3d) antigen.

Disease relevance: biallelic CD19 loss causes a CVID-like antibody deficiency. Clinical relevance: target of CD19 CAR T cells (tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, brexucabtagene), the bispecific blinatumomab (CD19×CD3), tafasitamab and loncastuximab tesirine; CD19-negative relapse is a known escape mechanism. Flow-cytometric pan-B-cell marker.

attrs.anecdote: The CD19 CAR T-cell product tisagenlecleucel (2017) was the first gene therapy approved by the FDA.

items.gloss_md: Pan-B-cell co-receptor that amplifies BCR signalling; the main target of CAR T-cell therapy in B-cell malignancies.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane glycoprotein of the Ig superfamily with two extracellular C2-type Ig domains and a long cytoplasmic tail whose phosphorylated tyrosines recruit LYN, VAV and PI3K.

Forms a complex with CD21 (CR2, binds C3d on opsonised antigen), CD81 (needed for CD19 surface transport) and CD225; co-ligation with the BCR lowers the antigen threshold for B-cell activation by orders of magnitude.

Encoded by *CD19*. Used as pan-B marker in flow cytometry (B-cell aplasia monitoring after CAR T or rituximab therapy), and targeted by CAR T cells, blinatumomab and antibody–drug conjugates; CD19 CAR T cells are also being tested in refractory autoimmune diseases such as lupus.

attrs.anecdote: Emily Whitehead, a 6-year-old with relapsed ALL, was the first child to receive CD19 CAR T cells (Philadelphia, 2012); she survived a severe cytokine storm that was controlled with tocilizumab and stayed in remission.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD20, the B-cell surface protein targeted by rituximab.
items.body_md:
Membrane spanning 4-domains A1. Aliases CD20, B1, Bp35. Located on 11q12.2 in the MS4A cluster.

Encodes CD20, expressed from the late pre-B stage to memory B cells but not on pro-B cells or plasma cells; therefore anti-CD20 therapy depletes B cells without abolishing existing antibody production from long-lived plasma cells.

Clinical relevance: CD20 IHC is the standard B-cell marker in pathology (B-cell lymphoma diagnosis, B cells in rejection infiltrates and tertiary lymphoid structures). Anti-CD20 antibodies: rituximab, obinutuzumab, ofatumumab, ocrelizumab, ublituximab; bispecifics mosunetuzumab, glofitamab, epcoritamab. In transplantation rituximab is used in ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation, desensitisation, treatment of antibody-mediated rejection and EBV-associated post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD).

attrs.mnemonic: MS4A1 = 'membrane-spanning 4-domains': CD20 crosses the membrane four times and is never shed – the perfect antibody target.

items.gloss_md: Tetraspanning B-cell surface protein from pre-B to memory B cells; the target of rituximab and other anti-CD20 antibodies.
items.body_md:
Non-glycosylated protein that crosses the membrane four times, with small extracellular loops (the large loop carries the rituximab epitope); it forms dimers or tetramers and is thought to participate in store-operated calcium influx after BCR activation. It has no known ligand and is not shed or rapidly internalised, which makes it an excellent antibody target.

Mechanisms of anti-CD20 antibodies: complement-dependent cytotoxicity, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity via CD16 on NK cells, phagocytosis and direct apoptosis (type I vs type II antibodies).

Encoded by *MS4A1*. Clinical use: lymphoma (R-CHOP), CLL, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis, multiple sclerosis, membranous nephropathy, PTLD and transplant desensitisation.

attrs.mnemonic: CD20 sits on B cells from 'pre' to 'memory' but leaves before the Plasma cell – so rituximab spares existing antibodies.
attrs.anecdote: Rituximab, approved by the FDA in 1997 for follicular lymphoma, was the first monoclonal antibody approved to treat cancer.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD14, the LPS co-receptor that marks classical monocytes.
items.body_md:
CD14 molecule, located on 5q31.3.

Encodes CD14, a GPI-anchored pattern-recognition co-receptor expressed strongly by monocytes and, more weakly, by macrophages and neutrophils; hepatocytes produce soluble CD14 as an acute-phase protein.

Function: together with LPS-binding protein (LBP) it transfers lipopolysaccharide to the TLR4–MD-2 complex and enables TLR4 endocytosis and TRIF signalling.

Clinical relevance: CD14 and CD16 define human monocyte subsets (classical CD14++CD16−, about 85 %; intermediate CD14++CD16+; non-classical CD14+CD16++). Soluble CD14 (sCD14) and LBP are markers of bacterial translocation and monocyte activation, studied in cirrhosis and HIV. CD14 is a standard monocyte marker in scRNA-seq.

items.gloss_md: GPI-anchored LPS co-receptor on monocytes and macrophages that hands LPS to TLR4; the classical monocyte marker.
items.body_md:
Horseshoe-shaped leucine-rich-repeat protein anchored by glycosylphosphatidylinositol (no cytoplasmic tail), also present in soluble form (shed or secreted, including from hepatocytes).

Binds LPS monomers delivered by LBP and transfers them to MD-2/TLR4; it also helps recognise peptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acid and apoptotic cells and is required for LPS-induced TLR4 internalisation and the TRIF–IRF3 interferon response.

Encoded by *CD14*. In flow cytometry, CD14 versus CD16 separates monocyte subsets; CD14 loss is used in PNH testing (GPI-anchor deficiency, with FLAER). Elevated sCD14 indicates monocyte activation in cirrhosis, sepsis and chronic infection.

attrs.mnemonic: Monocytes: 'fourteen comes before sixteen' – classical monocytes are CD14 bright, non-classical ones swap to CD16 bright.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD16a (FcγRIIIa), the low-affinity IgG receptor mediating ADCC by NK cells.
items.body_md:
Fc gamma receptor IIIa. Aliases CD16, CD16a, FCGR3. Located on 1q23.3 in the Fcγ receptor cluster, next to *FCGR3B* (CD16b, the GPI-anchored neutrophil form).

Encodes CD16a, a transmembrane receptor associated with FcRγ or CD3ζ chains, expressed on CD56dim NK cells, non-classical and intermediate monocytes, macrophages and some γδ T cells.

Polymorphism: the common F158V variant (rs396991); the V158 allele binds IgG1 with higher affinity, and some studies linked it to better rituximab or trastuzumab response, although results are inconsistent.

Clinical relevance: NK-cell CD16 mediates antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity of therapeutic antibodies; Fc-engineered antibodies (e.g. afucosylated obinutuzumab) increase CD16a binding. In kidney transplant biopsies, NK-cell transcripts including FCGR3A are part of the molecular signature of antibody-mediated rejection.

attrs.role: IgG Fc receptor / NK and monocyte marker

items.gloss_md: Low-affinity IgG Fc receptor on NK cells, monocytes and neutrophils that triggers antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
items.body_md:
Two isoforms: CD16a (FcγRIIIa, from *FCGR3A*) is transmembrane and signals through ITAM-bearing FcRγ or CD3ζ chains; CD16b (FcγRIIIb, from *FCGR3B*) is GPI-anchored on neutrophils and has no signalling chain. Both bind IgG1 and IgG3 immune complexes rather than monomeric IgG.

On CD56dim NK cells CD16a ligation is sufficient to trigger killing (ADCC) and IFN-γ release; it is shed by ADAM17 after activation. CD16 defines non-classical (CD14+CD16++) monocytes.

Clinical relevance: mediator of the cytotoxicity of rituximab, trastuzumab and other IgG1 antibodies; in antibody-mediated transplant rejection donor-specific antibodies engage CD16 on NK cells and monocytes in the microcirculation (microvascular inflammation).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD56 (neural cell adhesion molecule), the defining marker of NK cells and of neuroendocrine tumours.
items.body_md:
Neural cell adhesion molecule 1. Aliases CD56, NCAM. Located on 11q23.2.

Encodes NCAM, a homophilic adhesion molecule of the Ig superfamily with major isoforms NCAM-120 (GPI-anchored), NCAM-140 and NCAM-180 (transmembrane); polysialylated NCAM (PSA-NCAM) regulates neural plasticity.

Clinical relevance: in immunology, NK cells are CD3−CD56+ and split into CD56bright (cytokine-producing, lymph-node-enriched, about 10 % in blood; also enriched among liver-resident NK cells) and CD56dim CD16+ (cytotoxic, about 90 %). In pathology, CD56 is a neuroendocrine marker (with synaptophysin, chromogranin A, INSM1), stains NK/T-cell lymphomas, myeloma plasma cells (aberrant expression) and reactive cholangiocytes / ductular reaction in liver disease.

items.gloss_md: Neural cell adhesion molecule used as the defining marker of NK cells and as a neuroendocrine IHC marker.
items.body_md:
Homophilic adhesion glycoprotein with five Ig domains and two fibronectin type III repeats; the polysialic acid modification (PSA-NCAM) reduces adhesion and is prominent in developing neurons.

Immunology: NK cells are defined as CD3−CD56+; CD56bright CD16− NK cells secrete IFN-γ, TNF and GM-CSF, whereas CD56dim CD16+ NK cells are cytotoxic. CD56 is also found on NKT cells, some γδ and CD8+ T cells and activated monocytes.

Encoded by *NCAM1*. Pathology use: neuroendocrine neoplasms (including pancreatic NETs), small-cell carcinoma, NK/T-cell lymphoma, aberrant myeloma plasma cells; in the liver it highlights immature ductular reaction cells. Target of the antibody–drug conjugate lorvotuzumab mertansine (investigational).

attrs.mnemonic: NK cells: 'CD3 minus, 56 plus' – no T-cell receptor, but the nerve-cell glue.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD68, a lysosomal glycoprotein used as the pan-macrophage marker.
items.body_md:
CD68 molecule, alias macrosialin (mouse homologue), gp110, LAMP4, SCARD1. Located on 17p13.1.

Encodes CD68, a heavily glycosylated type I membrane protein of the LAMP family located mainly in late endosomes and lysosomes of monocytes, macrophages (including Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages, microglia and osteoclasts) and to a lesser extent dendritic cells, neutrophils, fibroblasts and some tumour cells.

Clinical relevance: CD68 IHC (clones KP1 and PG-M1) is the classic pan-macrophage marker for tumour-associated macrophage density, Kupffer cell assessment, and macrophage-rich lesions. CD68 is not fully specific, so combinations (CD68+CD163+, CD68+CD206+) are used to approximate polarisation. In scRNA-seq CD68 is a standard macrophage/monocyte marker together with CD14, LYZ, C1QA and CD163.

attrs.mnemonic: Macrophage pair: CD68 marks all macrophages (lysosomes), CD163 the calm, M2-like and resident ones (haem scavenger).

items.gloss_md: Lysosome-associated glycoprotein used in IHC as a pan-macrophage marker.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane glycoprotein with a mucin-like domain and a LAMP-like domain; about 80 % of the protein is in endosomal/lysosomal membranes, a minor fraction cycles to the cell surface. It can bind oxidised LDL and is upregulated by inflammatory stimuli.

Expression: monocytes and macrophages in all tissues (Kupffer cells in the liver), osteoclasts, microglia; weaker in dendritic cells, neutrophils and some non-myeloid cells.

Encoded by *CD68*. Main use is as an IHC and multiplex-imaging marker of macrophage infiltration, e.g. tumour-associated macrophages in PDAC, macrophage infiltration in transplant biopsies, and hepatic macrophage expansion in MASH and alcohol-related liver disease.

attrs.mnemonic: Macrophage pair: CD68 = all macrophages, CD163 = M2-like and resident macrophages; Kupffer cells are positive for both.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD163, the haemoglobin–haptoglobin scavenger receptor of 'M2-like' and resident macrophages.
items.body_md:
CD163 molecule, alias M130, haemoglobin scavenger receptor. Located on 12p13.31.

Encodes CD163, a scavenger receptor cysteine-rich (SRCR) family member restricted to monocytes and macrophages. Expression is induced by glucocorticoids and IL-10 and reduced by pro-inflammatory stimuli, so it marks alternatively activated / anti-inflammatory and tissue-resident macrophages, including Kupffer cells.

Clinical relevance: CD163 IHC identifies 'M2-like' tumour-associated macrophages (adverse prognosis in many tumours, including PDAC). Soluble CD163 (sCD163, shed by ADAM17) reflects macrophage activation; in cirrhosis it rises with portal hypertension and predicts decompensation and mortality, and it is elevated in macrophage activation syndrome.

items.gloss_md: Macrophage scavenger receptor for haemoglobin–haptoglobin complexes; marker of anti-inflammatory and resident macrophages and, as sCD163, of macrophage activation.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane protein with nine SRCR domains. Binds haemoglobin–haptoglobin complexes and internalises them; the released haem is degraded by haem oxygenase-1 into biliverdin, CO and iron, an anti-inflammatory process. CD163 also binds bacteria and TWEAK.

Expression is upregulated by IL-10, IL-6 and glucocorticoids and downregulated by LPS, IFN-γ and TNF. Upon TLR activation it is cleaved by ADAM17, releasing soluble CD163.

Encoded by *CD163*. Clinical use: IHC marker of 'M2-like' macrophages and Kupffer cells; serum sCD163 as a Kupffer-cell/macrophage activation marker in cirrhosis, acute-on-chronic liver failure, MASLD and macrophage activation syndrome.

attrs.mnemonic: CD163 cleans up haem – it is the 'garbage collector' receptor of calm (M2-like) macrophages.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD11c (integrin αX), the classical dendritic-cell marker.
items.body_md:
Integrin subunit alpha X. Aliases CD11c, p150,95. Located on 16p11.2 near *ITGAM* (CD11b) and *ITGAL* (CD11a).

Encodes CD11c, which pairs with the β2 integrin CD18 (*ITGB2*) to form complement receptor 4 (CR4), binding iC3b, fibrinogen and ICAM-1.

Expressed at high levels on conventional dendritic cells, and also on alveolar and some tissue macrophages, monocytes, activated T and NK cells, and on age-associated / atypical memory B cells (CD11c+ T-bet+), which expand in autoimmunity and chronic infection.

Clinical relevance: CD11c is used to identify dendritic cells (HLA-DR+ lineage− CD11c+) and is strongly positive in hairy cell leukaemia. Itgax-Cre and CD11c-DTR mice are standard tools to target or deplete dendritic cells.

items.gloss_md: β2-integrin α chain (complement receptor 4) used as the classical dendritic-cell marker.
items.body_md:
Integrin α subunit with an I (inserted) domain that binds ligands; it pairs with CD18 (β2) to form αXβ2 (CR4), which binds iC3b-opsonised particles, fibrinogen, ICAM-1 and denatured proteins and supports adhesion and phagocytosis.

Expression: conventional dendritic cells (cDC1 and cDC2), alveolar macrophages, monocyte-derived cells, some activated CD8+ T and NK cells, age-associated B cells; plasmacytoid dendritic cells are CD11c low.

Encoded by *ITGAX*. Used in flow cytometry and multiplex imaging to identify dendritic cells (CD11c+ HLA-DR+); hairy cell leukaemia is CD11c+, CD25+, CD103+, CD123+. β2-integrin deficiency (*ITGB2*) causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding interleukin-2, the T-cell growth factor whose transcription is blocked by calcineurin inhibitors.
items.body_md:
Interleukin 2, alias TCGF (T-cell growth factor). Located on 4q27 next to *IL21*.

Encodes IL-2, produced mainly by activated CD4+ T cells (also CD8+ T cells, NK cells and dendritic cells). Transcription requires NFAT (activated by calcineurin), AP-1 and NF-κB, which is why tacrolimus and ciclosporin act largely by preventing IL-2 production.

Discovery: described in 1976 (Morgan, Ruscetti, Gallo) as a factor in conditioned medium that let T cells grow in culture; cloned in 1983 (Taniguchi).

Clinical relevance: high-dose recombinant IL-2 (aldesleukin) was approved for metastatic renal cell carcinoma and melanoma with durable responses in a minority but severe capillary leak; low-dose IL-2 expands Tregs and is tested in autoimmunity and transplant tolerance. IL-2 is also used to expand tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes for TIL therapy.

attrs.anecdote: Before 1976 T cells could not be kept growing in culture; 'T-cell growth factor' (IL-2) changed that and soon enabled the isolation of the first human retrovirus, HTLV-1, from cultured T cells.

items.gloss_md: T-cell growth factor that drives clonal expansion of activated T cells and is indispensable for regulatory T cells.
items.body_md:
Four-α-helix-bundle cytokine (15 kDa). Receptors: intermediate-affinity IL-2Rβγc (CD122/CD132, on NK and memory CD8+ T cells) and high-affinity IL-2Rαβγc (with CD25, on Tregs and activated T cells). Signals via JAK1/JAK3 to STAT5, PI3K–AKT–mTOR and MAPK.

Effects: proliferation and effector differentiation of T cells, NK-cell activation, activation-induced cell death, and above all Treg maintenance – IL-2- or CD25-deficient mice and humans develop autoimmunity rather than immunodeficiency.

Encoded by *IL2*. Its production is inhibited by calcineurin inhibitors (via NFAT), and its signalling by basiliximab (anti-CD25), JAK inhibitors and mTOR inhibitors (downstream proliferation). Aldesleukin (high-dose) for cancer; engineered IL-2 variants and low-dose IL-2 for Treg expansion are under investigation.

attrs.mnemonic: Transplant drug chain: tacrolimus blocks IL-2 production, basiliximab blocks its receptor CD25, sirolimus blocks the signal downstream (mTOR) – 'make it, hear it, use it'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding interleukin-6, the master inducer of the hepatic acute-phase response.
items.body_md:
Interleukin 6. Previous names BSF-2 (B-cell stimulatory factor 2), IFN-β2, hepatocyte-stimulating factor (HSF), plasmacytoma growth factor. Located on 7p15.3.

Encodes IL-6, produced by monocytes/macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, adipocytes, muscle (as a myokine during exercise) and many tumours. Expression is induced by IL-1, TNF and TLR signalling through NF-κB.

Discovery: cloned in 1986 by Kishimoto, Hirano and colleagues as BSF-2; it then turned out to be identical to several factors described in different fields.

Clinical relevance: serum IL-6 is a sepsis and CRS biomarker; tocilizumab and sarilumab (anti-IL-6R) treat rheumatoid arthritis, giant-cell arteritis, CAR-T cytokine release syndrome and severe COVID-19; siltuximab (anti-IL-6) treats idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease. In the liver IL-6 primes hepatocyte proliferation after partial hepatectomy; in PDAC it contributes to cachexia and immunosuppression.

attrs.anecdote: IL-6 was discovered several times under different names (B-cell stimulatory factor 2, interferon-β2, hepatocyte-stimulating factor, plasmacytoma growth factor) before cloning showed that all were one molecule.

items.gloss_md: Pleiotropic pro-inflammatory cytokine signalling via IL-6R/gp130–JAK–STAT3 that drives fever, the acute-phase response (CRP) and B-cell differentiation.
items.body_md:
Four-helix-bundle cytokine (about 21–28 kDa depending on glycosylation). Classic signalling: IL-6 binds membrane IL-6R (CD126; on hepatocytes, some leukocytes) which recruits gp130 (CD130), activating JAK1/JAK2/TYK2 → STAT3 (and STAT1, SHP2–MAPK). Trans-signalling: IL-6 bound to soluble IL-6R activates gp130 on any cell; this is considered the more pro-inflammatory branch. SOCS3 provides negative feedback.

Effects: hepatic acute-phase proteins (CRP, serum amyloid A, fibrinogen, hepcidin – hence anaemia of inflammation) with reduced albumin and transferrin; fever; Th17 differentiation with TGF-β; plasma-cell differentiation; thrombopoiesis.

Encoded by *IL6*. Blocked by tocilizumab, sarilumab (receptor) and siltuximab (ligand); during IL-6R blockade CRP can stay low despite infection, an important clinical pitfall.

attrs.mnemonic: IL-6 is the liver's alarm: CRP up, albumin down – CRP is basically an IL-6 bioassay.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding tumour necrosis factor, a central pro-inflammatory cytokine located in the MHC class III region.
items.body_md:
Tumor necrosis factor. Previous names TNFA, TNF-α, cachectin. Located on 6p21.33 in the MHC class III region, next to *LTA* and *LTB*.

Encodes TNF, produced mainly by macrophages, monocytes, T cells and NK cells, as a transmembrane trimer that is cleaved by ADAM17 (TACE) to release soluble TNF.

Discovery: described in 1975 (Carswell, Old and colleagues) as a serum factor of endotoxin-treated, BCG-primed mice that caused haemorrhagic necrosis of transplanted tumours; independently identified as cachectin, a mediator of wasting, and shown to be the same protein in 1985.

Clinical relevance: anti-TNF agents (infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab pegol, etanercept) transformed treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis and spondyloarthritis; screening for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B is mandatory before treatment. Anti-TNF therapy was harmful in trials of severe alcohol-related hepatitis. Promoter polymorphisms (e.g. −308G>A) were widely studied with inconsistent results.

attrs.anecdote: Its story begins with William Coley's 1890s 'Coley's toxins': bacterial extracts that sometimes shrank sarcomas; in 1975 the serum factor induced by such bacterial products was named tumour necrosis factor.

items.gloss_md: Prototypical pro-inflammatory cytokine of macrophages and T cells that activates NF-κB and can trigger cell death; target of anti-TNF biologics.
items.body_md:
Homotrimer, made as a 26 kDa transmembrane precursor and released as a 17 kDa soluble form by ADAM17. Receptors: TNFR1 (TNFRSF1A, ubiquitous, has a death domain) and TNFR2 (TNFRSF1B, mainly immune and endothelial cells, best activated by membrane TNF).

TNFR1 signalling forms complex I (TRADD, TRAF2, RIPK1, cIAP, LUBAC) → NF-κB and MAPK activation (survival, inflammation); if NF-κB is blocked, complex II triggers caspase-8 apoptosis or RIPK3–MLKL necroptosis.

Effects: endothelial activation, fever, cachexia, insulin resistance, granuloma maintenance (hence TB reactivation under blockade), hepatocyte apoptosis in fulminant hepatitis models. Elevated in alcohol-related hepatitis and MASH.

Encoded by *TNF*. Biologics: infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab, certolizumab pegol (antibodies) and etanercept (TNFR2–Fc fusion).

attrs.mnemonic: Anti-TNF drugs end in -mab (antibodies) except etaner-CEPT – the receptor fusion; before any of them: screen for TB and HBV.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding interferon-γ, the type II interferon that activates macrophages and induces MHC and PD-L1.
items.body_md:
Interferon gamma, alias IFG, IFI, type II interferon. Located on 12q15.

Encodes IFN-γ, produced by Th1 cells, CD8+ T cells, NK cells, NKT cells and ILC1s, induced by IL-12 and IL-18 and by TCR signalling (T-bet, STAT4).

Disease relevance: inborn errors in IFN-γ immunity (*IFNGR1*, *IFNGR2*, *IL12RB1*, *STAT1*) cause Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD).

Clinical relevance: interferon-γ release assays (QuantiFERON, T-SPOT.TB) detect latent tuberculosis before biologics or transplantation; an 'IFN-γ-related' tumour gene-expression signature (e.g. CXCL9, CXCL10, IDO1, STAT1, HLA-DR) predicts response to PD-1 blockade; emapalumab (anti-IFN-γ) is approved for primary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis; recombinant IFN-γ-1b is used in chronic granulomatous disease. Loss-of-function mutations in *JAK1*/*JAK2* make tumours resistant to IFN-γ and to checkpoint blockade.

attrs.mnemonic: Type I interferons (α, β) are the antiviral alarm of every cell; type II (γ) is the 'immune interferon' of T and NK cells that arms macrophages.

items.gloss_md: Type II interferon from Th1, CD8+ T and NK cells that activates macrophages and induces antigen presentation, CXCL9/10 and PD-L1.
items.body_md:
Homodimeric cytokine (each chain about 17 kDa, glycosylated) structurally unrelated to type I interferons. Receptor IFNGR1/IFNGR2 activates JAK1 and JAK2 → STAT1 homodimers (gamma-activated factor), which bind GAS elements and induce IRF1 and hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes.

Effects: macrophage classical activation (M1; iNOS, antimicrobial killing), upregulation of MHC class I and II and the immunoproteasome, Th1 polarisation, IgG class switching, induction of CXCL9/CXCL10 (recruiting CXCR3+ T cells), IDO1 and PD-L1 (adaptive resistance), anti-proliferative effects on tumour and stellate cells.

Encoded by *IFNG*. Measured in IGRA tests for tuberculosis and in ELISpot assays; neutralised by emapalumab in HLH. High IFN-γ is the driver of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

attrs.mnemonic: IFN-γ signals through STAT1 dimers binding GAS elements – Gamma-Activated Sequences; it is also the 'G' measured in an IGRA (interferon-gamma release assay).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding TGF-β1, the key immunosuppressive and pro-fibrotic cytokine that activates hepatic stellate cells.
items.body_md:
Transforming growth factor beta 1. Alias TGFB, CED, LAP. Located on 19q13.2.

Encodes the pre-pro-protein that is cleaved by furin into the latency-associated peptide (LAP) and mature TGF-β1, which stay non-covalently bound (small latent complex), usually linked to latent TGF-β binding proteins (LTBPs) in the extracellular matrix. Activation requires release from LAP, e.g. by integrins αvβ6/αvβ8, thrombospondin-1, proteases or low pH.

Disease relevance: the central driver of fibrosis in liver, kidney and lung; in PDAC it shapes the dense desmoplastic stroma and excludes T cells, while the TGF-β pathway is genetically inactivated in many tumours (SMAD4 loss, TGFBR2 mutations). Gain-of-function TGFB1 mutations cause Camurati–Engelmann disease (progressive diaphyseal dysplasia).

Clinical relevance: TGF-β signalling is an investigational drug target (galunisertib, bintrafusp alfa – both without approval) and part of the 'TGF-β fibroblast' signatures of immune exclusion.

attrs.anecdote: Its downstream SMAD proteins are named after the C. elegans gene sma ('small') and the Drosophila gene Mad ('Mothers against decapentaplegic').

items.gloss_md: Latent, matrix-bound cytokine that suppresses immune responses, induces Tregs and Th17 cells and drives fibrosis via SMAD2/3.
items.body_md:
Disulfide-linked 25 kDa homodimer secreted in latent form with LAP; activated TGF-β binds TGFBR2, which recruits and phosphorylates TGFBR1 (ALK5); ALK5 phosphorylates SMAD2/3, which form complexes with SMAD4 and regulate transcription. Non-canonical arms: TAK1–p38/JNK, PI3K–AKT, RHOA.

Immunology: inhibits T-cell proliferation and cytotoxic programmes, NK cells and dendritic-cell maturation; induces peripheral FOXP3+ Tregs, and together with IL-6 or IL-1β promotes Th17 differentiation; promotes IgA class switching.

Fibrosis: in the liver it is the key signal turning quiescent hepatic stellate cells into α-SMA+ collagen-producing myofibroblasts, and it drives epithelial–mesenchymal transition. In cancer it acts as a tumour suppressor early and a pro-metastatic and immune-excluding factor late.

Encoded by *TGFB1* (paralogues TGF-β2 and -β3).

attrs.mnemonic: TGF-β is the 'Tissue Glue Factor': it scars (fibrosis) and calms (Tregs).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding interleukin-1β, the inflammasome-processed pyrogenic cytokine.
items.body_md:
Interleukin 1 beta. Previous names IL1F2, endogenous pyrogen, lymphocyte-activating factor. Located on 2q14.1 in the IL-1 cluster with *IL1A* and *IL1RN* (IL-1 receptor antagonist).

Encodes pro-IL-1β, which is induced transcriptionally by NF-κB (priming signal) and must be cleaved by caspase-1 in an inflammasome (typically NLRP3) to become active; it is released mainly through gasdermin D pores during pyroptosis.

Clinical relevance: IL-1 blockade (anakinra, a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist; canakinumab, anti-IL-1β; rilonacept, a decoy receptor) treats cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, Still's disease, gout flares and recurrent pericarditis. In the CANTOS trial canakinumab reduced cardiovascular events and, in an exploratory analysis, lung cancer incidence. IL-1 signalling contributes to alcohol-related hepatitis and MASH inflammation; anakinra was tested in severe alcohol-related hepatitis without survival benefit.

attrs.mnemonic: Cytokine trio of the acute phase: IL-1 makes fever, IL-6 makes the liver respond (CRP), TNF makes wasting (cachexia).

items.gloss_md: Pro-inflammatory, fever-inducing cytokine produced as an inactive precursor and activated by caspase-1 in the inflammasome.
items.body_md:
Synthesised as a 31 kDa cytosolic precursor without a signal peptide; caspase-1 cleaves it into the 17 kDa active form, which is released by an unconventional route (gasdermin D pores, pyroptosis). β-trefoil structure.

Signals through IL-1R1 plus the IL-1 receptor accessory protein (IL-1RAcP) → MyD88 → IRAK → TRAF6 → NF-κB and MAPK. Counter-regulators: IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) and the decoy receptor IL-1R2.

Effects: fever (via prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus), endothelial activation, neutrophilia, acute-phase response together with IL-6, Th17 differentiation, pain and joint destruction.

Encoded by *IL1B*. Targeted by canakinumab; the IL-1 receptor is blocked by anakinra. Gain-of-function NLRP3 mutations (CAPS) cause IL-1β-driven autoinflammation.

attrs.mnemonic: Inflammasome makes IL-1β and IL-18: 'one-beta and eighteen, the caspase-1 cut'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding IL-17A, the signature cytokine of Th17 cells that recruits neutrophils.
items.body_md:
Interleukin 17A, previous symbols IL17, CTLA8. Located on 6p12.2 next to *IL17F*.

Encodes IL-17A, produced by Th17 cells (differentiated by TGF-β plus IL-6/IL-1β, transcription factor RORγt, maintained by IL-23), γδ T cells, ILC3s, MAIT cells and some CD8+ T cells (Tc17).

Disease relevance: inborn errors of IL-17 immunity (*IL17RA*, *IL17F*, *STAT3* in hyper-IgE syndrome, *AIRE* through autoantibodies) cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Th17 cells are implicated in psoriasis, spondyloarthritis, MASH progression and allograft rejection.

Clinical relevance: anti-IL-17A antibodies (secukinumab, ixekizumab), the IL-17A/F antibody bimekizumab and the receptor antibody brodalumab treat psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis; IL-17 blockade worsened Crohn's disease in trials.

items.gloss_md: Th17 signature cytokine that induces neutrophil-recruiting chemokines and antimicrobial peptides in epithelial and stromal cells.
items.body_md:
Disulfide-linked homodimer (or heterodimer with IL-17F) of the cystine-knot family. Signals through the IL-17RA/IL-17RC receptor complex via the adaptor ACT1 and TRAF6 → NF-κB, C/EBP and mRNA stabilisation of target transcripts.

Targets are mainly non-haematopoietic cells: keratinocytes, epithelial cells, fibroblasts and endothelium, which produce CXCL1/CXCL8, G-CSF, IL-6, β-defensins and S100 proteins. This defends mucosae against extracellular bacteria and fungi (Candida) but drives psoriatic and arthritic inflammation.

Encoded by *IL17A*. Biologics: secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab, brodalumab. In the liver, IL-17 promotes neutrophil infiltration and stellate-cell activation in experimental fibrosis.

attrs.mnemonic: Th17 = 'neutrophil caller': IL-17 tells epithelium to call neutrophils (via IL-8) and fight Candida.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding interleukin-10, the prototypical anti-inflammatory cytokine.
items.body_md:
Interleukin 10, previous names CSIF (cytokine synthesis inhibitory factor), IL10A, TGIF. Located on 1q32.1.

Encodes IL-10 (described in the separate IL-10 protein item), produced by Tregs, Tr1 cells, regulatory B cells, Th2 cells, macrophages and dendritic cells. It was discovered in 1989 (Fiorentino, Mosmann and colleagues) as a Th2 product inhibiting Th1 cytokine synthesis.

Disease relevance: loss-of-function mutations in *IL10*, *IL10RA* or *IL10RB* cause very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease, curable by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation; Il10-knockout mice develop spontaneous colitis. Promoter polymorphisms influence production levels.

Viral mimicry: Epstein–Barr virus and cytomegalovirus encode IL-10 homologues (viral IL-10) to evade immunity.

Clinical relevance: serum IL-10 is elevated in sepsis-associated immunoparalysis and some lymphomas; pegylated IL-10 (pegilodecakin) failed in a phase 3 PDAC trial.

attrs.anecdote: Epstein–Barr virus carries its own copy of IL-10 (BCRF1), stolen from its host to calm down the immune response against infected cells.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding IL-8 (CXCL8), the main neutrophil-attracting chemokine.
items.body_md:
C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 8. Previous symbol IL8; aliases NAP-1, GCP-1. Located on 4q13.3 within the CXC chemokine cluster. There is no mouse orthologue (mice use CXCL1/KC and CXCL2/MIP-2 instead), a common pitfall in translating mouse data.

Encodes IL-8, produced by macrophages, epithelial and endothelial cells, hepatocytes and tumour cells in response to IL-1, TNF, TLR ligands, hypoxia and oncogenic RAS signalling.

Discovered in 1987 as a neutrophil-activating peptide from stimulated monocytes, it was one of the first chemokines characterised.

Clinical relevance: CXCL8 expression is high in alcohol-related hepatitis, where hepatic neutrophil infiltration is characteristic, and correlates with severity; in PDAC the CXCL8/CXCL1–CXCR2 axis recruits myeloid-derived suppressor cells and neutrophils, and CXCR2 antagonists were tested in combination therapy. Serum IL-8 rises in tumours treated with ineffective checkpoint blockade and predicts poor outcome.

items.gloss_md: ELR+ CXC chemokine that recruits and activates neutrophils via CXCR1 and CXCR2.
items.body_md:
Small chemokine (72 or 77 amino acids) with the CXC motif and the N-terminal ELR (Glu-Leu-Arg) motif typical of neutrophil-attracting and angiogenic CXC chemokines. Binds glycosaminoglycans on endothelium, forming haptotactic gradients.

Receptors: CXCR1 (IL-8 specific) and CXCR2 (shared with CXCL1–3, 5–7), G-protein-coupled receptors on neutrophils, monocytes and endothelial cells. Effects: neutrophil chemotaxis, degranulation, respiratory burst, NET formation, and angiogenesis.

Encoded by *CXCL8*. Elevated in alcohol-related hepatitis, sepsis, cytokine release syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease and many cancers including PDAC; CXCR1/2 inhibitors (e.g. reparixin, navarixin, AZD5069) are investigational.

attrs.mnemonic: 'IL-8 calls the neutrophils that ate the bacteria' – CXC chemokines with ELR attract neutrophils.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the heavy chain of the classical HLA class I molecule HLA-A, a highly polymorphic transplantation antigen.
items.body_md:
Major histocompatibility complex, class I, A. Located in the MHC class I region on 6p21.3 (6p22.1).

Encodes the α (heavy) chain of HLA-A, which pairs with β2-microglobulin and presents 8–11-mer peptides to CD8+ T cells. Polymorphism concentrates in exons 2 and 3 (α1 and α2 domains forming the peptide-binding groove); several thousand alleles are listed in the IPD-IMGT/HLA database.

Nomenclature: HLA-A*02:01 – the first field is the allele group (often equal to the serological antigen, A2), the second the specific protein; third and fourth fields denote synonymous and non-coding differences. HLA-A*02:01 is the most common allele in Europeans and the restriction element of many peptide vaccines and TCR therapies (e.g. tebentafusp).

Clinical relevance: HLA-A, -B and -DR are the three loci counted for mismatch grades in kidney allocation (e.g. 1-1-0). Pharmacogenetics: HLA-A*31:01 is associated with carbamazepine hypersensitivity (DRESS) in Europeans.

attrs.full_name: major histocompatibility complex, class I, A
attrs.anecdote: Jean Dausset described the first human leukocyte antigen (MAC, today HLA-A2) in 1958 from antibodies in multiply transfused patients; he shared the 1980 Nobel Prize with Baruj Benacerraf and George Snell.

items.gloss_md: Classical HLA class I molecule present on all nucleated cells that presents intracellular peptides to CD8+ T cells and is a major transplant antigen.
items.body_md:
Heterodimer of a polymorphic 45 kDa heavy chain (α1, α2, α3 domains, transmembrane and cytoplasmic tail) and invariant β2-microglobulin. α1 and α2 form the peptide-binding groove with pockets (notably B and F) that define the peptide motif of each allotype; α3 binds CD8.

Peptides come from proteasomal degradation of cytosolic proteins, are transported into the ER by TAP and loaded in the peptide-loading complex (tapasin, calreticulin, ERp57). Some HLA-A allotypes (A*03, A*11) are ligands for KIR3DL2, and all HLA-A leader peptides can load HLA-E.

Encoded by *HLA-A* (heavy chain) and *B2M*. Transplant relevance: target of donor-specific antibodies detected by single-antigen bead assays; mismatches count in kidney matching. Antibodies are directed against eplets, small polymorphic surface patches shared between alleles.

attrs.mnemonic: Class I = A, B, C (one letter each, on every nucleated cell); class II = D-something (DR, DQ, DP) on antigen-presenting cells.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the heavy chain of HLA-B, the most polymorphic HLA locus, with major pharmacogenetic and disease associations.
items.body_md:
Major histocompatibility complex, class I, B. Located on 6p21.3 (6p21.33), near *HLA-C* and *MICA*.

Encodes the heavy chain of HLA-B, the most polymorphic human gene (more alleles than any other HLA locus). Serological groups Bw4 and Bw6 are defined by residues 77–83; Bw4 allotypes are ligands of the NK receptor KIR3DL1.

Disease associations: HLA-B*27 with ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis; HLA-B*57 with slow HIV progression; HLA-B*51 with Behçet disease.

Pharmacogenetics (well established): HLA-B*57:01 – abacavir hypersensitivity (testing mandatory before therapy) and flucloxacillin drug-induced liver injury; HLA-B*58:01 – allopurinol SJS/TEN; HLA-B*15:02 – carbamazepine SJS/TEN in people of Southeast Asian ancestry.

Transplant relevance: one of the three loci (A, B, DR) used for mismatch grading in kidney allocation.

attrs.full_name: major histocompatibility complex, class I, B
attrs.mnemonic: B is for 'Bad reactions': B*57:01 abacavir and flucloxacillin, B*58:01 allopurinol, B*15:02 carbamazepine, B*27 Bechterew (ankylosing spondylitis).

items.gloss_md: Classical HLA class I molecule with the greatest polymorphism, presenting peptides to CD8+ T cells; key transplant antigen and drug-hypersensitivity risk factor.
items.body_md:
Same architecture as other class I molecules: polymorphic heavy chain with α1–α3 domains plus β2-microglobulin, presenting 8–10-mer peptides from cytosolic proteins. The polymorphic B pocket and F pocket define peptide specificity; e.g. HLA-B*27 favours arginine at peptide position 2.

Drug hypersensitivity mechanisms are known in detail for abacavir: the drug binds inside the HLA-B*57:01 groove, changes the repertoire of presented self-peptides and triggers a polyclonal CD8+ T-cell response.

Encoded by *HLA-B* and *B2M*. Important in transplantation (DSA, mismatches), in HIV control (B*57, B*27 restricted CD8+ responses) and as a ligand for KIR3DL1 (Bw4 epitope). HLA-B leader peptides with methionine at position −21 load HLA-E efficiently and educate NKG2A+ NK cells.

attrs.mnemonic: HLA-B*57:01: test before abacavir – and remember it also predisposes to flucloxacillin liver injury.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the heavy chain of HLA-C, the class I molecule that is the main ligand of KIR2D receptors on NK cells.
items.body_md:
Major histocompatibility complex, class I, C. Located on 6p21.3 (6p21.33), next to *HLA-B*.

Encodes the heavy chain of HLA-C, expressed at lower cell-surface levels than HLA-A and -B. All HLA-C allotypes fall into two groups defined by residue 80: C1 (asparagine 80, ligand of KIR2DL2/3) and C2 (lysine 80, ligand of KIR2DL1). HLA-C is also the main classical class I molecule on extravillous trophoblast, where it interacts with maternal uterine NK cells.

Disease associations: HLA-C*06:02 is the major psoriasis risk allele. Variants affecting HLA-C expression level influence HIV viral load.

Transplant relevance: HLA-C is typed and antibodies against it are considered in virtual crossmatching, although it is not part of the classical A-B-DR mismatch count; it is matched in haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (10/10 match = A, B, C, DRB1, DQB1).

attrs.full_name: major histocompatibility complex, class I, C
attrs.mnemonic: The numbers cross over: KIR2DL1 binds HLA-C group C2, KIR2DL2/3 bind group C1.

items.gloss_md: Classical HLA class I molecule with low surface expression that is the dominant ligand for KIR2D receptors on NK cells.
items.body_md:
Class I heavy chain plus β2-microglobulin, presenting peptides to CD8+ T cells, but with lower cell-surface density than HLA-A/B because of less efficient assembly, a less stable mRNA and miRNA-148 regulation of some alleles.

KIR ligand groups: C1 (Asn80) binds inhibitory KIR2DL2/KIR2DL3, C2 (Lys80) binds inhibitory KIR2DL1 and the activating KIR2DS1. NK-cell education and alloreactivity in haploidentical stem cell transplantation are predicted from donor KIR genotype and recipient HLA-C group.

Encoded by *HLA-C* and *B2M*. Former serological name 'Cw' (w for workshop) is still seen in older papers.

attrs.mnemonic: The numbers cross over: KIR2DL1 binds group C2 (Lys80), KIR2DL2/3 bind group C1 (Asn80).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the polymorphic β chain of HLA-DR, the most important HLA class II locus in transplantation and autoimmunity.
items.body_md:
Major histocompatibility complex, class II, DR beta 1. Located in the class II region on 6p21.32.

Encodes the β1 chain of HLA-DR; the α chain (*HLA-DRA*) is nearly monomorphic, so DR polymorphism is essentially DRB1 polymorphism. Depending on the haplotype, a second expressed β gene (*HLA-DRB3*, *-DRB4* or *-DRB5*; serologically DR52, DR53, DR51) is present.

Disease associations: the 'shared epitope' alleles (e.g. DRB1*04:01, *04:04, *01:01) with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis; DRB1*15:01 with multiple sclerosis; DR3 and DR4 haplotypes with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune hepatitis (DRB1*03:01 and *04:01 in Europeans).

Transplant relevance: DR mismatches have the strongest effect on kidney graft survival among the A-B-DR loci and are weighted most in matching; DRB1 is one of the five loci in 10/10 matching for stem cell transplantation.

attrs.full_name: major histocompatibility complex, class II, DR beta 1
attrs.mnemonic: In kidney matching, mismatches are counted A-B-DR (e.g. 1-1-0), and DR weighs most.

items.gloss_md: The most abundant HLA class II molecule, presenting extracellular peptides to CD4+ T cells; a key transplant antigen and activation marker.
items.body_md:
