Heterodimer of a monomorphic α chain (DRA) and a polymorphic β chain (DRB1, or DRB3/4/5); the α1 and β1 domains form an open-ended groove that binds peptides of about 13–25 amino acids derived from endocytosed proteins. Peptide loading occurs in the MIIC compartment after removal of the invariant chain (CD74) fragment CLIP by HLA-DM.

Constitutively expressed on dendritic cells, B cells, monocytes/macrophages and thymic epithelium; induced by IFN-γ on endothelium, epithelium and activated human T cells (HLA-DR+ CD38+ = activated T cells).

Encoded by *HLA-DRA* and *HLA-DRB1* (plus *DRB3/4/5*). Clinical uses: monocytic HLA-DR expression (mHLA-DR) by flow cytometry is a marker of sepsis-induced immunosuppression; HLA-DR mismatch and DR-DSA matter in kidney transplantation; HLA-DR is a standard antigen-presenting cell marker in scRNA-seq.

attrs.anecdote: Joseph Murray's first successful kidney transplant (Boston, 1954) sidestepped HLA entirely: donor and recipient were identical twins, Ronald and Richard Herrick. Murray received the 1990 Nobel Prize.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the polymorphic α chain of HLA-DQ.
items.body_md:
Major histocompatibility complex, class II, DQ alpha 1. Located on 6p21.32 next to *HLA-DQB1*.

Encodes the DQα chain. Unlike DR, both DQ chains are polymorphic, and α and β chains can pair in cis or in trans, so a heterozygous person can form up to four different DQ heterodimers.

Disease relevance: DQA1*05 together with DQB1*02 forms HLA-DQ2.5, the main coeliac disease risk molecule; DQA1*03 with DQB1*03:02 forms DQ8.

Transplant relevance: donor-specific antibodies can target epitopes on the DQα chain, so DQA1 typing of donor and recipient is increasingly part of virtual crossmatching; high-resolution DQA1/DQB1 typing improves the interpretation of DQ single-antigen bead results.

attrs.full_name: major histocompatibility complex, class II, DQ alpha 1

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the polymorphic β chain of HLA-DQ, the most frequent target of de novo donor-specific antibodies.
items.body_md:
Major histocompatibility complex, class II, DQ beta 1. Located on 6p21.32.

Encodes the DQβ chain; HLA-DQ is in strong linkage disequilibrium with DR, so DR-DQ haplotypes are inherited together (e.g. DR3-DQ2, DR4-DQ8).

Disease associations: DQ2.5 (DQA1*05-DQB1*02) and DQ8 (DQA1*03-DQB1*03:02) are carried by nearly all coeliac disease patients, so their absence practically excludes coeliac disease; DQ2/DQ8 also confer type 1 diabetes risk; DQB1*06:02 is associated with narcolepsy type 1 and is protective against type 1 diabetes.

Transplant relevance: anti-DQ antibodies are the most common de novo donor-specific antibodies after kidney and liver transplantation and are associated with chronic antibody-mediated rejection and graft loss; DQB1 is part of 10/10 stem cell matching.

attrs.full_name: major histocompatibility complex, class II, DQ beta 1
attrs.mnemonic: Coeliac disease: 'DQ2 and DQ8 – no gluten on the plate'; without DQ2/DQ8 coeliac disease is practically excluded.

items.gloss_md: HLA class II molecule with polymorphic α and β chains; carrier of coeliac disease risk (DQ2/DQ8) and frequent target of de novo DSA.
items.body_md:
αβ heterodimer of DQA1 and DQB1 chains presenting endosomal peptides to CD4+ T cells; expressed at lower density than HLA-DR on antigen-presenting cells and inducible on endothelium.

In coeliac disease, tissue transglutaminase deamidates gluten peptides, creating negatively charged residues that bind DQ2.5 or DQ8 pockets with high affinity and trigger gluten-specific CD4+ T cells.

Transplantation: DQ-directed donor-specific antibodies (often high MFI, IgG3 or complement-binding) dominate de novo DSA and associate with transplant glomerulopathy and graft loss; since both chains are polymorphic, antibodies can be specific for DQα, DQβ or a particular α–β combination.

Encoded by *HLA-DQA1* and *HLA-DQB1*.

attrs.mnemonic: Coeliac: 'DQ 2 and 8 – no gluten on the plate'. Negative DQ2/DQ8 typing virtually rules coeliac disease out.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the polymorphic β chain of HLA-DP, important in stem cell transplantation and sensitisation.
items.body_md:
Major histocompatibility complex, class II, DP beta 1. Located on 6p21.32, centromeric to DQ, separated from the rest of the MHC by a recombination hotspot; therefore DP is often mismatched even in otherwise HLA-identical unrelated donors.

Encodes the DPβ chain; the α chain (*HLA-DPA1*) is less polymorphic.

Clinical relevance: in unrelated haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, DPB1 mismatches are classified as permissive or non-permissive by the T-cell epitope (TCE) algorithm; non-permissive mismatches increase GVHD and mortality. In solid organ transplantation, anti-DP donor-specific antibodies can cause antibody-mediated rejection and positive crossmatches. DPB1*02:01 is associated with chronic beryllium disease (Glu69 variants) – a classic gene–environment interaction.

attrs.full_name: major histocompatibility complex, class II, DP beta 1

items.gloss_md: HLA class II molecule (DPA1/DPB1) with lower expression than DR; relevant for stem cell matching and as a target of donor-specific antibodies.
items.body_md:
αβ heterodimer of DPA1 and DPB1 presenting endosomal peptides to CD4+ T cells; expressed on professional antigen-presenting cells and inducible by IFN-γ, at lower levels than HLA-DR.

Because of weak linkage disequilibrium with DR/DQ, DP is mismatched in most 10/10-matched unrelated stem cell transplants; the TCE groups classify these mismatches by immunogenicity. DPB1 polymorphism at position 69 (Glu69) underlies susceptibility to beryllium-induced granulomatous lung disease.

Encoded by *HLA-DPA1* and *HLA-DPB1*. Anti-DP antibodies occur in sensitised patients (pregnancy, transfusions, previous transplant) and are included in single-antigen bead panels.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding β2-microglobulin, the invariant light chain of all HLA class I molecules.
items.body_md:
Beta-2-microglobulin, located on 15q21.1 – outside the MHC.

Encodes β2-microglobulin, required for folding and surface expression of HLA class I (A, B, C, E, F, G), CD1 and the neonatal Fc receptor FcRn, which recycles IgG and albumin.

Disease relevance: loss-of-function mutations of B2M are a frequent mechanism of tumour escape from CD8+ T cells and of acquired resistance to checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. melanoma, MSI-high colorectal cancer). Germline B2M deficiency causes familial hypoproteinaemia (low IgG and albumin, because FcRn fails). Amyloidogenic variants (D76N) cause hereditary systemic amyloidosis.

Clinical relevance: serum β2-microglobulin is a marker of tumour burden in myeloma (ISS/R-ISS stage) and lymphoma and of glomerular filtration. B2M knockout is used to create 'hypoimmunogenic' stem-cell-derived grafts.

items.gloss_md: Small invariant protein forming the light chain of all HLA class I molecules; serum marker of myeloma tumour burden and kidney function.
items.body_md:
Single Ig-like domain protein of about 12 kDa, non-covalently bound to the class I heavy chain (α3 domain), CD1 and FcRn; it stabilises the peptide-binding groove. Free β2m is filtered by the glomerulus and reabsorbed and degraded in the proximal tubule.

Clinical chemistry: serum β2m rises with reduced GFR and with high cell turnover; it is a component of the International Staging System for multiple myeloma (ISS stage III: β2m ≥ 5.5 mg/L). Urinary β2m indicates tubular damage. In long-term haemodialysis β2m accumulates and forms amyloid fibrils (dialysis-related amyloidosis, carpal tunnel syndrome).

Encoded by *B2M*. Loss of β2m on tumour cells removes all classical class I and makes the tumour invisible to CD8+ T cells but a target for NK cells ('missing self').

attrs.mnemonic: ISS for myeloma is just two numbers: β2m and albumin ('B and A').

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding MICA, a stress-induced, polymorphic MHC-like ligand of the NKG2D receptor and a non-HLA transplant antigen.
items.body_md:
MHC class I polypeptide-related sequence A, located on 6p21.33 about 46 kb centromeric of *HLA-B*; the related *MICB* lies nearby.

Encodes MICA, a class I-like molecule that does not bind β2-microglobulin or peptides. It is barely expressed on healthy cells but induced by cellular stress, DNA damage, heat shock, viral infection and transformation (especially on epithelial tumours), and is recognised by the activating NK/T-cell receptor NKG2D.

Polymorphism: over 100 alleles; a common transmembrane microsatellite variant (A5.1, in MICA*008) produces a truncated protein that is released in exosomes.

Clinical relevance: anti-MICA antibodies are among the best characterised non-HLA antibodies; they are associated with kidney graft rejection in several cohorts and are included in some single-antigen panels. Tumours shed soluble MICA (via ADAMs and ERp5), which downregulates NKG2D and is associated with poor prognosis.

attrs.full_name: MHC class I polypeptide-related sequence A

items.gloss_md: Stress-induced MHC class I-like protein that activates NK and CD8+ T cells via NKG2D; shed by tumours and targeted by non-HLA antibodies.
items.body_md:
Glycoprotein with α1, α2 and α3 domains like class I but without β2-microglobulin association and without a peptide in its groove. Expressed on gastrointestinal epithelium at low levels and strongly induced by stress (heat-shock elements in the promoter), DNA damage response and oncogenic transformation.

Binding to NKG2D (with DAP10) triggers NK-cell cytotoxicity and costimulates CD8+ and γδ T cells ('induced self'). Tumours escape by proteolytic shedding of MICA, producing soluble MICA that downmodulates NKG2D; antibodies that block shedding are in development.

Encoded by *MICA*. In transplantation, anti-MICA antibodies have been associated with acute and chronic rejection of kidney grafts, independent of HLA antibodies in some studies.

aliases: MHC class I chain-related protein A

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding cytochrome P450 3A5, whose genotype determines tacrolimus dose requirements.
items.body_md:
Cytochrome P450 family 3 subfamily A member 5, located on 7q22.1 in the CYP3A cluster with *CYP3A4*, *CYP3A7* and *CYP3A43*.

Encodes CYP3A5, expressed in liver, intestine and kidney. The common *3 allele (rs776746, intron 3) creates a cryptic splice site, so carriers of two *3 alleles make no functional enzyme ('non-expressers'); *6 and *7 are further loss-of-function alleles found mainly in people of African ancestry.

Frequencies: most Europeans (about 80–90 %) are *3/*3 non-expressers, whereas most people of African ancestry carry at least one functional *1 allele.

Clinical relevance: CYP3A5 expressers (*1/*1, *1/*3) clear tacrolimus faster and need about 1.5–2 times higher starting doses to reach target trough levels (CPIC guideline); otherwise they spend longer below target early after transplantation. In liver transplantation the donor liver's genotype matters for hepatic metabolism and the recipient's for intestinal metabolism.

attrs.full_name: cytochrome P450 family 3 subfamily A member 5
attrs.mnemonic: CYP3A5 *3 = 'switched off'. Expressers (*1 carriers) need more tacrolimus – think '*1 burns it fast'.

items.gloss_md: Polymorphically expressed cytochrome P450 enzyme that metabolises tacrolimus; expressers need higher tacrolimus doses.
items.body_md:
Haem-containing monooxygenase of the endoplasmic reticulum (about 84 % sequence identity with CYP3A4) that hydroxylates and demethylates lipophilic drugs, using electrons from NADPH–cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase.

Substrate overlap with CYP3A4 is large, but CYP3A5 contributes notably to the metabolism of tacrolimus (13-O-demethylation), less to ciclosporin and sirolimus; its expression in the kidney may contribute to local tacrolimus metabolism.

Encoded by *CYP3A5*. In expressers it can account for a substantial part of total hepatic CYP3A activity. Genotype-guided tacrolimus dosing is recommended by CPIC; therapeutic drug monitoring (trough levels) remains mandatory regardless of genotype.

attrs.mnemonic: CYP3A5*3 = switched off: most Europeans are non-expressers; *1 carriers ('expressers') burn tacrolimus faster and need about 1.5–2 × the dose.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CYP3A4, the most abundant hepatic and intestinal drug-metabolising enzyme.
items.body_md:
Cytochrome P450 family 3 subfamily A member 4, located on 7q22.1 next to *CYP3A5*.

Encodes CYP3A4, the dominant cytochrome P450 in adult liver and small-intestinal enterocytes, responsible for the metabolism of roughly a third to half of clinically used drugs. Expression is induced by the nuclear receptors PXR and CAR (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) and reduced in inflammation (IL-6).

Genetic variation is less important than for CYP3A5: the reduced-expression allele CYP3A4*22 (rs35599367) lowers tacrolimus dose requirements by about a fifth to a third.

Clinical relevance: CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, azole antifungals, ritonavir-boosted antivirals such as nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, diltiazem, grapefruit) raise calcineurin and mTOR inhibitor levels to toxic ranges; inducers cause subtherapeutic levels and rejection. Midazolam is the classic probe substrate.

attrs.full_name: cytochrome P450 family 3 subfamily A member 4
attrs.mnemonic: Tacrolimus level up with grapefruit, azoles, macrolides and ritonavir (inhibitors); down with rifampicin, carbamazepine and St John's wort (inducers).

items.gloss_md: The most important drug-metabolising cytochrome P450 in liver and gut, responsible for many clinically relevant drug interactions (e.g. with tacrolimus).
items.body_md:
ER-membrane haem monooxygenase with a large, flexible active site that accommodates large substrates (tacrolimus, ciclosporin, sirolimus, everolimus, statins, many kinase inhibitors, opioids, benzodiazepines, steroids) and can bind several molecules at once, which complicates interaction prediction.

Intestinal CYP3A4, together with P-glycoprotein, limits oral bioavailability (first-pass effect); this is why grapefruit (furanocoumarins, mechanism-based intestinal inactivation) raises levels of oral but not intravenous substrates.

Encoded by *CYP3A4*. Clinically: check every new drug in a transplant recipient for CYP3A interactions; strong inhibitors (ritonavir, cobicistat, posaconazole, voriconazole, clarithromycin) require tacrolimus dose reductions or pauses, strong inducers (rifampicin) multiply dose needs.

attrs.mnemonic: Tacrolimus level up with grapefruit, azoles, macrolides and ritonavir (inhibitors); down with rifampicin, carbamazepine and St John's wort (inducers).
attrs.anecdote: The grapefruit juice effect was discovered by accident in 1989: Canadian researchers used grapefruit juice to mask the taste of alcohol in a felodipine interaction study and found unexpectedly high drug levels.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding P-glycoprotein (MDR1), the ATP-driven efflux pump for many drugs including tacrolimus and ciclosporin.
items.body_md:
ATP binding cassette subfamily B member 1. Previous symbols MDR1, PGY1; alias P-gp, CD243. Located on 7q21.12 next to *ABCB4*.

Encodes P-glycoprotein, expressed on the apical membrane of enterocytes, the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes, proximal tubule cells, the blood–brain barrier, placenta and haematopoietic stem cells.

History: identified in 1976 by Juliano and Ling as a surface glycoprotein of colchicine-resistant hamster cells; 'P' stands for permeability. Overexpression causes multidrug resistance of tumour cells to anthracyclines, taxanes and vinca alkaloids.

Clinical relevance: limits oral absorption and brain entry of substrates (tacrolimus, ciclosporin, sirolimus, digoxin, dabigatran, loperamide). Polymorphisms such as C3435T (rs1045642) were extensively studied for tacrolimus and ciclosporin pharmacokinetics, with inconsistent results; they are not used for dosing. Many CYP3A inhibitors also inhibit P-gp.

attrs.full_name: ATP binding cassette subfamily B member 1

items.gloss_md: ATP-binding-cassette efflux pump that exports many drugs out of cells, limiting their absorption, brain penetration and tumour accumulation.
items.body_md:
ABC transporter with two transmembrane domains (6 helices each) and two nucleotide-binding domains; ATP hydrolysis drives a switch from inward- to outward-facing conformation, extruding hydrophobic, amphipathic substrates from the inner membrane leaflet.

Physiological roles: protection of brain, testis and fetus from xenobiotics; excretion into bile and urine; intestinal barrier. Loperamide is an opioid that lacks central effects only because P-gp keeps it out of the brain.

Encoded by *ABCB1*. Drug interactions: inhibitors (verapamil, amiodarone, clarithromycin, ciclosporin itself, ritonavir) and inducers (rifampicin, St John's wort) change exposure of P-gp substrates such as digoxin, dabigatran and tacrolimus. In oncology, P-gp inhibitors failed to reverse multidrug resistance clinically.

attrs.anecdote: Loperamide (Imodium) is an opioid; you do not feel it only because P-glycoprotein pumps it out of the brain. Overdoses with P-gp inhibitors have caused opioid-like toxicity.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding FKBP12, the intracellular receptor that tacrolimus and sirolimus must bind to act.
items.body_md:
FKBP prolyl isomerase 1A. Aliases FKBP12, FKBP1. Located on 20p13.

Encodes FKBP12, a small, abundant cytosolic peptidyl-prolyl cis–trans isomerase (immunophilin). Physiologically, FKBP12 binds and stabilises the ryanodine receptor RyR1 and the IP3 receptor, and binds the GS domain of the TGF-β type I receptor (ALK5), preventing ligand-independent activation.

Pharmacology: both tacrolimus (FK506) and sirolimus (rapamycin) bind FKBP12 in the same pocket, but the drug–protein complexes have different gain-of-function targets: FKBP12–tacrolimus inhibits calcineurin, FKBP12–sirolimus inhibits mTORC1. Ciclosporin uses a different immunophilin, cyclophilin A (*PPIA*). The FKBP12–drug binding concept (chemical inducers of dimerisation, e.g. rapalogs, AP1903) is used in synthetic biology and in CAR-T safety switches.

items.gloss_md: Immunophilin that binds tacrolimus or sirolimus; the drug–FKBP12 complex then inhibits calcineurin or mTORC1, respectively.
items.body_md:
12 kDa peptidyl-prolyl cis–trans isomerase whose hydrophobic active-site pocket binds FK506 (tacrolimus) and rapamycin (sirolimus, everolimus) with nanomolar affinity, inhibiting the isomerase activity – which is not the relevant effect.

Gain-of-function complexes: FKBP12–tacrolimus binds the calcineurin A/B interface and blocks access of NFAT; FKBP12–rapamycin binds the FRB domain of mTOR and allosterically inhibits mTORC1. Ciclosporin acts analogously with cyclophilin A.

Encoded by *FKBP1A*. Explains why tacrolimus and sirolimus were thought to compete, though in practice they are combined at lower doses.

attrs.mnemonic: Two drugs, one ring-holder: FKBP12 is the shared 'handle'; tacrolimus+handle hits calcineurin, sirolimus+handle hits mTOR.
attrs.anecdote: Tacrolimus (FK506) was isolated in 1984 from Streptomyces tsukubaensis in a soil sample from Tsukuba, Japan; rapamycin from Streptomyces hygroscopicus in soil from Easter Island – Rapa Nui, hence its name.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the catalytic α subunit of calcineurin, the target of tacrolimus and ciclosporin.
items.body_md:
Protein phosphatase 3 catalytic subunit alpha. Aliases calcineurin A α, CNA, CALNA. Located on 4q24.

Encodes the main catalytic subunit of calcineurin (protein phosphatase 2B), a Ca²⁺/calmodulin-dependent serine/threonine phosphatase formed with the regulatory subunit calcineurin B (*PPP3R1*). Paralogues *PPP3CB* and *PPP3CC* encode the β and γ catalytic isoforms.

Function: after TCR engagement raises intracellular calcium, calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT transcription factors, which then enter the nucleus and, with AP-1, induce IL-2, IL-4, TNF, CD40L and other activation genes. Calcineurin also has key functions in neurons, cardiomyocytes (hypertrophy), kidney and pancreatic β cells.

Disease relevance: de novo PPP3CA variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with epilepsy. Clinical relevance: calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, ciclosporin, voclosporin) are the backbone of maintenance immunosuppression after solid organ transplantation.

attrs.mnemonic: Ca²⁺ → calcineurin → NFAT → IL-2: block calcineurin and the T cell cannot make IL-2.

items.gloss_md: Calcium/calmodulin-activated phosphatase that activates NFAT in T cells; inhibited by tacrolimus and ciclosporin (calcineurin inhibitors).
items.body_md:
Heterodimer of a catalytic subunit (calcineurin A: α, β or γ isoform) and a Ca²⁺-binding regulatory subunit (calcineurin B), activated by Ca²⁺–calmodulin binding, which displaces an autoinhibitory domain. Also called protein phosphatase 2B (PP2B).

In T cells, TCR-induced Ca²⁺ influx activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT, exposing its nuclear localisation signal; nuclear NFAT drives IL-2 and other cytokine genes.

Inhibitors: tacrolimus–FKBP12 and ciclosporin–cyclophilin complexes block the substrate-binding groove. Typical calcineurin-inhibitor toxicities: nephrotoxicity (afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, chronic striped interstitial fibrosis, arteriolar hyalinosis), hypertension, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, tremor and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, post-transplant diabetes (more with tacrolimus), thrombotic microangiopathy, and with ciclosporin gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism.

Encoded by *PPP3CA* (main catalytic isoform), *PPP3CB*, *PPP3CC* and *PPP3R1*.

attrs.mnemonic: Calcineurin inhibitor side effects – (de) 'Niere, Nerven, Zucker, Zahnfleisch': nephrotoxicity, tremor/PRES, post-transplant diabetes, gingival hyperplasia (ciclosporin).
attrs.anecdote: Ciclosporin's immunosuppressive effect was found in 1972 at Sandoz by Jean-François Borel in an extract of the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum from a Norwegian soil sample; it made routine organ transplantation possible in the 1980s.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding IMPDH2, the lymphocyte-induced isoform of the rate-limiting guanine-synthesis enzyme inhibited by mycophenolic acid.
items.body_md:
Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 2, located on 3p21.31.

Encodes IMPDH type II, which catalyses the NAD⁺-dependent oxidation of IMP to XMP, the rate-limiting step of de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis. IMPDH2 is induced in proliferating cells and activated lymphocytes, whereas IMPDH1 is constitutive in most cells.

Pharmacology: activated T and B lymphocytes rely heavily on the de novo purine pathway, so IMPDH inhibition selectively suppresses their proliferation. Mycophenolic acid (from mycophenolate mofetil, CellCept, or enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium, Myfortic) inhibits IMPDH2 about 4-fold more potently than IMPDH1. Ribavirin also inhibits IMPDH. IMPDH2 forms filaments ('rods and rings') in cells under nucleotide stress.

items.gloss_md: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase type II, the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo GTP synthesis in activated lymphocytes and the target of mycophenolate.
items.body_md:
Homotetrameric NAD⁺-dependent oxidoreductase with a catalytic TIM-barrel domain and a regulatory Bateman (CBS) domain that mediates allosteric regulation by ATP/GTP and filament formation. It converts IMP to XMP, which GMP synthase turns into GMP.

Mycophenolic acid binds the NAD⁺ site after hydride transfer, trapping the covalent intermediate (uncompetitive inhibitor). Guanine depletion arrests lymphocyte proliferation and reduces glycosylation of adhesion molecules.

Mycophenolate in practice: standard antiproliferative agent with tacrolimus and steroids after kidney and liver transplantation, also in autoimmune hepatitis and lupus nephritis. Adverse effects: diarrhoea, leukopenia, anaemia, CMV and BK virus infections, teratogenicity. MPA is glucuronidated by UGT1A9 to inactive MPAG with enterohepatic recirculation (ciclosporin lowers MPA exposure by blocking biliary MRP2 export).

Encoded by *IMPDH2*.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding IMPDH1, the constitutive isoform of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, mutated in a form of retinitis pigmentosa.
items.body_md:
Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase 1, located on 7q32.1.

Encodes IMPDH type I, the constitutively expressed isoform (about 84 % identical to IMPDH2), with high expression in the retina, where specific splice variants dominate.

Disease relevance: heterozygous missense mutations (e.g. D226N) cause autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (RP10) and Leber congenital amaurosis 11.

Pharmacology: less sensitive to mycophenolic acid than IMPDH2. Polymorphisms in IMPDH1 and IMPDH2 have been associated with rejection risk or MMF side effects in some transplant cohorts, but they are not used clinically.

items.gloss_md: Constitutive inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase isoform, less sensitive to mycophenolic acid; essential in photoreceptors.
items.body_md:
Homotetrameric NAD⁺-dependent enzyme catalysing IMP → XMP in de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis, with the same catalytic and Bateman domains as IMPDH2. Retinal isoforms with N- and C-terminal extensions are highly expressed in photoreceptors, which need large amounts of GTP for cGMP-based phototransduction.

Mutations in the Bateman domain that impair allosteric regulation and filament assembly cause retinitis pigmentosa, illustrating that photoreceptors are uniquely sensitive to GTP imbalance.

Encoded by *IMPDH1*. Pharmacologically it is a secondary target of mycophenolic acid; the relative IMPDH2 selectivity of MPA is part of the rationale for its lymphocyte selectivity.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding thiopurine S-methyltransferase; deficiency causes severe myelotoxicity on azathioprine.
items.body_md:
Thiopurine S-methyltransferase, located on 6p22.3.

Encodes TPMT, a cytosolic enzyme that S-methylates thiopurines (azathioprine's active metabolite 6-mercaptopurine and thioguanine), diverting them from formation of the active, cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides.

Genetics: common loss-of-function alleles TPMT*2, *3A (the most common in Europeans), *3B and *3C. About 1 in 10 Europeans is heterozygous with intermediate activity and about 1 in 300 is homozygous deficient, with life-threatening myelosuppression on standard doses. *NUDT15* variants play the analogous role in East Asian and Hispanic populations.

Clinical relevance: TPMT genotype or enzyme activity (with NUDT15) should be tested before azathioprine or mercaptopurine (CPIC guideline), e.g. in autoimmune hepatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, after transplantation and in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; thiopurine metabolite levels (6-TGN, 6-MMP) guide therapy.

items.gloss_md: Thiopurine S-methyltransferase, the enzyme that inactivates azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine; its deficiency predicts severe bone marrow toxicity.
items.body_md:
Cytosolic S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferase. It methylates 6-mercaptopurine to 6-methylmercaptopurine (6-MMP) and thioinosine monophosphate to methylated metabolites; the alternative pathway (HGPRT) yields the active 6-thioguanine nucleotides (6-TGN) that incorporate into DNA and inhibit RAC1 in T cells.

Low TPMT activity → excess 6-TGN → myelotoxicity; very high activity ('shunters') → high 6-MMP → hepatotoxicity and poor efficacy, which allopurinol co-therapy (with dose-reduced azathioprine) can correct. Variant proteins (e.g. TPMT*3A with A154T and Y240C) are degraded rapidly by the proteasome.

Encoded by *TPMT*. Activity is measured in erythrocytes (falsely normal after recent transfusion) or inferred from genotype.

attrs.mnemonic: Test TPMT before 'AZA': no methylation, all goes to the toxic TGN.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD52, the lymphocyte surface glycoprotein targeted by alemtuzumab.
items.body_md:
CD52 molecule, alias CAMPATH-1 antigen, HE5. Located on 1p36.11.

Encodes CD52, a very small GPI-anchored glycopeptide (12 amino acids in its mature form) carried at high density on T and B lymphocytes, NK cells, monocytes and some dendritic cells, and on epithelial cells of the male reproductive tract; its function is not well understood (it may dampen T-cell activation via Siglec-10).

Clinical relevance: alemtuzumab, a humanised anti-CD52 antibody, causes profound and long-lasting lymphocyte depletion; it is used for induction in some kidney transplant programmes, in relapsing multiple sclerosis (Lemtrada), formerly in CLL (MabCampath) and in conditioning for stem cell transplantation; secondary autoimmunity (thyroid disease, ITP, anti-GBM disease) is a typical late complication.

items.gloss_md: Small GPI-anchored glycoprotein on lymphocytes and monocytes, target of the depleting antibody alemtuzumab.
items.body_md:
Mature CD52 consists of 12 amino acids with a large N-linked glycan and a GPI anchor; it is abundant (several hundred thousand copies per lymphocyte), which makes it an efficient target for complement-mediated and antibody-dependent killing.

Alemtuzumab depletes circulating T and B cells within hours; B cells recover over months, CD4+ T cells over a year or longer. Because of the GPI anchor, PNH-like CD52-negative T-cell clones can emerge after treatment.

Encoded by *CD52*. Alemtuzumab is used for induction in kidney transplantation (often with steroid avoidance), in multiple sclerosis and in stem cell transplant conditioning.

attrs.anecdote: 'Campath' comes from Cambridge Pathology: the antibody was developed in Herman Waldmann's group at the University of Cambridge pathology department in the 1980s and was one of the first humanised antibodies.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding complement C3, the central component where all three complement pathways converge.
items.body_md:
Complement C3, located on 19p13.3. Produced mainly by hepatocytes (as an acute-phase protein) and locally by macrophages, epithelial cells and kidney tubular cells.

Encodes the C3 precursor, processed into a disulfide-linked β and α chain; cleavage by C3 convertases releases C3a and C3b, which with its internal thioester binds covalently to surfaces.

Disease relevance: complete C3 deficiency causes recurrent pyogenic infections and immune-complex disease; gain-of-function C3 mutations predispose to atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome; C3 glomerulopathy (dense deposit disease, C3 glomerulonephritis) results from alternative pathway dysregulation, often with C3 nephritic factor. The C3 S/F polymorphism has been linked to kidney transplant outcomes.

Clinical relevance: serum C3 (with C4) is used to assess complement consumption (e.g. lupus nephritis, post-infectious glomerulonephritis); low C3 in cirrhosis reflects reduced hepatic synthesis and correlates with infections and mortality. Pegcetacoplan (C3 inhibitor) is approved for PNH and C3G.

items.gloss_md: Most abundant complement protein (about 1–1.5 g/L); its cleavage to C3a and C3b is the convergence point of all complement pathways.
items.body_md:
185 kDa protein with α and β chains and an internal thioester. Classical/lectin C3 convertase C4b2b (formerly 'C4b2a') and alternative convertase C3bBb cleave it into the anaphylatoxin C3a and C3b, which attaches to nearby surfaces and amplifies the alternative pathway loop.

Regulation: factor I with cofactors (factor H, CD46/MCP, CR1) inactivates C3b to iC3b, then C3c and C3dg/C3d; C3d bound to antigen engages CR2 (CD21) on B cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity. iC3b is the main opsonin for CR3 (CD11b/CD18) and CR4 (CD11c/CD18).

Encoded by *C3*. Clinical use: serum C3 measurement; C3d deposition in biopsies; C3d-binding single-antigen bead assays identify complement-fixing donor-specific antibodies; inhibitors such as pegcetacoplan (C3) and iptacopan (factor B) block the amplification loop.

attrs.mnemonic: All roads lead to C3: classical, lectin and alternative pathways all build a C3 convertase.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding complement C4A, one of two copy-number-variable C4 isotypes in the MHC class III region.
items.body_md:
Complement C4A (Rodgers blood group), located on 6p21.33 in the MHC class III region in the RCCX module (with *RP*/*STK19*, *CYP21A2*/*CYP21A1P* and *TNXB*). Each haplotype carries one to several C4 genes, and each copy is either C4A or C4B, differing by only four amino acids that change thioester reactivity: C4A binds preferentially to amino groups (protein antigens, immune complexes), C4B to hydroxyl groups (carbohydrate surfaces).

Disease relevance: low C4A copy number and complete C4 deficiency are strong risk factors for systemic lupus erythematosus; higher C4A copy number and expression in the brain were associated with schizophrenia risk through synaptic pruning (Sekar et al., 2016). C4A carries the Rodgers blood group antigens.

Clinical relevance: encodes the C4 protein whose split product C4d is a key biopsy marker of antibody-mediated rejection.

attrs.anecdote: In 2016 the strongest common genetic signal for schizophrenia in the MHC region was traced to C4A copy number: more C4A, more synaptic pruning in the developing brain.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding complement C4B, the second C4 isotype, carrying the Chido blood group antigens.
items.body_md:
Complement C4B (Chido blood group), located on 6p21.33 in the RCCX module of the MHC class III region next to *C4A*; the two genes are almost identical, differing in a few residues of the α chain (C4d region) that determine isotype and blood group antigens.

C4B has a more reactive thioester towards hydroxyl groups and higher haemolytic activity than C4A. Gene copy number of C4B, like C4A, varies between individuals; partial C4B deficiency has been associated with susceptibility to bacterial infections in some studies.

Clinical relevance: together with *C4A* it encodes the C4 protein whose degradation product C4d serves as a durable footprint of classical-pathway activation in transplant biopsies. Serum C4 measured clinically is the sum of both isotypes; low C4 indicates classical pathway consumption (lupus, cryoglobulinaemia, hereditary angioedema).

items.gloss_md: Classical and lectin pathway complement protein; its cleavage fragment C4b forms the C3 convertase and its degradation product C4d marks antibody-mediated injury.
items.body_md:
Three-chain (α, β, γ) protein of about 200 kDa with an internal thioester. C1s (classical pathway) or MASP-2 (lectin pathway) cleaves C4 into C4a and C4b; C4b binds covalently to surfaces near the antibody or lectin, binds C2, which is then cleaved to form the C3 convertase C4b2b.

C4b is inactivated by factor I with cofactors C4-binding protein, CR1 or CD46 to iC4b and then into C4c (released) and C4d (remaining covalently bound).

Encoded by *C4A* and *C4B*. Serum C4 is low in active lupus, cryoglobulinaemia (often very low), hereditary angioedema (C1-inhibitor deficiency, even between attacks) and hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis.

attrs.mnemonic: Low C4 alone (with normal C3) – think hereditary angioedema or cryoglobulinaemia.

items.gloss_md: Covalently bound degradation fragment of complement C4 that persists on endothelium and serves as the biopsy footprint of antibody-mediated rejection.
items.body_md:
A 44.5 kDa fragment of the C4 α chain containing the thioester site; after factor I cleaves C4b, C4d stays covalently attached to endothelial cell surfaces and basement membranes for days to weeks, outlasting the antibodies that triggered classical-pathway activation.

Banff classification (kidney): linear C4d staining of peritubular capillaries (C4d2–3 by immunofluorescence on frozen tissue, or C4d > 0 by IHC on paraffin) is one criterion for 'current/recent antibody interaction with the endothelium' in active or chronic active antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR), together with histological injury (microvascular inflammation) and donor-specific antibodies. Since Banff 2013 C4d-negative ABMR is recognised, because many antibody-mediated rejections are C4d-negative. C4d positivity without injury is typical of ABO-incompatible grafts (accommodation).

Also used in liver (Banff 2016 liver AMR criteria), heart and lung allograft pathology. Product of *C4A* and *C4B*.

attrs.mnemonic: C4d = 'C4 detective': it stays at the crime scene (capillaries) after the antibodies have left.
attrs.anecdote: C4d as a marker of humoral rejection was introduced in the early 1990s by Helmut Feucht and colleagues in Munich, who found capillary C4d deposits associated with early kidney graft loss.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding complement C5, the starting point of the terminal pathway and target of eculizumab.
items.body_md:
Complement C5, located on 9q33.2. Produced mainly by hepatocytes.

Encodes C5, which C5 convertases cleave into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates the membrane attack complex (C5b–9).

Disease relevance: inherited C5–C9 deficiencies predispose to recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal and gonococcal) infections. A C5 polymorphism (R885H) explains non-response to eculizumab in some Japanese patients.

Clinical relevance: anti-C5 antibodies eculizumab (Soliris) and the long-acting ravulizumab (Ultomiris), and the peptide zilucoplan, treat paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (including recurrence after kidney transplantation), generalised myasthenia gravis and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder; they have been used off-label in refractory antibody-mediated rejection. Meningococcal vaccination (and often antibiotic prophylaxis) is mandatory. Avacopan blocks the C5a receptor (C5aR1) in ANCA vasculitis.

items.gloss_md: Terminal complement protein whose cleavage releases the anaphylatoxin C5a and starts the membrane attack complex; blocked by eculizumab.
items.body_md:
190 kDa two-chain protein structurally related to C3 and C4 but without a reactive thioester. Cleaved by C5 convertases (C4b2b3b, C3bBb3b) into C5a (strongest anaphylatoxin; chemotaxis and activation of neutrophils and monocytes via C5aR1) and C5b, which recruits C6, C7, C8 and multiple C9 molecules to form the membrane attack complex (C5b-9, MAC), a pore that lyses cells and bacteria.

Host cells are protected by CD59, which blocks C9 polymerisation; loss of GPI-anchored CD59 and CD55 explains complement-mediated haemolysis in PNH.

Encoded by *C5*. Drugs: eculizumab, ravulizumab, crovalimab, zilucoplan (all prevent C5 cleavage); soluble C5b-9 in plasma is a marker of terminal pathway activation.

attrs.mnemonic: Terminal complement (C5–C9) defects or eculizumab = 'Neisseria needs the MAC': vaccinate against meningococci.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding KIR2DL1, the inhibitory killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptor for HLA-C group C2; prototype for KIR basics.
items.body_md:
Killer cell immunoglobulin like receptor, two Ig domains and long cytoplasmic tail 1. Alias CD158a. Located in the leukocyte receptor complex on 19q13.42.

KIR basics: the KIR genes (about 15 genes and pseudogenes) vary in gene content between haplotypes – group A haplotypes carry mainly inhibitory KIRs, group B haplotypes additional activating ones – and are highly polymorphic. Their HLA class I ligands are on chromosome 6, so receptor and ligand segregate independently.

KIR2DL1 recognises HLA-C allotypes with lysine at position 80 (group C2). NK cells expressing an inhibitory KIR for a self-HLA ligand become 'licensed' (educated) and functionally potent.

Clinical relevance: in haploidentical stem cell transplantation for AML, donor NK cells lacking an inhibitory ligand in the recipient (KIR-ligand mismatch) were associated with less relapse (Ruggeri, Velardi et al., 2002); KIR genotyping is used in some donor-selection algorithms. KIR–HLA combinations also affect viral control and pregnancy outcomes. Lirilumab is an investigational anti-KIR2DL antibody.

attrs.full_name: killer cell immunoglobulin like receptor, two Ig domains and long cytoplasmic tail 1

items.gloss_md: Inhibitory killer-cell Ig-like receptor (CD158a) on NK cells that binds HLA-C group C2 and blocks killing of healthy cells.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane receptor with two extracellular Ig-like domains (2D) and a long (L) cytoplasmic tail with two ITIMs that recruit SHP-1/SHP-2 to dephosphorylate activating signals. Activating KIRs (e.g. KIR2DS1, same ligand with lower affinity) have a short (S) tail and pair with the ITAM adaptor DAP12.

Ligand recognition depends on HLA-C residue 80 (Lys80 = C2) and is modulated by the presented peptide. Expressed stochastically on subsets of NK cells and some memory CD8+ T cells.

Encoded by *KIR2DL1*. Lost recognition of self HLA (tumour HLA loss, allogeneic cells lacking C2) releases NK-cell killing – the basis of NK alloreactivity in haploidentical transplantation.

attrs.mnemonic: KIR names decode themselves: 2D/3D = number of Ig domains; L = Long tail = inhibitory (ITIM); S = Short tail = Stimulatory (DAP12).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding NKG2A, the inhibitory NK and CD8 T-cell receptor for HLA-E and target of monalizumab.
items.body_md:
Killer cell lectin like receptor C1. Aliases NKG2A, CD159a. Located on 12p13.2 in the NK gene complex, near *KLRC2* (NKG2C), *KLRK1* (NKG2D) and *KLRD1* (CD94).

Encodes NKG2A, a C-type lectin-like receptor that forms a heterodimer with CD94 and binds HLA-E. Expressed on about half of blood NK cells (especially CD56bright and immature NK cells) and induced on tumour-infiltrating CD8+ T cells.

Clinical relevance: NKG2A is an emerging checkpoint; HLA-E is often upregulated on tumours (IFN-γ-inducible). The blocking antibody monalizumab has been tested with cetuximab and durvalumab; results in phase 3 have been mixed and it is not approved. The activating counterpart NKG2C defines adaptive NK cells that expand after CMV infection, including in transplant recipients.

attrs.full_name: killer cell lectin like receptor C1

items.gloss_md: Inhibitory C-type lectin receptor on NK and CD8+ T cells that binds HLA-E loaded with class I leader peptides.
items.body_md:
Type II transmembrane protein that dimerises with CD94 (*KLRD1*); its cytoplasmic ITIMs recruit SHP-1 to inhibit activation. CD94/NKG2A senses overall class I expression indirectly: HLA-E is only stabilised at the surface when loaded with leader-sequence peptides of HLA-A, -B, -C or -G, so loss of classical class I reduces HLA-E and releases NKG2A inhibition.

Expressed on early-differentiated NK cells, which acquire KIRs as they mature, and on chronically stimulated CD8+ T cells in tumours.

Encoded by *KLRC1*. Investigational target of monalizumab; NKG2A-high NK cells are 'educated' via HLA-B −21M haplotypes.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding NKG2D, the activating receptor that recognises stress ligands such as MICA, MICB and ULBPs.
items.body_md:
Killer cell lectin like receptor K1. Aliases NKG2D, CD314. Located on 12p13.2 in the NK gene complex. Despite its name it is not structurally a member of the NKG2 family that pairs with CD94.

Encodes NKG2D, expressed on all NK cells, CD8+ T cells, γδ T cells, NKT cells and some CD4+ T cells under chronic inflammation.

Clinical relevance: NKG2D–ligand interactions mediate immunosurveillance of stressed and transformed cells ('induced self'); tumours evade through ligand shedding and chronic ligand exposure. NKG2D-based CAR T cells and antibodies blocking MICA/B shedding are investigational. NKG2D ligand expression on stressed hepatocytes and cholangiocytes contributes to liver injury in experimental models and has been studied in primary sclerosing cholangitis and coeliac disease.

attrs.full_name: killer cell lectin like receptor K1

items.gloss_md: Activating homodimeric receptor on NK and CD8+ T cells that recognises stress-induced ligands (MICA, MICB, ULBP1–6) on infected or transformed cells.
items.body_md:
Type II transmembrane C-type lectin-like homodimer that signals via the adaptor DAP10 (YINM motif → PI3K and GRB2–VAV1); in mice also via DAP12. On NK cells it can trigger killing alone; on CD8+ T cells it acts as a costimulator.

Ligands: MICA and MICB (MHC-encoded) and the ULBP/RAET1 family, induced by DNA damage response, heat shock, viral infection and oncogenic signalling. Persistent soluble or tumour-bound ligands downregulate NKG2D. Cytomegalovirus encodes several proteins that retain NKG2D ligands intracellularly, a sign of the receptor's importance.

Encoded by *KLRK1*.

attrs.mnemonic: NKG2D = 'D for Danger': it detects the danger (stress) ligands MICA/B and ULBPs; NKG2A = 'A for Anti' (inhibitory).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding HLA-E, a minimally polymorphic non-classical class I molecule that presents class I leader peptides to CD94/NKG2A.
items.body_md:
Major histocompatibility complex, class I, E. Located on 6p21.3 (6p22.1) within the MHC class I region.

Encodes the heavy chain of HLA-E, a class Ib molecule with only two common protein variants (E*01:01 and E*01:03, differing at position 107) and broad but low-level expression. It presents nonamer peptides derived from the signal sequences of HLA-A, -B, -C and -G (e.g. VMAPRTLLL), thereby reporting overall class I biosynthesis to NK cells.

Clinical relevance: HLA-E is upregulated on many tumours and senescent cells, protecting them from NKG2A+ NK and CD8+ T cells; cytomegalovirus encodes UL40, whose leader peptide loads HLA-E to escape NK cells. In regenerative medicine, B2M-knockout cells engineered to express single-chain HLA-E evade both T and NK cells. HLA-E can also present pathogen peptides (e.g. from Mycobacterium tuberculosis) to non-conventional CD8+ T cells.

attrs.full_name: major histocompatibility complex, class I, E

items.gloss_md: Non-classical HLA class I molecule that presents leader peptides of other class I molecules and is the ligand of the CD94/NKG2A and CD94/NKG2C receptors.
items.body_md:
Heavy chain plus β2-microglobulin with a groove adapted to the conserved leader nonamers of classical class I; surface expression depends on availability of these peptides and on TAP function.

Recognition: CD94/NKG2A (inhibitory, high affinity) and CD94/NKG2C (activating, lower affinity); peptide sequence modulates the balance. CMV's UL40 peptide mimics the HLA-C leader, promoting expansion of NKG2C+ adaptive NK cells.

Encoded by *HLA-E* and *B2M*. Low polymorphism makes HLA-E an attractive universal 'don't kill me' signal for engineered allogeneic cell products and a target of NKG2A checkpoint blockade.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding serum albumin, the most abundant plasma protein and a classic marker of hepatic synthetic function.
items.body_md:
Albumin, located on 4q13.3 in the albumin gene family cluster with *AFP*, *AFM* (afamin) and *GC* (vitamin D-binding protein), which arose by gene duplication.

Encodes pre-pro-albumin, expressed almost exclusively by hepatocytes (about 10–15 g per day). Transcription is driven by liver-enriched factors (HNF1α, HNF4α, C/EBP) and falls during the acute-phase response (IL-6, TNF), making albumin a negative acute-phase protein.

Disease relevance: congenital analbuminaemia (biallelic loss) is rare and surprisingly mild; familial dysalbuminaemic hyperthyroxinaemia is caused by variants increasing thyroxine binding, which yields falsely high free T4 in some assays.

Clinical relevance: serum albumin is part of the Child-Pugh and ALBI scores; the ALB promoter/enhancer is widely used to drive hepatocyte-specific transgene expression (Alb-Cre mice), and highly expressed ALB transcripts are a frequent ambient-RNA contaminant in liver single-cell/nucleus RNA-seq.

attrs.mnemonic: Albumin's half-life is about 3 weeks, so it reflects chronic liver failure; acute failure shows first in the INR (factor VII half-life about 6 hours).

items.gloss_md: Most abundant plasma protein, made by hepatocytes, maintaining oncotic pressure and transporting many ligands; low levels indicate impaired liver synthesis, inflammation or loss.
items.body_md:
Non-glycosylated 66.5 kDa protein of three homologous domains with multiple binding sites (Sudlow sites I and II) for bilirubin, fatty acids, hormones, metals and drugs. Normal serum level about 35–50 g/L; half-life about 3 weeks, so it reflects chronic rather than acute liver dysfunction. It provides about 75 % of plasma oncotic pressure and has antioxidant and endothelial-stabilising functions. FcRn recycling explains its long half-life.

Causes of hypoalbuminaemia: cirrhosis, inflammation, malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, burns, dilution.

Clinical use in hepatology: Child-Pugh and ALBI scores; intravenous albumin after large-volume paracentesis (6–8 g per litre removed when >5 L), in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3) and with terlipressin in hepatorenal syndrome–AKI; long-term albumin in decompensated cirrhosis improved survival in the Italian ANSWER trial. In cirrhosis, albumin is also functionally damaged (oxidised), so quality matters, not only quantity.

Encoded by *ALB*.

attrs.mnemonic: Albumin in SBP: '1.5 on day 1, 1 on day 3' (g/kg).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding α-fetoprotein, the fetal serum protein re-expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk-sac tumours.
items.body_md:
Alpha fetoprotein, located on 4q13.3 next to *ALB*, with which it shares a three-domain structure.

Encodes AFP, the dominant serum protein of the fetus, produced by the yolk sac and fetal liver; expression is switched off after birth (partly by the transcriptional repressors ZHX2 and ZBTB20) and reactivated in hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatoblastoma, yolk-sac (endodermal sinus) tumours, during liver regeneration and in some gastric cancers (hepatoid adenocarcinoma).

Hereditary persistence of AFP is a benign condition with high AFP due to promoter variants (HNF1-binding site).

Clinical relevance: serum AFP is the classic HCC tumour marker (see AFP protein), a germ-cell tumour marker (with β-hCG and LDH; elevated AFP excludes pure seminoma), and maternal serum AFP screens for open neural tube defects and is part of second-trimester screening.

attrs.anecdote: Garri Abelev in Moscow showed in 1963 that mouse hepatomas secrete the fetal protein, and Yuri Tatarinov found it in the blood of patients with liver cancer in 1964 – the start of AFP as the first oncofetal tumour marker.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding C-reactive protein, the hepatic acute-phase pentraxin used everywhere as an inflammation marker.
items.body_md:
C-reactive protein, located on 1q23.2 near the serum amyloid P component gene *APCS*, its pentraxin relative.

Encodes CRP, produced by hepatocytes; transcription is induced mainly by IL-6 (via STAT3 and C/EBPβ), enhanced by IL-1β. Serum levels can rise more than 1000-fold within 24–48 h of an inflammatory stimulus.

Genetics: common variants in CRP and in genes of the IL-6 pathway (e.g. *IL6R*, *HNF1A*) affect baseline CRP; Mendelian randomisation using CRP variants showed that CRP itself is not causal for coronary heart disease, whereas IL-6 receptor signalling is.

Clinical relevance: the routine marker of inflammation and infection (see CRP protein); in liver disease, hepatic production is preserved in most cirrhotic patients, so CRP stays useful, although levels may be lower in advanced liver failure.

attrs.mnemonic: CRP rises within hours, peaks at about 2 days and halves in about a day – a fast readout of IL-6.

items.gloss_md: Hepatic acute-phase pentraxin whose serum level rises rapidly with IL-6-driven inflammation; the standard laboratory marker of inflammation.
items.body_md:
Pentamer of five identical 23 kDa subunits (pentraxin). Binds phosphocholine on bacterial surfaces and damaged or apoptotic cell membranes in a Ca²⁺-dependent way, then activates the classical complement pathway via C1q and engages Fcγ receptors – an opsonin of innate immunity.

Kinetics: rises within 6–8 h, peaks at about 48 h, half-life about 19 h, so falling CRP reflects resolving inflammation. Typical values: < 5 mg/L normal; high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) 1–3 mg/L range is used for cardiovascular risk stratification.

Pitfalls: IL-6 receptor blockade (tocilizumab) and JAK inhibitors suppress CRP despite infection. In cirrhosis, CRP predicts infections and mortality and is part of the CRP/albumin ratio. Encoded by *CRP*.

attrs.mnemonic: C for the pneumococcal C-polysaccharide it reacts with; CRP is basically a readout of IL-6.
attrs.anecdote: CRP was discovered in 1930 by Tillett and Francis, who found that serum from acutely ill pneumonia patients precipitated the 'C' polysaccharide of pneumococci – hence 'C-reactive'.

items.gloss_md: Gene whose I148M variant is the strongest common genetic risk factor for steatotic liver disease (MASLD, ALD) and its progression.
items.body_md:
Patatin like phospholipase domain containing 3. Alias adiponutrin (ADPN), iPLA2ε. Located on 22q13.31.

Encodes PNPLA3, a lipid-droplet-associated triglyceride lipase / transacylase expressed in hepatocytes (induced by insulin and carbohydrate via SREBP-1c and ChREBP), hepatic stellate cells and adipose tissue.

The missense variant rs738409 C>G, p.I148M, was discovered in 2008 (Romeo, Cohen, Hobbs et al.) in a GWAS of liver fat measured by proton MR spectroscopy in the Dallas Heart Study. It increases liver fat, inflammation, fibrosis, cirrhosis and HCC risk across aetiologies (MASLD, alcohol-related liver disease, chronic hepatitis C, haemochromatosis); the risk allele is most frequent in Hispanic populations (around 50 %) and has an allele frequency of roughly 20–25 % in Europeans.

Clinical relevance: part of polygenic risk scores (with TM6SF2, MBOAT7, GCKR, HSD17B13) for liver disease; liver-targeted antisense and siRNA silencing of PNPLA3 in I148M homozygous carriers is in clinical trials.

attrs.anecdote: It was found by measuring liver fat non-invasively by MR spectroscopy in more than 2,000 Dallas residents of different ancestries; the higher Hispanic carrier frequency matched the higher fatty liver prevalence in that group.

items.gloss_md: Lipid-droplet triglyceride hydrolase whose I148M variant accumulates on droplets, blocks lipolysis and promotes fatty liver and fibrosis.
items.body_md:
481-amino-acid protein with a patatin-like domain (catalytic dyad Ser47–Asp166) related to ATGL (PNPLA2). It hydrolyses triglycerides and transfers polyunsaturated fatty acids, and in stellate cells hydrolyses retinyl palmitate.

Mechanism of I148M: the variant narrows the substrate-binding pocket and reduces enzymatic activity, but its main effect is gain of function: it escapes ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation, accumulates on lipid droplets and sequesters CGI-58 (ABHD5), the co-activator of ATGL, thereby inhibiting triglyceride mobilisation. In stellate cells it impairs retinol release and promotes fibrogenesis.

Encoded by *PNPLA3*. Its expression is nutritionally regulated (high with carbohydrate feeding via SREBP-1c), explaining strong gene–diet interaction: carriers with obesity or high sugar intake show the largest effect.

attrs.mnemonic: I148M: the variant protein should be degraded, but it sticks to the lipid droplet and blocks the fat-burning lipase ATGL.

items.gloss_md: Gene whose E167K loss-of-function variant raises liver fat and MASLD risk but lowers plasma lipids and cardiovascular risk.
items.body_md:
Transmembrane 6 superfamily member 2, located on 19p13.11.

Encodes TM6SF2, a multi-pass ER/ERGIC membrane protein of hepatocytes and enterocytes required for lipidation of VLDL particles (it partners with APOB and helps load triglyceride and polyunsaturated phospholipids).

The variant rs58542926 C>T, p.E167K (about 7 % allele frequency in Europeans), was identified in 2014 by an exome-wide association study of hepatic fat (Kozlitina et al.). It causes protein misfolding and degradation, reducing VLDL secretion: liver fat, MASH and fibrosis rise, while LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and coronary risk fall.

Clinical relevance: a textbook example of the 'catch-22' between liver and heart risk; included in polygenic risk scores for MASLD and HCC.

attrs.mnemonic: TM6SF2 E167K: fat stays in the liver instead of the arteries – 'bad for the liver, good for the heart'.

items.gloss_md: ER membrane protein needed to load VLDL particles with lipids; its loss traps triglycerides in hepatocytes.
items.body_md:
Hydrophobic protein with about ten transmembrane helices located in the endoplasmic reticulum and ER–Golgi intermediate compartment of hepatocytes and enterocytes, with a sterol-sensing-like domain.

Function: supports the lipidation of nascent APOB-100 (with MTTP) and enrichment of membranes with polyunsaturated phosphatidylcholines; loss of function produces small, lipid-poor VLDL particles and hepatic triglyceride accumulation, while plasma lipids decrease.

Encoded by *TM6SF2*. The E167K variant protein is misfolded and degraded, effectively a loss-of-function allele.

Because E167K carriers have more liver fat but lower plasma lipids, the variant shows that hepatic steatosis and cardiovascular risk can diverge; this matters when interpreting MASLD as a cardiometabolic risk marker.

items.gloss_md: Gene whose loss-of-function splice variant protects against progression of fatty liver to MASH, cirrhosis and HCC; an RNAi drug target.
items.body_md:
Hydroxysteroid 17-beta dehydrogenase 13, located on 4q22.1. Also called SCDR9.

Encodes a hepatocyte-specific lipid-droplet enzyme of the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase family with retinol dehydrogenase activity.

The splice variant rs72613567:TA (insertion of an adenine adjacent to the exon 6 donor site) produces a truncated, unstable, inactive protein. In 2018 Abul-Husn et al. (Regeneron Genetics Center, DiscovEHR cohort) showed that it reduces the risk of alcohol-related and non-alcoholic liver disease, cirrhosis and HCC in a dose-dependent manner, and mitigates the effect of PNPLA3 I148M. It does not reduce steatosis itself but reduces inflammation and fibrosis.

Clinical relevance: a 'protective human knockout' that made HSD17B13 a drug target; siRNAs (e.g. rapirosiran, GSK4532990) and small molecules are in clinical trials for MASH and alcohol-related liver disease.

attrs.mnemonic: The 'good' fatty liver gene: PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 variants hurt, the HSD17B13 truncation protects – a natural knockout turned drug target.

items.gloss_md: Hepatocyte lipid-droplet dehydrogenase whose genetic loss protects against MASH and fibrosis.
items.body_md:
Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase anchored to lipid droplets by an N-terminal hydrophobic segment; it uses NAD⁺ and has retinol dehydrogenase activity in vitro (retinol → retinal); other substrates (steroids, bioactive lipids, leukotriene B4) have been proposed. Expression rises in human MASLD.

The protective truncated variant lacks enzymatic activity; carriers show lower pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic gene expression and altered hepatic phospholipids, possibly via pyrimidine catabolism effects.

Encoded by *HSD17B13*. Its physiological substrate in vivo remains uncertain, which is notable for a protein with drugs already in clinical testing.

items.gloss_md: Gene whose reduced-expression variant (rs641738) increases risk of fatty liver disease and fibrosis by altering phosphatidylinositol remodelling.
items.body_md:
Membrane bound O-acyltransferase domain containing 7. Aliases LPIAT1, BB1, LENG4. Located on 19q13.42 in the leukocyte receptor complex region, next to *TMC4*.

Encodes an ER enzyme that incorporates arachidonic acid into lysophosphatidylinositol (Lands' cycle remodelling).

The variant rs641738 C>T (in the 3' region of *TMC4*, about 40 % allele frequency in Europeans) lowers hepatic MBOAT7 expression and was identified in 2015 as a risk locus for alcohol-related cirrhosis (Buch et al., a German-led GWAS that also confirmed PNPLA3 and TM6SF2); it was later linked to MASLD, inflammation, fibrosis and HCC. Hyperinsulinaemia also downregulates MBOAT7, so the pathway may be affected beyond genotype.

Clinical relevance: part of MASLD polygenic risk scores; biallelic loss-of-function mutations cause intellectual disability with epilepsy, showing its importance in brain phosphoinositide metabolism.

items.gloss_md: ER acyltransferase that adds arachidonic acid to lysophosphatidylinositol; reduced activity promotes hepatic fat and fibrosis.
items.body_md:
Multi-pass membrane protein of the membrane-bound O-acyltransferase family with an invariant catalytic histidine. It re-acylates lysophosphatidylinositol with arachidonoyl-CoA, producing the arachidonic-acid-rich phosphatidylinositol species that dominate cell membranes.

Reduced MBOAT7 activity raises lysophosphatidylinositol and saturated phosphatidylinositol, which in experimental models activates triglyceride synthesis (via phosphatidylinositol turnover and SREBP-1c-independent pathways) and inflammation in hepatocytes and Kupffer cells.

Encoded by *MBOAT7*; also expressed in neutrophils, where it regulates arachidonic acid availability for eicosanoids.

Effects of the MBOAT7 risk variant are strongest in people with obesity and are additive with PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 variants in polygenic risk scores for liver disease.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the glucokinase regulatory protein; its P446L variant increases hepatic lipogenesis, triglycerides and liver fat.
items.body_md:
Glucokinase regulator, located on 2p23.3.

Encodes glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP), which binds and sequesters glucokinase in the hepatocyte nucleus during fasting.

The common missense variant rs1260326 C>T, p.P446L (about 40 % allele frequency in Europeans), weakens fructose-6-phosphate-dependent inhibition of glucokinase; carriers have more hepatic glucose uptake and glycolysis, providing substrate for de novo lipogenesis. Result: lower fasting glucose and insulin and less type 2 diabetes risk, but higher triglycerides, liver fat and MASLD/fibrosis risk – one of the most pleiotropic loci in GWAS (also linked to CRP, uric acid, kidney function).

Clinical relevance: part of MASLD polygenic risk scores; earlier glucokinase activators raised triglycerides in diabetes trials, consistent with the GCKR biology.

items.gloss_md: Hepatocyte protein that binds and inhibits glucokinase in the nucleus during fasting and releases it after meals.
items.body_md:
About 68 kDa protein with two sugar isomerase (SIS) domains. Fructose-6-phosphate strengthens and fructose-1-phosphate (from dietary fructose) weakens its binding to glucokinase; high glucose also promotes release. Released glucokinase moves to the cytosol and phosphorylates glucose, driving glycogen synthesis and glycolysis.

The P446L variant protein binds fructose-6-phosphate less well, so more glucokinase is active in the fasting state, increasing malonyl-CoA and de novo lipogenesis.

Encoded by *GCKR*. Explains the dual effect of the variant: better glucose control, but more triglycerides and liver fat.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding apolipoprotein B, the structural protein of chylomicrons, VLDL and LDL, edited into ApoB-100 and ApoB-48.
items.body_md:
Apolipoprotein B, located on 2p24.1.

Encodes ApoB-100 in hepatocytes and, through APOBEC1-mediated C→U mRNA editing of codon 2153 (CAA → UAA stop codon) in enterocytes, the truncated ApoB-48. It was the first described example of mammalian mRNA editing (1987).

Disease relevance: the missense variant R3527Q (familial defective apoB-100) impairs LDL receptor binding and causes familial hypercholesterolaemia; truncating mutations cause familial hypobetalipoproteinaemia with very low LDL, fat malabsorption and hepatic steatosis (a monogenic cause of fatty liver). Abetalipoproteinaemia, with absent ApoB lipoproteins, is caused by *MTTP* mutations.

Clinical relevance: the antisense drug mipomersen lowered LDL but caused hepatic steatosis and was withdrawn; ApoB concentration measures the number of atherogenic particles.

attrs.anecdote: ApoB mRNA editing (1987) was the first known case of RNA editing in mammals: a single C-to-U change in the gut turns ApoB-100 into ApoB-48 – '48' because it is 48 % of the full length.

items.gloss_md: Non-exchangeable structural protein of atherogenic lipoproteins: ApoB-100 on VLDL/IDL/LDL from the liver, ApoB-48 on intestinal chylomicrons.
items.body_md:
ApoB-100 (4536 amino acids, about 550 kDa) is one of the largest proteins; it wraps around the lipoprotein particle, one molecule per particle, and its C-terminal region contains the LDL receptor-binding domain. ApoB-48 contains the N-terminal 48 % and lacks the receptor-binding region, so chylomicron remnants are cleared via ApoE.

Assembly requires microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP) in the ER; poorly lipidated ApoB is degraded, and impaired ApoB secretion (MTTP inhibitors, ApoB antisense, TM6SF2 loss) leads to hepatic steatosis.

Encoded by *APOB*. Plasma ApoB (or non-HDL cholesterol) is considered a better marker of atherogenic risk than LDL cholesterol in hypertriglyceridaemia; lipoprotein(a) is an LDL-like particle whose ApoB is linked to apolipoprotein(a).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding apolipoprotein E, whose ε2/ε3/ε4 alleles influence lipid levels and, most strongly, Alzheimer disease risk.
items.body_md:
Apolipoprotein E, located on 19q13.32 in a cluster with *APOC1*, *APOC4* and *APOC2*.

Encodes ApoE, synthesised mainly by hepatocytes and, in the brain, by astrocytes and microglia. Three common alleles are defined by two SNPs (rs429358 and rs7412) at amino acid positions 112 and 158: ε2 (Cys/Cys), ε3 (Cys/Arg, the most common) and ε4 (Arg/Arg).

Disease relevance: ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer disease (roughly 3-fold risk in heterozygotes and about 8- to 12-fold in homozygotes) and increases LDL cholesterol and coronary risk; ε2/ε2 homozygosity with a second hit causes dysbetalipoproteinaemia (type III hyperlipoproteinaemia, palmar xanthomas); ε2 is protective for Alzheimer disease.

Clinical relevance: APOE genotyping is recommended before anti-amyloid antibody therapy (lecanemab, donanemab) because ε4 homozygotes have the highest risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA).

attrs.mnemonic: ApoE4 = 'for' Alzheimer; ApoE2 = 'too' many remnants (type III dyslipidaemia).

items.gloss_md: Exchangeable apolipoprotein that mediates hepatic uptake of chylomicron and VLDL remnants via LDL receptor and LRP1; key lipid carrier in the brain.
items.body_md:
299-amino-acid protein with an N-terminal receptor-binding domain (residues 136–150) and a C-terminal lipid-binding domain. Present on chylomicron remnants, VLDL, IDL and some HDL; ligand for the LDL receptor, LRP1 and heparan sulfate proteoglycans.

Isoform effects: ApoE2 binds the LDL receptor poorly (less than 2 % of ApoE3), so remnants accumulate; ApoE4 has a domain interaction (Arg112 → Arg61–Glu255 salt bridge) that favours VLDL binding and is less efficient in amyloid-β clearance and lipid transport in the brain.

Encoded by *APOE*. In liver disease, ApoE deficiency is a model for atherosclerosis (ApoE−/− mice); the ε4 allele has been reported to be protective against MASLD/ALD in some genetic studies.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding thyroid hormone receptor β, the liver-predominant receptor targeted by resmetirom for MASH.
items.body_md:
Thyroid hormone receptor beta. Previous names NR1A2, ERBA2, THR1. Located on 3p24.2.

Encodes THR-β (isoforms β1 and β2), a nuclear receptor that binds T3 and, as a heterodimer with RXR, regulates transcription. THR-β is the predominant thyroid hormone receptor in liver (where it increases fatty acid β-oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, LDL receptor expression and cholesterol conversion to bile acids), whereas THR-α (*THRA*) predominates in heart and bone. THR-β2 mediates T3 feedback in the pituitary and hypothalamus.

Disease relevance: heterozygous dominant-negative THRB mutations cause resistance to thyroid hormone β (RTHβ): high free T4/T3 with non-suppressed TSH, goitre, tachycardia.

Clinical relevance: resmetirom (Rezdiffra), an oral liver-directed THR-β-selective agonist, was the first drug approved for MASH (FDA accelerated approval March 2024, for non-cirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis F2–F3, based on the MAESTRO-NASH trial).

attrs.mnemonic: THR-α rules the heart, THR-β the liver: resmetirom is β-selective, so it burns liver fat without racing the heart.

items.gloss_md: Nuclear receptor for T3 that is dominant in the liver; its selective activation by resmetirom reduces liver fat and fibrosis in MASH.
items.body_md:
Nuclear receptor with a DNA-binding zinc-finger domain and a ligand-binding domain; it binds thyroid hormone response elements as a heterodimer with RXR. Without ligand it recruits corepressors (NCoR, SMRT); T3 binding switches to coactivators.

Hepatic actions: increased fatty acid oxidation and mitophagy, lipophagy, reduced de novo lipogenesis, increased LDL receptor and CYP7A1 expression, lowering LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and lipoprotein(a).

Drug: resmetirom (MGL-3196) is about 28-fold selective for THR-β over THR-α and is taken up mainly by the liver (via OATP1B1), limiting cardiac and bone effects; in MAESTRO-NASH it improved MASH resolution and fibrosis by at least one stage versus placebo. Encoded by *THRB*.

attrs.mnemonic: THR-α rules the heart, THR-β the liver: resmetirom is β-selective, so it burns liver fat without racing the heart.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the GLP-1 receptor, the target of semaglutide, liraglutide and tirzepatide (diabetes, obesity, MASH).
items.body_md:
Glucagon like peptide 1 receptor, located on 6p21.2.

Encodes GLP-1R, a class B G-protein-coupled receptor expressed in pancreatic β cells, the brain (hypothalamus, brainstem – appetite and nausea), stomach (delayed emptying), heart, kidney and some immune cells; hepatocytes express little or no GLP-1R, so liver benefits in MASLD are largely indirect (weight loss, insulin sensitivity).

Clinical relevance: GLP-1 receptor agonists (exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide) and the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide treat type 2 diabetes and obesity and reduce cardiovascular events. Semaglutide 2.4 mg improved MASH resolution and fibrosis in the ESSENCE trial and received FDA accelerated approval for MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis in 2025. Side effects: nausea, vomiting, gallstones, rarely pancreatitis.

attrs.anecdote: Exenatide, the first GLP-1 receptor agonist (2005), is a synthetic version of exendin-4 from the saliva of the Gila monster, discovered by John Eng in 1992.

items.gloss_md: Class B GPCR for glucagon-like peptide 1 that enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion and satiety; target of semaglutide and related drugs.
items.body_md:
Seven-transmembrane receptor with a large N-terminal extracellular domain that captures the C-terminal helix of GLP-1; couples mainly to Gαs → cAMP → PKA/EPAC2, augmenting insulin exocytosis only when glucose is elevated, hence low hypoglycaemia risk. Also recruits β-arrestins, leading to internalisation.

Physiological effects: insulin secretion, glucagon suppression, slowed gastric emptying, central satiety, β-cell protection in rodents.

Drugs: peptide agonists resistant to DPP-4 and with extended half-life (liraglutide via fatty-acid albumin binding, semaglutide once weekly or oral); multi-agonists (tirzepatide GIP/GLP-1, retatrutide GIP/GLP-1/glucagon, survodutide glucagon/GLP-1) are being tested in MASH; small-molecule oral agonists (orforglipron) exist. Encoded by *GLP1R*.

attrs.anecdote: The first GLP-1 drug, exenatide, is a synthetic copy of exendin-4, a peptide found in 1992 by John Eng in the venom (saliva) of the Gila monster – a lizard that eats only a few times a year.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding FGF21, a liver-derived stress and fasting hormone whose analogues are in late-stage trials for MASH.
items.body_md:
Fibroblast growth factor 21, located on 19q13.33.

Encodes FGF21, an endocrine FGF (with FGF19 and FGF23) secreted mainly by the liver, induced by fasting and ketogenic diets (PPARα), protein restriction (ATF4), carbohydrate and fructose intake (ChREBP), alcohol and mitochondrial stress.

Genetics: common FGF21 variants are associated with higher sugar and alcohol intake preference.

Clinical relevance: serum FGF21 is high in obesity, MASLD and mitochondrial myopathies (suggesting FGF21 resistance). Long-acting FGF21 analogues (efruxifermin, pegozafermin) reduced liver fat and improved MASH and fibrosis in phase 2 trials, with signals of fibrosis regression even in compensated cirrhosis, and are in phase 3.

items.gloss_md: Endocrine fibroblast growth factor from the liver that improves insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism and reduces sweet and alcohol preference.
items.body_md:
Hormone of about 20 kDa that lacks the heparin-binding affinity of paracrine FGFs and signals through FGF receptors (mainly FGFR1c) only in the presence of the co-receptor β-Klotho (*KLB*), restricting action to adipose tissue, liver, pancreas and the brain (hypothalamus, hindbrain). Inactivated by fibroblast activation protein (FAP) cleavage.

Effects: increased insulin sensitivity, adiponectin release, thermogenesis and fatty acid oxidation, reduced hepatic lipogenesis and fibrogenic signalling, central suppression of sweet and alcohol intake.

Drugs: efruxifermin (Fc fusion), pegozafermin (glycopegylated) and others for MASH and severe hypertriglyceridaemia; adverse effects include gastrointestinal symptoms and possible effects on bone. Encoded by *FGF21*.

attrs.mnemonic: FGF21 is the 'fasting' FGF: the liver sends it when you fast, feast on sugar or drink alcohol.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding PPARα, the fasting-activated nuclear receptor for fatty acid oxidation and target of fibrates.
items.body_md:
Peroxisome proliferator activated receptor alpha. Alias NR1C1. Located on 22q13.31.

Encodes PPARα, highly expressed in liver, heart, kidney and brown fat. It is activated by fatty acids and fatty-acid-derived ligands during fasting and induces genes for mitochondrial and peroxisomal β-oxidation, ketogenesis, FGF21 and lipoprotein lipase activation (reducing APOC3).

History: named after the observation that certain chemicals cause peroxisome proliferation and liver tumours in rodents; this effect does not occur in humans.

Clinical relevance: fibrates (fenofibrate, bezafibrate, pemafibrate) are PPARα agonists lowering triglycerides; bezafibrate improves pruritus and biochemistry in primary biliary cholangitis. Dual and pan agonists – elafibranor (PPARα/δ, approved for PBC in 2024) and lanifibranor (pan-PPAR, phase 3 in MASH) – target it too.

items.gloss_md: Fatty-acid-sensing nuclear receptor that switches on hepatic fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis during fasting; activated by fibrates.
items.body_md:
Ligand-activated transcription factor of the nuclear receptor superfamily that heterodimerises with RXR and binds peroxisome proliferator response elements (PPREs, DR1 motifs). Endogenous ligands include fatty acids, oxidised phospholipids and eicosanoids; synthetic ligands are fibrates.

Targets: CPT1A, ACOX1, ACADM, HMGCS2 (ketogenesis), FGF21, ANGPTL4, PDK4; it also represses inflammatory NF-κB and AP-1 signalling. Reduced hepatic PPARα activity correlates with MASH severity in human biopsies.

Encoded by *PPARA*. Drugs: fenofibrate, bezafibrate, pemafibrate (selective), elafibranor and lanifibranor (multi-PPAR).

In rodents, chronic PPARα activation causes peroxisome proliferation and liver tumours; this does not occur in humans, owing to lower hepatic receptor expression and species differences in target genes.

attrs.mnemonic: PPAR-α = 'Alpha burns' (fatty acid oxidation in liver); PPAR-γ = 'Gamma stores' (adipocytes); PPAR-δ = 'Delta does both, in muscle and bile'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding PPARγ, the master regulator of adipogenesis and target of the thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone).
items.body_md:
Peroxisome proliferator activated receptor gamma. Alias NR1C3. Located on 3p25.2.

Encodes PPARγ, with isoforms γ1 (broadly expressed, including macrophages and colon) and γ2 (adipose-specific, alternative promoter). PPARγ is necessary and sufficient for adipocyte differentiation and lipid storage, and promotes alternatively activated macrophages; in hepatic stellate cells it maintains quiescence.

Genetics: the common Pro12Ala variant reduces type 2 diabetes risk; dominant-negative loss-of-function mutations cause familial partial lipodystrophy type 3 with severe insulin resistance and fatty liver.

Clinical relevance: thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) are PPARγ agonists; pioglitazone improves MASH histology and is recommended by some guidelines for MASH with type 2 diabetes. Side effects: weight gain, fluid retention, heart failure, bone fractures. Lanifibranor is a pan-PPAR agonist in MASH phase 3. PPARG fusions (PAX8–PPARG) occur in follicular thyroid carcinoma.

items.gloss_md: Nuclear receptor that drives adipocyte differentiation and insulin sensitivity; activated by pioglitazone.
items.body_md:
Ligand-activated transcription factor that heterodimerises with RXR on PPREs. Ligands: polyunsaturated fatty acids and their oxidised derivatives (e.g. 15-deoxy-Δ12,14-prostaglandin J2), and synthetic thiazolidinediones.

Effects: adipogenesis (with C/EBPα), safe storage of lipids in subcutaneous fat (reducing ectopic fat in liver and muscle), adiponectin induction, anti-inflammatory macrophage programme, maintenance of quiescent stellate cells.

Encoded by *PPARG*. Drugs: pioglitazone (used off-label for MASH, particularly with diabetes), rosiglitazone (restricted use), lanifibranor (pan-PPAR). Cdk5 phosphorylation at Ser273 is linked to insulin resistance, a target of non-agonist PPARγ ligands.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding PPARδ, the nuclear receptor targeted by seladelpar and elafibranor in primary biliary cholangitis.
items.body_md:
Peroxisome proliferator activated receptor delta. Aliases PPARβ, NR1C2, NUC1. Located on 6p21.31.

Encodes PPARδ (also called PPARβ), expressed ubiquitously, highly in skeletal muscle, liver, macrophages and cholangiocytes. It promotes fatty acid oxidation, oxidative muscle fibres and anti-inflammatory macrophage polarisation, and in the liver reduces bile acid synthesis (via FGF21 and CYP7A1 repression).

Clinical relevance: seladelpar (selective PPARδ agonist, Livdelzi) and elafibranor (PPARα/δ, Iqirvo) received accelerated approval in 2024 as second-line therapy for primary biliary cholangitis with insufficient response to ursodeoxycholic acid; both also reduce pruritus (seladelpar more consistently).

items.gloss_md: Nuclear receptor regulating fatty acid oxidation and inflammation; agonists (seladelpar, elafibranor) treat primary biliary cholangitis.
items.body_md:
PPAR family transcription factor (also called PPARβ) acting with RXR on PPREs; activated by fatty acids and synthetic agonists. Targets include CPT1, PDK4 and ANGPTL4; it shifts muscle towards oxidative metabolism and raises HDL cholesterol.

In cholestatic liver disease, PPARδ activation lowers bile acid synthesis, reduces cholangiocyte and macrophage inflammation and decreases alkaline phosphatase in PBC.

Encoded by *PPARD*. Drugs: seladelpar and elafibranor (PBC).

Both PBC drugs are given in addition to ursodeoxycholic acid (or alone if it is not tolerated). Typical adverse effects are abdominal discomfort and nausea; elafibranor can raise creatine kinase.

attrs.anecdote: The PPARδ agonist GW501516 ('cardarine') was dropped in 2007 after it caused cancers in rodents, yet it is still sold illicitly as an endurance doping agent and is on the WADA prohibited list.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding FXR, the bile-acid-sensing nuclear receptor targeted by obeticholic acid.
items.body_md:
