Nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group H member 4. Alias FXR (farnesoid X receptor), BAR, HRR1. Located on 12q23.1.

Encodes FXR, highly expressed in liver, intestine, kidney and adrenal. It was named after weak activation by farnesol; bile acids (chenodeoxycholic acid most potent) turned out to be its physiological ligands in 1999.

Function: master regulator of bile acid homeostasis – it suppresses bile acid synthesis (hepatic SHP induction; intestinal FGF19 release acting on FGFR4/β-Klotho in hepatocytes) and promotes bile acid export (BSEP, OSTα/β), and influences lipid and glucose metabolism and intestinal barrier function.

Disease relevance: biallelic loss-of-function mutations cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 5 (PFIC5) with neonatal cholestasis and coagulopathy.

Clinical relevance: obeticholic acid (Ocaliva), a semisynthetic FXR agonist, received conditional approval as second-line PBC therapy (2016), but the EU authorisation was revoked in 2024 after the confirmatory trial; it was not approved for MASH (pruritus, LDL increase, hepatic decompensation risk in advanced cirrhosis). Non-steroidal FXR agonists are in development.

attrs.full_name: nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group H member 4

items.gloss_md: Nuclear bile acid receptor that limits bile acid synthesis and promotes their export; activated by obeticholic acid.
items.body_md:
Ligand-activated transcription factor that binds IR-1 elements as a heterodimer with RXRα. Ligands: CDCA > deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid > cholic acid; synthetic: obeticholic acid (6α-ethyl-CDCA, about 100-fold more potent than CDCA), cilofexor, tropifexor.

Hepatocyte: induces SHP (represses CYP7A1 and CYP8B1), BSEP (*ABCB11*), MDR3 (*ABCB4*) and OSTα/β. Enterocyte: induces FGF19 (FGF15 in mice), which travels in portal blood to repress CYP7A1 – the gut–liver bile acid feedback loop.

Encoded by *NR1H4*. Obeticholic acid side effects: dose-dependent pruritus and LDL increase; severe liver injury in patients with decompensated cirrhosis led to restrictions.

attrs.mnemonic: FXR = 'Fix X-cess bile': too much bile acid → FXR shuts down CYP7A1 (synthesis) and opens BSEP (export).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding SREBP-1, the insulin-activated transcription factor that drives hepatic de novo lipogenesis.
items.body_md:
Sterol regulatory element binding transcription factor 1. Alias SREBP1, bHLHd1. Located on 17p11.2 (within the Smith–Magenis syndrome region).

Encodes SREBP-1a and SREBP-1c from alternative promoters/first exons. SREBP-1c is the dominant liver isoform, induced by insulin (via mTORC1 and LXR), and activates genes of fatty acid synthesis (ACLY, ACACA, FASN, SCD1, ELOVL6). The paralogue *SREBF2* controls cholesterol synthesis and LDL receptor expression.

Discovery: SREBPs were cloned in 1993 by the laboratory of Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein, who had won the 1985 Nobel Prize for the LDL receptor.

Clinical relevance: in insulin-resistant states, hepatic SREBP-1c stays active (selective insulin resistance: glucose production is not suppressed, but lipogenesis is still stimulated), a central mechanism of MASLD; de novo lipogenesis inhibitors (ACC inhibitor firsocostat, FASN inhibitor denifanstat) target its output.

attrs.full_name: sterol regulatory element binding transcription factor 1

items.gloss_md: Membrane-bound transcription factor activated by insulin that switches on hepatic fatty acid synthesis.
items.body_md:
bHLH-leucine zipper transcription factor synthesised as an ER membrane precursor bound to SCAP; INSIG proteins retain the complex in the ER. Upon activation, COPII vesicles carry SCAP–SREBP to the Golgi, where site-1 and site-2 proteases (S1P, S2P) release the N-terminal nuclear form, which binds sterol regulatory elements and E-boxes.

SREBP-1c is regulated mainly by insulin (transcriptional induction through LXR, mTORC1-dependent processing, reduced INSIG2a), whereas SREBP-2 responds to cellular cholesterol. Targets: ACLY, ACC1, FASN, SCD1, GPAM, ELOVL6.

Encoded by *SREBF1*. Hepatic SREBP-1c activity and de novo lipogenesis are increased in MASLD and are suppressed by THR-β and FXR agonists and by ChREBP inhibition in experiments.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding leptin, the adipocyte hormone signalling energy stores to the brain.
items.body_md:
Leptin, previous symbol OB (obese). Located on 7q32.1.

Encodes leptin, secreted mainly by white adipocytes in proportion to fat mass. Its receptor (*LEPR*) long isoform signals via JAK2–STAT3 in hypothalamic neurons (POMC/AgRP), reducing appetite and permitting energy-costly functions (reproduction, immunity).

Discovery: the obese (ob/ob) mouse arose spontaneously at the Jackson Laboratory in 1949–1950; Jeffrey Friedman's group cloned the gene in 1994.

Disease relevance: congenital leptin deficiency causes severe early-onset obesity, hyperphagia and hypogonadism and responds dramatically to recombinant leptin; common obesity is characterised by high leptin and leptin resistance.

Clinical relevance: metreleptin is approved for generalised lipodystrophy and markedly reduces hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridaemia there; leptin promotes hepatic stellate cell activation and fibrogenesis in experimental models.

attrs.anecdote: Friedman cloned the obese gene in 1994 after an eight-year hunt; daily leptin injections made the massively obese ob/ob mice lose about 30 % of their weight in two weeks.

items.gloss_md: Adipocyte hormone that signals long-term energy stores to the hypothalamus, suppressing appetite; high in obesity due to leptin resistance.
items.body_md:
16 kDa four-helix-bundle cytokine-like hormone (class I cytokine family). Its receptor LEPR (Ob-R) signals through JAK2 → STAT3, also STAT5, PI3K and SHP2–ERK; SOCS3 and PTP1B terminate signalling and are implicated in leptin resistance.

Physiology: serum levels correlate with fat mass and fall rapidly with fasting, triggering hunger, reduced thyroid and reproductive axes and immune suppression ('starvation signal'). Leptin also acts on T cells (Th1 promotion) and is pro-fibrogenic in the liver.

Encoded by *LEP*. Drug: metreleptin (lipodystrophy). In MASLD, high leptin and low adiponectin (high leptin:adiponectin ratio) reflect adipose tissue dysfunction.

attrs.mnemonic: Greek 'leptos' = thin: leptin tells the brain 'enough fat stored, stop eating'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding adiponectin, an insulin-sensitising, anti-inflammatory adipokine that is low in obesity and MASLD.
items.body_md:
Adiponectin, C1Q and collagen domain containing. Aliases ACRP30, apM1, GBP28, ACDC. Located on 3q27.3.

Encodes adiponectin, secreted abundantly by adipocytes (one of the most abundant plasma proteins among hormones, µg/mL range). It was described independently by four groups in 1995–1996, explaining its many names.

Disease relevance: plasma adiponectin is inversely correlated with visceral fat, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and MASLD severity; PPARγ agonists raise it. Paradoxically it is elevated in cirrhosis (reduced clearance and altered production) and in heart failure. Common ADIPOQ variants influence circulating levels.

Clinical relevance: a biomarker in metabolic research (leptin:adiponectin ratio); adiponectin receptor agonists (e.g. AdipoRon) are experimental.

attrs.full_name: adiponectin, C1Q and collagen domain containing

items.gloss_md: Adipocyte-derived hormone that improves insulin sensitivity and fatty acid oxidation; low levels mark visceral obesity and MASLD.
items.body_md:
30 kDa protein with a collagen-like domain and a C-terminal globular C1q-like domain, circulating as trimers, hexamers and high-molecular-weight multimers (the most active form).

Receptors AdipoR1 (muscle, ubiquitous) and AdipoR2 (liver) – seven-transmembrane proteins with ceramidase activity, unrelated to GPCRs – activate AMPK and PPARα, increasing fatty acid oxidation and glucose uptake and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis and lipogenesis; T-cadherin binds the multimers in vascular and cardiac tissue.

Encoded by *ADIPOQ*. Anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects on Kupffer cells and stellate cells were shown in experimental liver disease.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the α1 chain of type I collagen, the main collagen of bone, skin and fibrotic scar tissue.
items.body_md:
Collagen type I alpha 1 chain, located on 17q21.33; the partner chain is encoded by *COL1A2* (7q21.3).

Encodes pro-α1(I) chains; type I collagen is a heterotrimer of two α1(I) and one α2(I) chain. In the liver it is produced mainly by activated hepatic stellate cells / myofibroblasts and portal fibroblasts; TGF-β1 is the strongest inducer. COL1A1 expression is a standard readout of fibrogenesis in cell culture, mouse models (Col1a1-GFP reporter mice) and single-cell data.

Disease relevance: mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 cause most cases of osteogenesis imperfecta (glycine substitutions in the Gly-X-Y repeat are typical) and some forms of Ehlers–Danlos syndrome. The COL1A1–PDGFB fusion from t(17;22) drives dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, treatable with imatinib.

attrs.mnemonic: Collagen types: type I = bONE (and scar), type II = carTWOlage, type III = reticulin (early fibrosis, vessels), type IV = under the fLOOR (basement membrane).

items.gloss_md: Fibrillar collagen of two α1 and one α2 chain; the dominant matrix protein of fibrotic liver scar, bone, skin and tendon.
items.body_md:
Triple-helical molecule (about 300 nm long) built from Gly-X-Y repeats, rich in proline and hydroxyproline. Synthesis requires prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases (vitamin C dependent), secretion as procollagen, cleavage of N- and C-propeptides (released PINP and PICP serve as markers of synthesis), and fibril cross-linking by lysyl oxidase (LOX/LOXL2), which makes scars resistant to degradation.

In liver fibrosis, collagen I and III accumulate in the space of Disse and fibrous septa; quantification uses Sirius red staining, collagen proportionate area or hydroxyproline content. Degradation is performed by interstitial collagenases (MMP-1, MMP-8, MMP-13), inhibited by TIMP-1.

Encoded by *COL1A1* and *COL1A2*. Serum neo-epitope markers of collagen formation (e.g. PRO-C3 for type III) are studied as fibrosis biomarkers.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), the marker of activated hepatic stellate cells, myofibroblasts and myCAFs.
items.body_md:
Actin alpha 2, smooth muscle. Aliases α-SMA, ACTSA, AAT6. Located on 10q23.31.

Encodes α-smooth muscle actin, the actin isoform of vascular smooth muscle that is also induced in myofibroblasts (by TGF-β and mechanical stress). Quiescent hepatic stellate cells do not express it; activation into proliferative, contractile, collagen-producing myofibroblasts is defined by α-SMA expression.

Disease relevance: heterozygous ACTA2 mutations are the most common cause of familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection (TAAD); R179 mutations cause multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome.

Clinical relevance: α-SMA IHC marks activated stellate cells in liver fibrosis, myofibroblasts in wound healing and cancer-associated fibroblasts; in PDAC, myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs, α-SMA high, adjacent to tumour cells) are distinguished from inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs, IL-6 high, α-SMA low).

items.gloss_md: Contractile actin isoform of smooth muscle cells that marks activated hepatic stellate cells, myofibroblasts and myofibroblastic CAFs.
items.body_md:
42 kDa globular actin isoform differing from cytoplasmic β- and γ-actin mainly in the N-terminal residues; incorporated into stress fibres, it gives myofibroblasts their contractile force (relevant for sinusoidal constriction and portal hypertension in cirrhosis).

Induction in fibroblasts and stellate cells requires TGF-β1, the ED-A splice variant of fibronectin and mechanical tension (via MRTF–SRF and YAP/TAZ signalling).

Encoded by *ACTA2*. IHC use: activated stellate cells in liver fibrosis, myofibroblasts in kidney and lung fibrosis, CAF subtypes in PDAC, smooth muscle tumours (leiomyoma, leiomyosarcoma) and myoepithelial cells. Not fully specific: pericytes and vascular smooth muscle stain too.

attrs.mnemonic: Stellate cell wakes up = vitamin A droplets out, α-SMA in: 'from storing A to Smooth-muscle Actin'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding TIMP-1, an inhibitor of matrix metalloproteinases and part of the ELF fibrosis test.
items.body_md:
TIMP metallopeptidase inhibitor 1. Aliases EPA (erythroid potentiating activity), CLGI. Located on Xp11.3, within intron 6 of *SYN1* on the opposite strand.

Encodes TIMP-1, secreted by activated hepatic stellate cells, macrophages and many tumour cells, induced by TGF-β, IL-1 and IL-6.

Clinical relevance: TIMP-1 is one of the three components of the Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) test, together with hyaluronic acid and the N-terminal propeptide of type III procollagen (PIIINP); ELF scores of 9.8 or higher indicate advanced fibrosis and predict liver-related events. High serum TIMP-1 is associated with poor prognosis in several cancers, including colorectal and pancreatic cancer.

items.gloss_md: Tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases 1, which blocks matrix degradation and protects activated stellate cells; component of the ELF test.
items.body_md:
28 kDa glycoprotein whose N-terminal domain inserts into the active site of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-1, -3, -9 and others; weak against membrane-type MMPs), inhibiting them 1:1. Beyond protease inhibition, it signals through CD63 and integrin β1 to promote cell survival.

In liver fibrosis TIMP-1 rises early, prevents collagen degradation by interstitial collagenases and inhibits stellate cell apoptosis; falling TIMP-1 accompanies fibrosis regression in experimental models.

Encoded by *TIMP1*. ELF test interpretation (NAFLD): < 7.7 none to mild, 7.7 – < 9.8 moderate, ≥ 9.8 severe fibrosis, ≥ 11.3 cirrhosis; NICE uses 10.51 as the threshold for advanced fibrosis in NAFLD.

attrs.mnemonic: ELF test = 'HA-P-T': Hyaluronic Acid, PIIINP, TIMP-1.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding cytokeratin 18, the hepatocyte intermediate filament whose caspase-cleaved fragments are a serum marker of cell death in MASH.
items.body_md:
Keratin 18, located on 12q13.13 in the type II keratin cluster (although CK18 itself is a type I keratin, an exception explained by its placement next to *KRT8*).

Encodes CK18, which pairs with the type II keratin CK8 to form the intermediate filaments of simple (single-layer) epithelia, including hepatocytes, cholangiocytes, pancreatic acinar and ductal cells and intestinal epithelium. Adult hepatocytes express only CK8/CK18; cholangiocytes additionally CK7 and CK19.

Disease relevance: KRT8 and KRT18 variants predispose to progression of acute and chronic liver injury; CK8/18 are major components of Mallory–Denk bodies in alcohol-related and metabolic steatohepatitis.

Clinical relevance: serum CK18 fragments (M30 neoepitope = caspase-cleaved, apoptosis; M65 = total, apoptosis plus necrosis) are studied as non-invasive MASH markers; diagnostic accuracy is moderate. CK8/18 (CAM5.2) IHC is used as a broad carcinoma marker.

items.gloss_md: Type I keratin of simple epithelia, including hepatocytes; its caspase-cleaved fragment (M30) in serum reflects hepatocyte apoptosis.
items.body_md:
Intermediate filament protein that heterodimerises with CK8; the filament network protects hepatocytes against mechanical and toxic stress and anchors organelles. Phosphorylation and glycosylation regulate its dynamics.

During apoptosis caspases cleave CK18 at Asp396, creating a neoepitope recognised by the M30 antibody; the M65 assay detects total soluble CK18. Ballooned hepatocytes in steatohepatitis lose CK8/18 staining, which pathologists can use to identify ballooning more reproducibly, and CK8/18 aggregates with ubiquitin and p62 form Mallory–Denk bodies.

Encoded by *KRT18*. Clinical use: research and some diagnostic panels for MASH activity; IHC for epithelial origin (CAM5.2, often with CK8).

items.gloss_md: Gene whose C282Y homozygosity causes HFE (type 1) hereditary haemochromatosis, the most common inherited iron overload.
items.body_md:
Homeostatic iron regulator, previously 'high Fe' / HLA-H. Located on 6p22.2, telomeric of the HLA class I region; it encodes an MHC class I-like protein.

The gene was identified in 1996 (Feder et al.). The C282Y variant (rs1800562) disrupts a disulfide bond, preventing association with β2-microglobulin and surface expression. About 1 in 200 people of northern European descent is C282Y homozygous, but clinical penetrance is incomplete (iron overload markers in most, organ damage in a minority, more often in men). H63D is common and mild; C282Y/H63D compound heterozygosity rarely causes overload without cofactors (alcohol, MASLD).

Clinical relevance: suspect when transferrin saturation > 45 % with raised ferritin; confirm by HFE genotyping. Ferritin > 1000 µg/L and raised transaminases indicate risk of fibrosis/cirrhosis and warrant liver assessment. Treatment: phlebotomy (venesection) to a ferritin of about 50–100 µg/L; cirrhosis carries a high HCC risk requiring surveillance.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) Hämochromatose = 'Bronzediabetes': Leber, Pankreas, Haut (bronze), Herz, Gelenke – Therapie: Aderlass.
attrs.anecdote: C282Y descends from a single ancestral mutation in northern Europe and is so frequent in Ireland and Brittany that haemochromatosis is nicknamed the 'Celtic curse'.

items.gloss_md: MHC class I-like membrane protein that senses iron via transferrin receptors and promotes hepcidin expression in hepatocytes.
items.body_md:
Membrane glycoprotein with α1–α3 domains associated with β2-microglobulin but with a narrow groove that binds no peptide. HFE binds transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) at a site overlapping the holotransferrin binding site; when iron-loaded transferrin rises, HFE is displaced and interacts with TfR2, enhancing BMP6–SMAD signalling and hepcidin transcription.

Loss of functional HFE (C282Y protein is retained in the ER) blunts hepcidin, so intestinal iron absorption via ferroportin stays inappropriately high, and iron deposits in hepatocytes (periportal zone 1 first), pancreas, heart, joints, skin and pituitary.

Encoded by *HFE*. Other haemochromatosis genes in the same pathway: *HJV*, *HAMP* (juvenile, type 2), *TFR2* (type 3) and *SLC40A1* (ferroportin disease, type 4).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding hepcidin, the liver hormone that controls systemic iron by degrading ferroportin.
items.body_md:
Hepcidin antimicrobial peptide. Aliases HEPC, LEAP-1. Located on 19q13.12.

Encodes pre-pro-hepcidin, expressed mainly by hepatocytes. Transcription rises with iron (BMP6–BMP receptors–HJV–SMAD1/5/8–SMAD4, modulated by HFE and TfR2) and inflammation (IL-6–STAT3), and falls with erythropoietic demand (erythroferrone from erythroblasts), hypoxia and iron deficiency (matriptase-2, *TMPRSS6*).

Discovery: isolated in 2000–2001 by two groups as an antimicrobial peptide from blood ultrafiltrate (LEAP-1) and urine; its role in iron came from mouse knockouts the same year.

Disease relevance: HAMP mutations cause juvenile haemochromatosis type 2B; inadequately low hepcidin underlies all forms of hereditary haemochromatosis and iron loading in β-thalassaemia and alcohol-related liver disease; excess hepcidin causes anaemia of inflammation and iron-refractory iron deficiency anaemia (*TMPRSS6* loss).

items.gloss_md: 25-amino-acid liver peptide hormone that lowers plasma iron by binding and degrading the iron exporter ferroportin.
items.body_md:
Small hairpin peptide with four disulfide bonds, secreted by hepatocytes and cleared by the kidney (measurable in urine and serum by mass spectrometry or immunoassay).

Mechanism: binds ferroportin (*SLC40A1*) on duodenal enterocytes, macrophages (iron recycling from old erythrocytes) and hepatocytes, occludes the iron export channel and triggers its ubiquitination and degradation, so dietary iron absorption and iron release from stores fall.

Clinical relevance: low hepcidin → iron overload (haemochromatosis, ineffective erythropoiesis); high hepcidin → iron-restricted erythropoiesis and anaemia of inflammation (chronic disease, CKD), explaining poor response to oral iron. Hepcidin mimetics (e.g. rusfertide in polycythaemia vera) and hepcidin-lowering agents are in development. Encoded by *HAMP*.

attrs.mnemonic: Hep-cidin = made in the liver (hepar), born as an antimicrobial (-cidin): it kills iron export to starve microbes of iron.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the copper-transporting ATPase whose biallelic mutations cause Wilson disease.
items.body_md:
ATPase copper transporting beta. Alias WND, Wilson disease protein. Located on 13q14.3; cloned in 1993.

Encodes a P-type ATPase of hepatocytes that loads copper onto apo-ceruloplasmin and exports excess copper into bile.

Wilson disease: autosomal recessive, prevalence about 1 in 30,000 (carrier frequency about 1 in 90), with more than 900 known variants; H1069Q is the most common in Central and Eastern Europe (including Germany), R778L in East Asia. Copper accumulates in liver (from steatosis to acute liver failure and cirrhosis), brain (basal ganglia: tremor, dystonia, psychiatric symptoms), cornea (Kayser–Fleischer rings) and kidney.

Diagnosis: low serum ceruloplasmin, high 24-h urinary copper, Kayser–Fleischer rings, liver copper > 250 µg/g dry weight, Coombs-negative haemolysis, genetic testing; combined in the Leipzig score. Treatment: chelators (D-penicillamine, trientine), zinc, or liver transplantation for acute liver failure.

attrs.mnemonic: Wilson = copper in liver, brain and eye: think of it in anyone under about 40 with unexplained liver disease, haemolysis or a movement disorder.
attrs.anecdote: Samuel Alexander Kinnier Wilson described 'progressive lenticular degeneration' with liver cirrhosis in 1912; the corneal copper rings had already been described by the ophthalmologists Kayser (1902) and Fleischer (1903).

items.gloss_md: Hepatocyte copper-transporting P-type ATPase that incorporates copper into ceruloplasmin and excretes excess copper into bile.
items.body_md:
About 165 kDa membrane protein with six N-terminal metal-binding domains (each MxCxxC), eight transmembrane helices, a phosphorylation (aspartate) and nucleotide-binding domain. Copper is delivered by the chaperone ATOX1.

At low copper ATP7B resides in the trans-Golgi network and pumps copper into the secretory pathway for apo-ceruloplasmin; at high copper it traffics to vesicles near the canalicular membrane for biliary excretion. Without functional ATP7B, ceruloplasmin is secreted without copper and degraded quickly (low serum ceruloplasmin), and copper builds up in hepatocytes and then spills into blood ('free' non-ceruloplasmin-bound copper).

Encoded by *ATP7B*. The paralogue ATP7A (Menkes disease) is responsible for intestinal copper absorption.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding α1-antitrypsin; the Z allele causes alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with liver disease and emphysema.
items.body_md:
Serpin family A member 1. Aliases A1AT, AAT, PI (protease inhibitor). Located on 14q32.13.

Encodes α1-antitrypsin, produced mainly by hepatocytes. Alleles are named by isoelectric focusing mobility (Pi system): M normal, S (E264V) mildly deficient, Z (E342K, rs28929474) severely deficient; null alleles produce no protein.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: PiZZ (about 1 in 2,000–5,000 in Europeans) causes (1) liver disease by toxic gain of function – misfolded Z protein polymerises in the hepatocyte ER, leading to neonatal cholestasis, cirrhosis and HCC – and (2) early panlobular emphysema by loss of function, accelerated by smoking. Heterozygous PiMZ (about 2–4 % of Europeans) is a modifier that increases cirrhosis risk in MASLD and alcohol-related liver disease.

Clinical relevance: diagnosis by serum AAT level, phenotyping and genotyping; liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules. Intravenous augmentation therapy treats lung disease only; liver-targeted siRNA (fazirsiran) lowers Z-AAT production and is in phase 3; liver transplantation cures the deficiency.

attrs.mnemonic: Z is the end of the alphabet and the worst allele: 'M is Most normal, S is Slightly low, Z is Zero-ish'.

items.gloss_md: Main serine protease inhibitor of plasma, made by hepatocytes, which protects the lung from neutrophil elastase; deficiency causes emphysema and liver disease.
items.body_md:
52 kDa glycoprotein of the serpin family; its reactive centre loop (Met358) acts as bait for neutrophil elastase, which cleaves it and becomes covalently trapped while the serpin springs into a stable conformation ('mousetrap' mechanism). It is an acute-phase protein (normal serum about 0.9–2.0 g/L), produced also by monocytes and intestinal cells.

Z-AAT misfolds and forms loop–sheet polymers that are retained in the ER of hepatocytes (PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules), causing ER stress, autophagy and hepatocyte injury, while plasma levels fall to about 10–15 % of normal, leaving lung elastin unprotected. Smoking oxidises Met358, inactivating even residual AAT.

Encoded by *SERPINA1*. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a missing α1 band in severe deficiency.

attrs.mnemonic: Z-AAT: the liver suffers from too much (polymers stuck in the ER, toxic gain of function), the lung from too little (no elastase brake, loss of function).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding transthyretin, whose destabilising variants cause hereditary ATTR amyloidosis, historically treated by liver transplantation.
items.body_md:
Transthyretin, previously prealbumin. Located on 18q12.1.

Encodes transthyretin, made mainly by the liver (over 95 % of plasma TTR) and the choroid plexus, and the retina.

Disease relevance: more than 100 amyloidogenic point mutations destabilise the TTR tetramer, causing hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (hATTR) with polyneuropathy and/or cardiomyopathy; V30M (p.Val50Met in current numbering) is endemic in Portugal, Sweden and Japan, V122I (p.Val142Ile) is carried by about 3–4 % of African Americans and causes cardiomyopathy. Wild-type TTR forms amyloid in the elderly heart (ATTRwt cardiomyopathy).

Clinical relevance: liver transplantation removes the source of mutant TTR and was the first disease-modifying therapy (since 1990). Now: tetramer stabilisers (tafamidis, acoramidis), RNA silencers (patisiran – the first approved siRNA drug, 2018 – vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen) and in vivo CRISPR editing (nexiguran ziclumeran, NTLA-2001) in trials.

attrs.anecdote: Because an hATTR liver is otherwise healthy, explanted livers from hATTR patients were given to older recipients in 'domino liver transplantation' – they usually take decades to cause amyloidosis in the new host.

items.gloss_md: Liver-made tetrameric transport protein for thyroxine and retinol-binding protein; misfolded monomers form ATTR amyloid.
items.body_md:
Homotetramer of 127-amino-acid subunits rich in β-sheet. It carries thyroxine (in the central channel; minor carrier in plasma, main one in cerebrospinal fluid) and retinol-binding protein with vitamin A – hence the name trans-thy-retin.

Amyloidogenesis: dissociation of the tetramer is rate-limiting; released monomers misfold and aggregate into amyloid fibrils in nerves, heart, kidney and eye. Stabilisers (tafamidis, acoramidis) bind the thyroxine sites and keep the tetramer intact.

Clinical chemistry: serum prealbumin (half-life about 2 days) was used as a nutritional marker but is lowered by inflammation and liver disease. Encoded by *TTR*.

attrs.mnemonic: Trans-THY-RETin = TRANSports THYroxine and RETinol.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CYP2E1, the ethanol-inducible P450 that also converts paracetamol to its toxic metabolite NAPQI.
items.body_md:
Cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily E member 1, located on 10q26.3.

Encodes CYP2E1, expressed mainly in pericentral (zone 3) hepatocytes. It is induced by chronic alcohol, isoniazid, fasting, obesity and diabetes, largely by protein stabilisation rather than transcription.

Function: oxidises small molecules – ethanol (part of the microsomal ethanol-oxidising system, MEOS, important at high and chronic intake), acetone, paracetamol (to NAPQI), halothane, isoniazid, CCl₄ and nitrosamines – and generates reactive oxygen species as a by-product.

Clinical relevance: explains why chronic drinkers and fasting patients are more susceptible to paracetamol hepatotoxicity and why the necrosis is centrilobular (zone 3). CYP2E1-derived oxidative stress contributes to alcohol-related and metabolic liver injury. Chlormethiazole and disulfiram inhibit it.

attrs.full_name: cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily E member 1
attrs.mnemonic: CYP2E1 = 'E for Ethanol' – induced by alcohol, it makes paracetamol's toxic NAPQI.

items.gloss_md: Ethanol-inducible cytochrome P450 of pericentral hepatocytes that oxidises ethanol and small toxins and activates paracetamol to NAPQI.
items.body_md:
ER membrane haem monooxygenase with a small active site suited to low-molecular-weight substrates. It is 'leaky': uncoupled catalysis produces superoxide and hydrogen peroxide even without substrate, which promotes lipid peroxidation.

Paracetamol: normally mostly glucuronidated and sulfated; a small fraction is oxidised by CYP2E1 (and CYP3A4/1A2) to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), which is detoxified by glutathione. When glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds mitochondrial proteins and causes zone 3 necrosis; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione.

Encoded by *CYP2E1*. Ethanol both induces CYP2E1 and, when present acutely, competitively inhibits it – explaining why acute intake can be protective while chronic intake is harmful for paracetamol toxicity.

items.gloss_md: Highly polymorphic P450 gene whose poor and ultrarapid metaboliser genotypes alter the effect of codeine, tamoxifen and many psychiatric and cardiovascular drugs.
items.body_md:
Cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily D member 6, located on 22q13.2 next to the pseudogenes *CYP2D7* and *CYP2D8*, which complicates genotyping.

Encodes CYP2D6, responsible for about a fifth of drug metabolism despite low hepatic abundance; it is not inducible. More than 100 star alleles exist, including deletions (*5), non-functional alleles (*4, most common in Europeans), decreased-function alleles (*10 in East Asians, *17 in Africans, *41) and gene duplications. About 5–10 % of Europeans are poor metabolisers; ultrarapid metabolisers (gene duplications) are especially common in North Africa and the Middle East.

Clinical relevance (CPIC guidelines): codeine and tramadol (prodrugs) – no effect in poor, morphine toxicity in ultrarapid metabolisers; tamoxifen activation to endoxifen; tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, ondansetron, metoprolol, atomoxetine, eliglustat. Strong inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, quinidine) convert normal metabolisers into poor metabolisers ('phenoconversion').

attrs.full_name: cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily D member 6
attrs.anecdote: The polymorphism was found in 1977 when pharmacologist Robert Smith took the antihypertensive debrisoquine himself and collapsed with severe hypotension – he turned out to be a poor metaboliser. Michel Eichelbaum in Germany independently found it with sparteine.

items.gloss_md: Polymorphic, non-inducible cytochrome P450 that metabolises about a fifth of drugs, including codeine, tamoxifen and many antidepressants.
items.body_md:
ER haem monooxygenase whose active site has an acidic residue (Asp301, Glu216) favouring basic, lipophilic amine substrates (antidepressants, antipsychotics, β-blockers, opioids, antiarrhythmics).

Phenotypes are predicted from the activity score of both alleles: poor (0), intermediate, normal and ultrarapid metaboliser. For prodrugs (codeine → morphine, tramadol → O-desmethyltramadol, tamoxifen → endoxifen), poor metabolisers lack efficacy and ultrarapid ones risk toxicity; for active drugs it is the opposite.

Encoded by *CYP2D6*. Liver disease reduces activity less than for other CYPs, but drug–drug inhibition is a frequent cause of phenoconversion.

attrs.mnemonic: 2D6 'never induced, often inhibited': fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, quinidine turn you into a poor metaboliser.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CYP2C9, whose *2 and *3 alleles reduce metabolism of warfarin, phenytoin and NSAIDs.
items.body_md:
Cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily C member 9, located on 10q23.33 in the CYP2C cluster with *CYP2C19*, *CYP2C8* and *CYP2C18*.

Encodes CYP2C9, one of the most abundant hepatic P450s; substrates include S-warfarin, phenytoin, NSAIDs (celecoxib, ibuprofen), sulfonylureas, losartan and siponimod.

Genetics: *2 (R144C) and *3 (I359L) reduce activity; about a third of Europeans carry at least one of them, while *3/*3 homozygotes are rare (under 1 %).

Clinical relevance: CPIC guidelines combine CYP2C9 and *VKORC1* genotypes for warfarin dosing (with *CYP4F2*), reduce phenytoin doses in poor metabolisers, and siponimod is contraindicated in *3/*3. Inhibited by fluconazole, amiodarone and sulfamethoxazole; induced by rifampicin.

attrs.full_name: cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily C member 9

items.gloss_md: Hepatic cytochrome P450 that metabolises warfarin, phenytoin, NSAIDs and sulfonylureas; reduced-function variants require dose reduction.
items.body_md:
ER haem monooxygenase preferring weakly acidic, lipophilic substrates (Arg108 binds anionic groups). It inactivates the more potent S-enantiomer of warfarin by 7-hydroxylation, so reduced activity prolongs warfarin action and increases bleeding risk.

Narrow-therapeutic-index substrates: warfarin, phenytoin, tolbutamide/glimepiride. Strong inhibitors (fluconazole, amiodarone, miconazole) frequently cause clinically relevant INR rises.

Encoded by *CYP2C9*. In cirrhosis, CYP2C activity is relatively reduced, contributing to altered drug handling.

Together with *VKORC1* (the warfarin target, vitamin K epoxide reductase), CYP2C9 genotype explains a large part of the interindividual variation in warfarin dose; genotype-guided dosing algorithms combine both with age, weight and interacting drugs.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CYP2C19, whose loss-of-function alleles impair clopidogrel activation and alter PPI and voriconazole exposure.
items.body_md:
Cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily C member 19, located on 10q23.33.

Encodes CYP2C19. Alleles: *2 (splicing defect, the most common loss-of-function allele) and *3 (stop codon; mainly East Asian) abolish function; *17 (promoter variant) increases expression. Poor metabolisers are about 2–5 % of Europeans and about 15 % of East Asians.

Clinical relevance (CPIC): clopidogrel, a prodrug, is poorly activated in poor and intermediate metabolisers (FDA boxed warning 2010; prasugrel or ticagrelor preferred after PCI); proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, pantoprazole) reach higher levels in poor metabolisers, which improves Helicobacter eradication; voriconazole, an antifungal used in transplant recipients, has subtherapeutic levels in ultrarapid and toxic levels in poor metabolisers; citalopram and escitalopram dosing are affected.

attrs.full_name: cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily C member 19

items.gloss_md: Polymorphic hepatic P450 that activates clopidogrel and metabolises proton pump inhibitors, voriconazole and citalopram.
items.body_md:
ER haem monooxygenase closely related to CYP2C9 (about 90 % identity) but with different substrate preference (neutral or weakly basic compounds), originally characterised as S-mephenytoin 4'-hydroxylase.

Bioactivation: clopidogrel is oxidised in two steps (CYP2C19 contributes to both) to its active thiol metabolite that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 receptor. Inactivation: omeprazole and other PPIs (omeprazole also inhibits CYP2C19), voriconazole, diazepam, citalopram.

Encoded by *CYP2C19*. Relevant in transplant medicine because voriconazole and PPIs are common co-medications and voriconazole also inhibits CYP3A4, raising tacrolimus levels.

attrs.mnemonic: Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 to 'switch on' – no 2C19, no platelet block.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the bilirubin-glucuronidating enzyme; variants cause Gilbert and Crigler–Najjar syndromes and irinotecan toxicity.
items.body_md:
UDP glucuronosyltransferase family 1 member A1, located on 2q37.1 in the complex *UGT1A* locus, where nine unique first exons are each spliced to shared exons 2–5.

Encodes UGT1A1, the only enzyme that substantially glucuronidates bilirubin in hepatocytes; it also conjugates SN-38 (active metabolite of irinotecan), oestradiol, ethinylestradiol and some drugs.

Disease relevance: Gilbert syndrome – mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, worse with fasting, illness or stress – mostly due to homozygosity for the promoter TATA-box variant A(TA)7TAA (UGT1A1*28) in Europeans (about 10 %) or *6 (G71R) in East Asians. Crigler–Najjar type I (no activity; kernicterus risk; liver transplantation or gene therapy) and type II (residual activity; responds to phenobarbital).

Clinical relevance: UGT1A1*28 homozygotes have increased neutropenia and diarrhoea with irinotecan (part of FOLFIRINOX and NALIRIFOX in PDAC); dose reduction is recommended. Atazanavir and pazopanib inhibit UGT1A1 and raise bilirubin harmlessly.

attrs.mnemonic: (de) Morbus Meulengracht = Gilbert: 'Fasten macht gelb' – fasting raises unconjugated bilirubin; harmless, but beware irinotecan.
attrs.anecdote: Gilbert syndrome is named after the French physician Augustin Gilbert, who described this benign familial jaundice in 1901; about 1 in 10 people carry the genotype without knowing it.

items.gloss_md: ER enzyme that conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid, making it water-soluble for biliary excretion; also inactivates SN-38 from irinotecan.
items.body_md:
Membrane-bound UDP-glucuronosyltransferase on the luminal side of the ER, with an N-terminal substrate (aglycone) domain encoded by the variable exon 1 and a C-terminal UDP-glucuronic acid-binding domain from shared exons. It forms bilirubin mono- and diglucuronides, which are exported into bile by MRP2 (*ABCC2*).

Reduced activity causes unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia: mild in Gilbert syndrome (about 30 % residual activity), severe in Crigler–Najjar. Neonatal jaundice reflects immature UGT1A1 expression. Inducers: phenobarbital, rifampicin (via CAR/PXR).

Encoded by *UGT1A1*. For irinotecan, low UGT1A1 activity means prolonged SN-38 exposure and toxicity.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding NTCP, the hepatocyte bile acid uptake transporter that hepatitis B and D viruses use as their entry receptor.
items.body_md:
Solute carrier family 10 member 1, alias NTCP (Na⁺–taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide). Located on 14q24.2.

Encodes NTCP, expressed on the basolateral (sinusoidal) membrane of hepatocytes, where it takes up conjugated bile acids from portal blood for enterohepatic circulation.

Discovery as viral receptor: in 2012 Yan et al. (Wenhui Li's laboratory, Beijing) identified NTCP as the functional receptor of hepatitis B and D viruses by binding to the preS1 domain of the large envelope protein; this enabled HBV infection systems in cell lines.

Disease relevance: the loss-of-function variant S267F, common in East Asia, causes hypercholanaemia and is associated with protection against chronic HBV infection.

Clinical relevance: bulevirtide (Hepcludex; formerly Myrcludex B, developed at Heidelberg University), a myristoylated preS1 peptide that blocks NTCP, was approved in the EU in 2020 (conditional, full approval 2023) for chronic hepatitis D; it raises serum bile acids as an on-target effect.

items.gloss_md: Basolateral hepatocyte transporter for conjugated bile acids that also serves as the entry receptor for HBV and HDV; blocked by bulevirtide.
items.body_md:
Membrane glycoprotein with nine transmembrane helices that couples uptake of conjugated bile acids (and some drugs, e.g. rosuvastatin) to two Na⁺ ions. Responsible for most sodium-dependent bile acid uptake from portal blood.

Viral entry: HBV and HDV first attach to heparan sulfate proteoglycans and then bind NTCP through the myristoylated N-terminus of preS1, followed by EGFR-dependent endocytosis. Cryo-EM structures (2022) revealed the bile-acid-binding tunnel that preS1 occupies.

Encoded by *SLC10A1*. Bulevirtide mimics preS1 and competitively blocks entry, lowering HDV RNA and ALT. Expression is reduced in cholestasis (downregulated by FXR–SHP) as a protective response.

attrs.mnemonic: NTCP: the bile acid door that HBV and HDV use as their key-hole – bulevirtide plugs the key-hole.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding glypican-3, an oncofetal heparan sulfate proteoglycan and IHC marker of hepatocellular carcinoma.
items.body_md:
Glypican 3, located on Xq26.2. Aliases SGB, OCI-5, DGSX.

Encodes glypican-3, a GPI-anchored heparan sulfate proteoglycan highly expressed in fetal liver and placenta and silenced in adult liver; it modulates Wnt, Hedgehog and other growth-factor signalling.

Disease relevance: loss-of-function mutations cause Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome type 1, an X-linked overgrowth syndrome with embryonal tumour risk.

Clinical relevance: GPC3 is re-expressed in most hepatocellular carcinomas (especially moderately to poorly differentiated) and hepatoblastomas, but not in normal liver, cirrhotic nodules or most adenomas; it is also positive in yolk sac tumours. GPC3 is a target of CAR T cells, bispecific antibodies and the antibody codrituzumab (unsuccessful in a phase 2 HCC trial).

items.gloss_md: Oncofetal GPI-anchored proteoglycan absent from normal adult liver but expressed in most HCCs; an IHC marker and immunotherapy target.
items.body_md:
About 70 kDa core protein (cleaved by furin into two subunits linked by disulfides) with heparan sulfate chains near the C-terminus and a GPI anchor; it can be shed by Notum/lipases into serum. It binds Wnt and promotes canonical Wnt signalling in HCC cells, and inhibits Hedgehog signalling in development.

Pathology use: in the differential diagnosis of well-differentiated HCC versus high-grade dysplastic nodule, positivity for at least two of three markers – GPC3, heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) and glutamine synthetase – supports HCC. Also positive in hepatoblastoma and yolk sac tumour.

Encoded by *GPC3*. Serum GPC3 has been studied as a complement to AFP.

attrs.mnemonic: HCC vs dysplastic nodule: 'GPC3, HSP70, GS – two of three, call it HCC'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding arginase-1, the final urea cycle enzyme, a sensitive IHC marker of hepatocytes and an immunosuppressive myeloid enzyme.
items.body_md:
Arginase 1, located on 6q23.2.

Encodes arginase-1, the cytosolic, liver-type arginase that hydrolyses arginine to ornithine and urea in the last step of the urea cycle. Outside the liver it is expressed in human neutrophils and granulocytic myeloid-derived suppressor cells and, prominently in mice, in alternatively activated macrophages.

Disease relevance: arginase-1 deficiency (hyperargininaemia) is a urea cycle disorder presenting with progressive spastic diplegia rather than early hyperammonaemic crises; pegzilarginase (enzyme therapy) was approved in the EU in 2023.

Clinical relevance: arginase-1 IHC is a highly sensitive and specific marker of hepatocellular differentiation, including poorly differentiated HCC (more sensitive than HepPar-1), useful to distinguish HCC from metastases and cholangiocarcinoma. Arginine depletion by myeloid ARG1 suppresses T-cell function (CD3ζ downregulation) in tumours.

items.gloss_md: Manganese-dependent urea-cycle enzyme of hepatocytes (arginine → ornithine + urea); IHC marker of hepatocellular origin and T-cell-suppressive myeloid enzyme.
items.body_md:
Homotrimeric metalloenzyme with a binuclear manganese cluster in each active site. In hepatocytes it completes the urea cycle and regenerates ornithine; urea is excreted by the kidney. The mitochondrial isoform arginase-2 (*ARG2*) is expressed in kidney and other tissues.

Immune function: arginase-1 from neutrophils, MDSCs and some macrophages depletes extracellular arginine, which T cells need for CD3ζ expression and proliferation – a mechanism of tumour immune escape; arginase inhibitors are in clinical trials.

Encoded by *ARG1*. Pathology: nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in benign and malignant hepatocytes, typically negative in other carcinomas.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding preproinsulin, the precursor of insulin and C-peptide, expressed in pancreatic β cells.
items.body_md:
Insulin, located on 11p15.5 next to *IGF2* and *TH*, within an imprinted region.

Encodes preproinsulin, translated almost exclusively in β cells of the islets of Langerhans; transcription is controlled by PDX1, MAFA and NEUROD1 and stimulated by glucose.

Disease relevance: dominant INS mutations disrupting proinsulin folding cause permanent neonatal diabetes and MODY10 (β-cell ER stress); a variable number tandem repeat (VNTR) upstream of INS (the IDDM2 locus) influences type 1 diabetes risk, likely via thymic insulin expression and tolerance. Proinsulin/insulin is a primary autoantigen in type 1 diabetes (insulin autoantibodies).

Clinical relevance: insulinomas are the most common functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (Whipple triad). Loss of β-cell mass after pancreatic resection or in chronic pancreatitis and PDAC causes pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes; new-onset diabetes in people over 50 can be an early sign of PDAC.

attrs.anecdote: Frederick Banting and Charles Best extracted insulin in Toronto in 1921; in January 1922 14-year-old Leonard Thompson became the first patient treated. Banting and Macleod received the 1923 Nobel Prize, and Banting shared his prize money with Best.

items.gloss_md: Peptide hormone of pancreatic β cells that lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis and suppressing hepatic glucose production.
items.body_md:
51-amino-acid hormone of an A chain (21 aa) and a B chain (30 aa) linked by two disulfide bonds (plus one intrachain bond in A). Made from proinsulin by prohormone convertases PC1/3 and PC2 and carboxypeptidase E, which release C-peptide; stored as zinc hexamers in secretory granules and secreted in response to glucose (via GLUT2/glucokinase, ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels and Ca²⁺ influx), amplified by incretins (GLP-1, GIP).

Signals through the insulin receptor tyrosine kinase → IRS → PI3K–AKT (GLUT4 translocation, glycogen synthesis, mTORC1, SREBP-1c) and RAS–MAPK. About half of portal insulin is cleared by the liver on first pass.

Encoded by *INS*. Therapy: human insulin and analogues (rapid-acting lispro, aspart; long-acting glargine, degludec). Hepatic insulin resistance with persistent lipogenesis is a core mechanism of MASLD.

attrs.anecdote: Insulin was the first protein to be fully sequenced (Frederick Sanger, Nobel Prize 1958) and human insulin from E. coli (1982) was the first recombinant drug approved.

items.gloss_md: Connecting peptide cleaved from proinsulin and secreted in equimolar amounts with insulin; the standard measure of endogenous insulin secretion.
items.body_md:
31-amino-acid peptide linking the B and A chains in proinsulin, which allows correct disulfide formation; cleaved off in the secretory granule and co-secreted with insulin.

Clinical use: unlike insulin, C-peptide is hardly extracted by the liver and has a longer half-life (about 30 min vs a few minutes), so it reflects β-cell secretion better than insulin; it is not present in therapeutic insulin. Applications: differentiating type 1 from type 2 diabetes and MODY in unclear cases, assessing residual β-cell function (e.g. before islet or pancreas transplantation and in type 3c diabetes after pancreatectomy), and investigating hypoglycaemia – high insulin with low C-peptide indicates exogenous insulin, high insulin with high C-peptide an insulinoma or sulfonylureas.

Derived from *INS*; renal failure raises C-peptide.

attrs.mnemonic: Insulin high + C-peptide low = insulin came from a syringe; both high = insulinoma or sulfonylurea.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding proglucagon, processed into glucagon in α cells and into GLP-1, GLP-2 and oxyntomodulin in intestinal L cells.
items.body_md:
Glucagon, located on 2q24.2.

Encodes proglucagon, which is cleaved tissue-specifically: in pancreatic α cells by prohormone convertase 2 (PC2) into glucagon, glicentin-related pancreatic polypeptide and the major proglucagon fragment; in intestinal L cells and the brainstem by PC1/3 into GLP-1, GLP-2, glicentin and oxyntomodulin.

Disease relevance: glucagonoma, a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, causes necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, weight loss and thrombosis. Hyperglucagonaemia contributes to hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes.

Clinical relevance: glucagon (injectable, nasal, dasiglucagon) treats severe hypoglycaemia and is used as a gut relaxant in radiology; GLP-1 analogues and glucagon/GLP-1 co-agonists (survodutide, pemvidutide) are developed for obesity and MASH. The 'liver–α-cell axis' links hepatic glucagon resistance in MASLD to raised amino acids and glucagon.

items.gloss_md: Peptide hormone of pancreatic α cells that raises blood glucose by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
items.body_md:
29-amino-acid peptide secreted by α cells in response to hypoglycaemia, amino acids and sympathetic activation; suppressed by glucose, insulin, somatostatin and GLP-1.

Acts on the glucagon receptor (*GCGR*), a class B GPCR mainly on hepatocytes → Gαs → cAMP → PKA, which activates glycogen phosphorylase, gluconeogenic genes (via CREB/CRTC2), amino acid catabolism and ureagenesis, and fatty acid oxidation/ketogenesis.

Derived from *GCG*. Clinical: emergency treatment of severe hypoglycaemia (it fails when hepatic glycogen is depleted, e.g. alcohol-related or starvation hypoglycaemia); antidote for β-blocker overdose; diagnostic test of β-cell reserve (glucagon stimulation of C-peptide).

attrs.anecdote: Glucagon was discovered in 1923 by Kimball and Murlin as a contaminant that caused blood sugar to rise before falling in early insulin extracts; they named it 'glucose agonist'.

items.gloss_md: Incretin hormone from intestinal L cells that enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon and appetite; the basis of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs.
items.body_md:
Produced from proglucagon by PC1/3 in L cells of the distal ileum and colon (and in brainstem neurons); the active forms are GLP-1(7–36)amide and GLP-1(7–37). Secreted within minutes after meals, it is degraded by dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) with a half-life of about 2 minutes.

Effects via the GLP-1 receptor: glucose-dependent insulin secretion (the incretin effect together with GIP), glucagon suppression, slower gastric emptying, satiety. The incretin effect is reduced in type 2 diabetes.

Derived from *GCG*. Drugs: DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin and other gliptins) raise endogenous GLP-1; GLP-1 receptor agonists (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide) and multi-agonists (tirzepatide) mimic it.

attrs.mnemonic: Incretin = INtestine seCRETion INsulin: gut hormones that make oral glucose stimulate more insulin than IV glucose.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), the classic serum marker of colorectal and other adenocarcinomas.
items.body_md:
CEA cell adhesion molecule 5. Aliases CEA, CD66e. Located on 19q13.2 in the CEA family cluster (with *CEACAM1*, *CEACAM6* and the pregnancy-specific glycoproteins).

Encodes carcinoembryonic antigen, expressed in fetal gut and on the apical surface of mature colonic epithelium; in carcinomas it loses polarity and spills into the blood.

Discovered in 1965 by Phil Gold and Samuel Freedman (Montreal) as an antigen shared by colon cancer and embryonic gut tissue – hence 'carcinoembryonic'.

Clinical relevance: serum CEA for colorectal cancer follow-up; elevated in a subset of PDAC (lower sensitivity than CA19-9, but useful in CA19-9 non-secretors), gastric, lung, breast and medullary thyroid cancer. In pancreatic cyst fluid, CEA ≥ 192 ng/mL is a classic cut-off for a mucinous cyst (IPMN, MCN). CEACAM5 is a target of antibody–drug conjugates and T-cell bispecifics in development.

items.gloss_md: GPI-anchored glycoprotein of fetal and colonic epithelium used as a serum tumour marker for colorectal and other adenocarcinomas, and in pancreatic cyst fluid.
items.body_md:
Heavily glycosylated (about 50 % carbohydrate) 180 kDa Ig-superfamily protein with seven Ig-like domains and a GPI anchor; it mediates homotypic adhesion and may inhibit anoikis and differentiation.

Serum reference: usually < 5 ng/mL (lower in non-smokers; smokers often have mildly elevated values). False elevations: smoking, cirrhosis and hepatitis (reduced hepatic clearance), cholestasis, pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, renal failure.

Clinical use: monitoring colorectal cancer after resection and during therapy (not for screening); complement to CA19-9 in PDAC and cholangiocarcinoma; cyst fluid CEA (≥ 192 ng/mL) for mucinous pancreatic cysts, often combined with cyst fluid glucose (low in mucinous cysts). IHC: positive in most adenocarcinomas; polyclonal CEA shows a canalicular pattern in HCC.

Encoded by *CEACAM5*.

attrs.mnemonic: CEA in pancreatic cyst fluid: 'one-nine-two, mucinous is true' (≥ 192 ng/mL).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding mucin 16, the giant transmembrane mucin that carries the CA-125 epitope.
items.body_md:
Mucin 16, cell surface associated. Alias CA125, located on 19p13.2.

Encodes one of the largest human proteins (over 14,000 amino acids, with a large tandem-repeat region of SEA domains), expressed on mesothelium (peritoneum, pleura, pericardium), Müllerian epithelium, ocular surface and airway epithelium, where it forms a protective glycocalyx.

Discovery: the CA-125 antigen was defined in 1981 by Robert Bast and colleagues with the OC125 antibody raised against an ovarian cancer cell line; the gene was cloned in 2001.

Clinical relevance: serum CA-125 monitors epithelial ovarian cancer (see CA-125 protein). MUC16 is frequently mutated in tumour sequencing data because of its enormous length, a classic example of a passenger 'false positive' gene. MUC16 binds mesothelin, which may support peritoneal metastasis; MUC16 is a target of bispecific antibodies (ubamatamab) in ovarian cancer.

attrs.mnemonic: MUC16 is a 'long gene, many mutations': like TTN, it appears in every mutation list just because it is huge.

items.gloss_md: Glycoprotein epitope on mucin 16 measured in serum as a tumour marker for ovarian cancer, and raised whenever serosal surfaces are irritated, e.g. by ascites.
items.body_md:
CA-125 is the antigen of the OC125 antibody on the tandem-repeat region of MUC16; the extracellular part is shed after cleavage and measured in serum (reference usually < 35 U/mL).

Clinical use: monitoring epithelial ovarian cancer, part of the Risk of Malignancy Index for adnexal masses. In PDAC it is elevated in about half of patients and adds information in CA19-9-negative (Lewis-negative) patients and in metastatic or peritoneal spread.

Major pitfall in hepatology and transplant medicine: any ascites, pleural or pericardial effusion, heart failure, cirrhosis, peritonitis, endometriosis, menstruation and pregnancy raise CA-125, so high values in a cirrhotic patient with ascites do not indicate ovarian cancer.

Encoded by *MUC16*.

attrs.mnemonic: CA-125 rises whenever the 'wrapping' (serosa) is irritated – ascites in cirrhosis is the classic false positive.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the Lewis fucosyltransferase; people lacking its activity (Lewis-negative) cannot make CA19-9.
items.body_md:
Fucosyltransferase 3 (Lewis blood group). Aliases Le, LE, FT3B. Located on 19p13.3.

Encodes an α(1,3/1,4)-fucosyltransferase that adds fucose in α1,4 linkage to type 1 chains, producing Lewis a (Leᵃ) and, after FUT2 action, Lewis b (Leᵇ), and sialyl-Lewis a (sLeᵃ) – the CA19-9 epitope – when the chain is first sialylated (by ST3GAL3).

Genetics: several common inactivating variants exist; about 5–10 % of people of European ancestry (more in people of African ancestry) are Lewis-negative, Le(a−b−), and do not produce CA19-9 even with large tumours. FUT2 (secretor) status modifies baseline CA19-9 levels (non-secretors have higher values).

Clinical relevance: explains false-negative CA19-9 in PDAC and cholangiocarcinoma; genotype- or Lewis-phenotype-adjusted CA19-9 cut-offs and alternative markers (CEA, CA-125) are recommended for these patients.

items.gloss_md: Golgi fucosyltransferase that makes Lewis antigens, including sialyl-Lewis a (CA19-9).
items.body_md:
Type II Golgi membrane glycosyltransferase that transfers fucose from GDP-fucose to N-acetylglucosamine in α1,3 or α1,4 linkage; its α1,4 activity on type 1 chains (Galβ1-3GlcNAc) is unique among human fucosyltransferases and is required for Leᵃ, Leᵇ and sialyl-Leᵃ synthesis.

Lewis antigens on red cells are not made by erythrocytes but adsorbed from plasma glycolipids produced in the gut, which is why Lewis phenotype can change in pregnancy.

Encoded by *FUT3*. Sialyl-Leᵃ and sialyl-Leˣ are selectin ligands, linking FUT3 activity to tumour cell adhesion to endothelium and metastasis.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding cytokeratin 19, the marker of ductal epithelium (cholangiocytes, pancreatic ducts), ductular reaction and progenitor-like HCC.
items.body_md:
Keratin 19, located on 17q21.2 in the type I keratin cluster.

Encodes CK19, the smallest keratin (it lacks a tail domain), which pairs with CK8 in simple and ductal epithelia: bile ducts, pancreatic ducts, gastrointestinal and urothelial epithelium, and mesothelium.

Clinical relevance: CK19 IHC marks cholangiocytes, the ductular reaction and hepatic progenitor cells in chronic liver disease, PDAC and cholangiocarcinoma (positive), and a subgroup of HCC with progenitor features (CK19-positive HCC is more aggressive, with higher recurrence after resection and transplantation). The serum fragment CYFRA 21-1 is a tumour marker for non-small cell lung cancer. In single-cell and spatial data, KRT19 is a standard marker of ductal and cholangiocyte populations, and Krt19-CreERT mice trace ductal cells.

items.gloss_md: Type I keratin of ductal epithelia used to identify cholangiocytes, pancreatic ductal cells, ductular reaction and progenitor-like HCC.
items.body_md:
40 kDa intermediate filament protein lacking the C-terminal tail domain of other keratins; it assembles with CK8 (and CK7) in ductal and simple epithelia and is relatively resistant to degradation in tumours.

Use in liver pathology: highlights bile ducts (duct loss in PBC, PSC, ductopenic rejection after liver transplantation), the ductular reaction that correlates with fibrosis stage, intermediate hepatobiliary cells, and progenitor-phenotype HCC. In the pancreas: normal ducts, PanIN, IPMN and PDAC are CK19-positive; acinar cells are negative, but become positive during acinar-to-ductal metaplasia.

Encoded by *KRT19*. Serum CYFRA 21-1 (a CK19 fragment) is a lung cancer marker.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding cytokeratin 7, used with CK20 to determine the origin of carcinomas and to detect cholangiocyte metaplasia in cholestasis.
items.body_md:
Keratin 7, located on 12q13.13 in the type II keratin cluster.

Encodes CK7, a type II keratin of glandular and ductal epithelia: bile ducts, pancreatic ducts, lung, breast, thyroid, female genital tract, urothelium and mesothelium; absent from hepatocytes, colorectal epithelium and prostate.

Clinical relevance: the CK7/CK20 immunoprofile is a cornerstone of carcinoma-of-unknown-primary workup (see CK7 protein). In chronic cholestatic liver disease, periportal hepatocytes acquire CK7 expression (biliary metaplasia), which is used in staging PBC and PSC; CK7 also highlights the ductular reaction.

items.gloss_md: Type II keratin of ductal and glandular epithelia; CK7 versus CK20 staining narrows down the origin of adenocarcinomas.
items.body_md:
54 kDa intermediate filament protein pairing with type I keratins (CK19, CK18, CK17) in ductal epithelia.

Classic CK7/CK20 patterns: CK7+/CK20− – lung, breast, thyroid, endometrium, ovarian serous, mesothelioma, many cholangiocarcinomas; CK7+/CK20+ – urothelial carcinoma, mucinous ovarian, and a substantial part of pancreatic and gastric adenocarcinomas (PDAC is usually CK7+ with variable CK20); CK7−/CK20+ – colorectal carcinoma, Merkel cell carcinoma; CK7−/CK20− – HCC, renal clear cell, prostate, adrenal, squamous carcinomas (often).

Hepatology: CK7-positive 'intermediate' hepatocytes in zone 1 indicate chronic cholestasis; aberrant CK7 in HCC is uncommon. Encoded by *KRT7*.

attrs.mnemonic: CK7−/CK20+ = colon ('20 is for the gut'); CK7+/CK20− = lung, breast; double negative = liver (HCC), kidney, prostate.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding cytokeratin 20, the marker of intestinal-type and urothelial differentiation.
items.body_md:
Keratin 20, located on 17q21.2 in the type I keratin cluster.

Encodes CK20, expressed in the surface epithelium of the stomach, small and large intestine (strongest at the villus/crypt surface), urothelial umbrella cells and Merkel cells.

Clinical relevance: CK20 is positive in colorectal adenocarcinoma (with SATB2 and CDX2), Merkel cell carcinoma (characteristic perinuclear dot pattern), urothelial and mucinous tumours; together with CK7 it guides the work-up of metastases of unknown origin, e.g. distinguishing colorectal liver metastases (CK7−/CK20+) from cholangiocarcinoma (usually CK7+/CK20−) and PDAC (CK7+, variable CK20). In IPMN, intestinal-type lesions express CK20 with MUC2 and CDX2. KRT20 mRNA in lymph nodes or blood was studied for occult tumour cell detection.

items.gloss_md: Type I keratin of intestinal surface epithelium, urothelial umbrella cells and Merkel cells; key IHC marker for colorectal origin.
items.body_md:
46 kDa intermediate filament protein of differentiated (non-proliferating) surface enterocytes and goblet cells; expression increases along the crypt–villus axis. Its phosphorylation regulates mucin secretion in goblet cells.

Pathology: colorectal adenocarcinoma (CK20+ in most, CK7−), Merkel cell carcinoma (paranuclear dot), urothelial carcinoma (CK7+/CK20+), mucinous tumours of various sites. Loss of CK20 in colorectal cancer is associated with MSI-high, right-sided tumours.

Encoded by *KRT20*.

In the liver, CK20 helps recognise colorectal metastases (CK7−/CK20+, with SATB2 and CDX2) and separate them from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, which is usually CK7+/CK20−. Intestinal-type IPMN and ampullary carcinomas of intestinal type also express CK20.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding vimentin, the intermediate filament of mesenchymal cells and a marker of epithelial–mesenchymal transition.
items.body_md:
Vimentin, located on 10p13.

Encodes vimentin, the type III intermediate filament of fibroblasts, endothelial cells, leukocytes, hepatic stellate cells (with desmin), Kupffer cells and most mesenchymal cells; also expressed in mesenchymal-like tumour cells.

Clinical relevance: vimentin IHC indicates mesenchymal origin (sarcomas, melanoma) and is co-expressed with keratins in renal cell, endometrial and some thyroid carcinomas. In carcinomas, vimentin gain with E-cadherin loss marks epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and is associated with invasion and poor prognosis; in PDAC, poorly differentiated, quasi-mesenchymal/basal-like tumours often express vimentin. Methylated VIM DNA in stool was used in early colorectal cancer screening tests.

attrs.anecdote: Vimentin knockout mice, reported in 1994, looked surprisingly normal – a lesson that even very abundant proteins can be dispensable under laboratory conditions; defects appeared only under stress such as wound healing.

items.gloss_md: Type III intermediate filament protein of mesenchymal cells; IHC marker of mesenchymal origin and of EMT in carcinomas.
items.body_md:
57 kDa protein forming homopolymeric filaments (and co-polymers with desmin, GFAP or nestin) that maintain cell shape, position organelles and resist mechanical stress; phosphorylation dynamically remodels the network during migration and mitosis.

Expression is driven by EMT transcription factors (SNAIL, SLUG, ZEB1, TWIST) downstream of TGF-β, and supports cell motility and invasion. Extracellular and surface vimentin act as a ligand/receptor for pathogens and immune cells.

Encoded by *VIM*. Pathology: positive in sarcomas, melanoma, lymphoma, renal cell carcinoma; activated hepatic stellate cells and portal fibroblasts are vimentin-positive.

attrs.mnemonic: Vimentin = Very Important Mesenchymal filament: keratins for epithelium, vimentin for mesenchyme.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding cationic trypsinogen; gain-of-function mutations cause autosomal dominant hereditary pancreatitis.
items.body_md:
Serine protease 1, alias cationic trypsinogen, TRY1. Located on 7q34, within the T-cell receptor β locus.

Encodes cationic trypsinogen, the most abundant trypsinogen isoform of pancreatic juice.

Disease relevance: in 1996 David Whitcomb and colleagues identified R122H as the cause of hereditary pancreatitis – the first gene linked to pancreatitis. R122H and N29I (most common) make trypsin resistant to autolysis or promote autoactivation; copy-number gains (triplications) have the same effect. Hereditary pancreatitis is autosomal dominant with high penetrance (about 80 %), starts in childhood with recurrent acute pancreatitis and progresses to chronic pancreatitis with exocrine and endocrine insufficiency; lifetime PDAC risk is markedly increased, especially in smokers. A common protective variant near PRSS1–PRSS2 lowers alcohol-related pancreatitis risk.

Clinical relevance: genetic testing (PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR, CTRC, CPA1, CEL) in young patients with idiopathic or familial pancreatitis.

attrs.mnemonic: Pancreatitis genetics = 'trypsin too strong or brakes too weak': PRSS1 (accelerator) gain-of-function; SPINK1 and CTRC (brakes) loss-of-function.

items.gloss_md: Inactive precursor of trypsin, the key pancreatic serine protease whose premature activation inside the pancreas triggers pancreatitis.
items.body_md:
Secreted by acinar cells as a zymogen; enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal brush border cleaves off the trypsinogen activation peptide (TAP), and trypsin then activates all other zymogens (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase, prophospholipase A2, colipase).

Protective mechanisms against intrapancreatic activation: storage as zymogen, SPINK1 (inhibits about 20 % of trypsin activity), trypsin autolysis at Arg122, degradation by chymotrypsin C, and low intracellular calcium. Premature activation (in co-localisation with cathepsin B in acinar vacuoles) initiates acinar injury in acute pancreatitis.

Encoded by *PRSS1*. Urinary TAP and serum trypsinogen-2 have been evaluated as pancreatitis markers; immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT) is the first-tier newborn screen for cystic fibrosis.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor; the N34S variant is a major risk factor for chronic pancreatitis.
items.body_md:
Serine peptidase inhibitor Kazal type 1. Aliases PSTI (pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor), TATI (tumour-associated trypsin inhibitor). Located on 5q32.

Encodes PSTI, synthesised by acinar cells as the first line of defence against prematurely activated trypsin; it is also an acute-phase-like protein induced by IL-6 and expressed by several tumours.

Disease relevance: the N34S haplotype (carried by about 1–2 % of Europeans; the causal variant within the haplotype is still debated) increases the risk of idiopathic chronic pancreatitis roughly 10-fold, acting as a disease modifier rather than a monogenic cause; it is common in tropical (fibrocalculous) pancreatitis in South Asia. Biallelic severe variants cause early-onset severe chronic pancreatitis.

Clinical relevance: part of genetic panels for idiopathic and early-onset chronic pancreatitis.

items.gloss_md: Kazal-type trypsin inhibitor secreted with pancreatic zymogens that blocks prematurely activated trypsin inside the pancreas.
items.body_md:
56-amino-acid peptide that acts as a competitive, pseudo-substrate inhibitor of trypsin with a Lys–Ile reactive site bond; inhibition is temporary because trypsin slowly degrades it. Stored in zymogen granules at about 1:100 ratio to trypsinogen, enough to neutralise roughly a fifth of potential trypsin activity.

Reduced SPINK1 lowers the threshold for trypsin-driven autodigestion; SPINK1 is also secreted by gut mucosa and acts as a growth factor via EGFR, which may explain its overexpression in some cancers.

Encoded by *SPINK1*.

In serum, SPINK1 (as tumour-associated trypsin inhibitor, TATI) rises in acute pancreatitis and in some tumours; it has been studied as a marker but is not used routinely.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the CFTR chloride/bicarbonate channel; biallelic mutations cause cystic fibrosis, milder variants predispose to pancreatitis.
items.body_md:
CF transmembrane conductance regulator. Alias ABCC7. Located on 7q31.2.

Encodes CFTR, an anion channel of the ABC transporter family expressed in airway, pancreatic duct, bile duct, intestinal, sweat gland and reproductive tract epithelia.

Cloned in 1989 by Lap-Chee Tsui, John Riordan and Francis Collins – one of the first human disease genes found by positional cloning. More than 2,000 variants are known; F508del (p.Phe508del) accounts for about 70 % of CF alleles in people of European ancestry.

Disease relevance: cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive, about 1 in 2,500–3,500 European newborns) with lung disease, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (about 85 %), CF-related diabetes and CF-associated liver disease (focal biliary cirrhosis); milder variants or heterozygosity increase the risk of chronic pancreatitis, congenital absence of the vas deferens and bronchiectasis.

Clinical relevance: diagnosis by newborn screening and sweat chloride (≥ 60 mmol/L); CFTR modulators (ivacaftor, 2012; elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor, 2019) restore function in most patients and have transformed prognosis.

attrs.anecdote: European folklore warned: 'Woe to the child who tastes salty when kissed on the brow, for he is bewitched and soon must die' – a description of cystic fibrosis centuries before the sweat test.

items.gloss_md: cAMP/PKA-regulated anion channel of epithelia that secretes chloride and bicarbonate; defective in cystic fibrosis.
items.body_md:
ABC-family protein with two membrane-spanning domains, two nucleotide-binding domains and a unique regulatory (R) domain; PKA phosphorylation of the R domain and ATP binding at the NBDs open the channel. It is the only ABC transporter that functions as an ion channel.

In pancreatic ducts CFTR drives bicarbonate-rich fluid secretion (with SLC26A6), which flushes digestive enzymes and neutralises gastric acid; failure leads to protein plugs, duct obstruction, acinar destruction and fibrosis. In bile ducts it supports bile alkalinisation and flow.

Mutation classes: no synthesis (e.g. G542X), misfolding/processing (F508del), gating (G551D), conductance (R117H), reduced quantity, instability. Modulators: potentiators (ivacaftor) increase opening, correctors (lumacaftor, tezacaftor, elexacaftor) improve folding and trafficking.

Encoded by *CFTR*.

attrs.mnemonic: CFTR: 'C'hloride 'F'or 'T'he 'R'ight mucus – no CFTR, no water, thick secretions in lungs, pancreas and bile ducts.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding chymotrypsin C, which degrades trypsin; loss-of-function variants increase chronic pancreatitis risk.
items.body_md:
Chymotrypsin C, alias caldecrin, ELA4. Located on 1p36.21.

Encodes chymotrypsin C, an acinar digestive protease that, unusually, protects the pancreas by degrading trypsinogen and trypsin (cleaving the Leu81–Glu82 bond within the calcium-binding loop) at low calcium concentrations, and by regulating activation of other zymogens.

Disease relevance: in 2008 Rosendahl and colleagues (a German-led consortium in Leipzig) identified loss-of-function CTRC variants (e.g. R254W, K247_R254del, and the common synonymous c.180C>T, p.G60=) as risk factors for chronic pancreatitis, including alcohol-related disease, acting synergistically with SPINK1 and CFTR variants.

Clinical relevance: included in genetic panels for idiopathic chronic pancreatitis.

items.gloss_md: Pancreatic serine protease that degrades trypsinogen and trypsin, providing an intrinsic brake against intrapancreatic trypsin activity.
items.body_md:
Chymotrypsin-like serine protease secreted as chymotrypsinogen C and activated by trypsin. At low calcium (as in the acinar cell) it cleaves trypsinogen in its calcium-binding loop, marking it for degradation; at high calcium in the duodenum trypsinogen is protected. It also processes procarboxypeptidase A1 and A2 and enhances trypsinogen autoactivation by cleaving its activation peptide.

Loss-of-function variants reduce secretion (misfolding with ER stress) or activity, thereby weakening the trypsin brake.

Encoded by *CTRC*.

Alcohol and smoking increase the disease risk of CTRC variant carriers considerably, a clear example of gene–environment interaction in chronic pancreatitis.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding carboxyl ester lipase; VNTR frameshifts cause MODY8 and a hybrid allele raises chronic pancreatitis risk.
items.body_md:
Carboxyl ester lipase, alias bile salt-stimulated lipase (BSSL), bile salt-dependent lipase. Located on 9q34.13, next to the pseudogene *CELP*.

Encodes CEL, a digestive lipase of pancreatic acinar cells and the lactating mammary gland (breast milk lipase that helps infants digest fat). Exon 11 contains a variable number of 33-bp tandem repeats (VNTR) encoding an O-glycosylated, proline-rich C-terminal tail.

Disease relevance: single-base deletions in the VNTR cause CEL-MODY (MODY8), a dominant syndrome of exocrine pancreatic dysfunction, lipomatosis and diabetes, through aggregation of the mutant protein. The CEL-HYB1 allele, a hybrid of CEL and CELP formed by non-allelic recombination, increases the risk of idiopathic chronic pancreatitis.

Clinical relevance: a model for proteotoxic pancreatic disease; genotyping the VNTR is technically difficult with short-read sequencing.

items.gloss_md: Broad-specificity pancreatic and breast-milk lipase activated by bile salts that hydrolyses cholesterol esters, fat-soluble vitamin esters and triglycerides.
items.body_md:
Serine hydrolase of the α/β-hydrolase fold, activated by primary bile salts; unlike pancreatic lipase, it hydrolyses cholesteryl esters, retinyl and tocopheryl esters, phospholipids and all three ester bonds of triglycerides. Its C-terminal mucin-like tandem-repeat tail affects stability and secretion.

In breast milk it compensates for the low pancreatic lipase of newborns; heat (pasteurisation) inactivates it, which is relevant for donor milk feeding of preterm infants.

Encoded by *CEL*. MODY8 frameshifts create a novel, aggregation-prone tail that damages acinar cells.

Unlike pancreatic triglyceride lipase, CEL depends on bile salts for activity, so it is active only in the intestinal lumen.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding pancreatic elastase 3B, the antigen measured in the faecal elastase-1 test for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
items.body_md:
Chymotrypsin like elastase 3B. Previous name elastase 1 (ELA3B), alias protease E. Located on 1p36.12, next to *CELA3A*, with which it is highly homologous.

Encodes an acinar serine protease secreted as a zymogen and activated by trypsin. Human 'pancreatic elastase-1' measured in stool corresponds to the CELA3 enzymes (CELA3B and its close paralogue CELA3A), which pass through the gut largely undegraded.

Clinical relevance: faecal elastase-1 (ELISA with monoclonal antibodies against human pancreatic elastase) is the standard non-invasive test for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (see protein item); because the antibodies do not detect porcine enzyme, the test remains valid during pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. A rare CELA3B variant was reported in a family with hereditary pancreatitis.

items.gloss_md: Acinar serine protease that survives intestinal passage; its concentration in stool (faecal elastase-1) is the main screening test for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
items.body_md:
Serine protease of the chymotrypsin family (CELA3 enzymes) secreted as a proenzyme and activated by trypsin; it degrades elastin and other proteins. It is stable in the intestine and concentrated about five-fold in stool relative to pancreatic juice.

Faecal elastase-1 interpretation (common cut-offs): > 200 µg/g stool normal; 100–200 µg/g mild to moderate insufficiency; < 100 µg/g severe insufficiency. False low values occur with watery (diluted) stool. Specificity for mild insufficiency is limited; sensitivity is high for severe insufficiency, as in chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, after pancreatic resection and in PDAC, where pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy improves nutrition and survival.

Encoded by *CELA3B* (and *CELA3A*). Because the test is specific for the human enzyme, patients need not stop enzyme supplements before testing.

attrs.mnemonic: Stool elastase: 'over 200 fine, under 100 bad' (µg/g).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding pancreatic triglyceride lipase, the main fat-digesting enzyme and the basis of the serum lipase test.
items.body_md:
Pancreatic lipase, alias PTL. Located on 10q25.3, near the related *PNLIPRP1* and *PNLIPRP2*.

Encodes pancreatic triacylglycerol lipase, secreted by acinar cells in large amounts; together with its cofactor colipase (*CLPS*) it hydrolyses dietary triglycerides at positions sn-1 and sn-3, producing 2-monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids.

Disease relevance: rare biallelic PNLIP mutations cause congenital pancreatic lipase deficiency with steatorrhoea.

Clinical relevance: serum lipase is the preferred laboratory test for acute pancreatitis (see protein item); lipase units are the dosing basis for pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy; orlistat, an anti-obesity drug, inhibits gastric and pancreatic lipases.

items.gloss_md: Acinar enzyme that digests dietary triglycerides with colipase; serum lipase above three times the upper limit is a diagnostic criterion of acute pancreatitis.
items.body_md:
About 50 kDa interfacial enzyme with a catalytic Ser–His–Asp triad covered by a lid that opens at the lipid–water interface; colipase anchors it to bile-salt-coated fat droplets.

Diagnostic use: according to the revised Atlanta classification (2012), acute pancreatitis requires two of three criteria – typical abdominal pain, serum lipase (or amylase) at least three times the upper limit of normal, characteristic imaging findings. Lipase is more specific and stays elevated longer than amylase; its level does not correlate with severity. Mild elevations occur in renal failure, bowel perforation or ischaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis.

Therapy: pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancreatin capsules, e.g. Kreon/Creon) is dosed in lipase units, often 40,000–50,000 units per main meal, with meals. Encoded by *PNLIP*.

attrs.mnemonic: Revised Atlanta: 'two out of three' – pain, lipase ≥ 3 × ULN, imaging.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding PDX1, the homeobox transcription factor required for pancreas development and β-cell identity.
items.body_md:
Pancreatic and duodenal homeobox 1. Previous names IPF1, STF-1, IDX-1. Located on 13q12.2.

Encodes PDX1, expressed in the early pancreatic and duodenal endoderm, where all pancreatic lineages originate, and later restricted mainly to β and δ cells, where it activates *INS*, *GCK* and *SLC2A2*.
