Disease relevance: homozygous loss causes pancreatic agenesis (first reported in 1997); heterozygous variants cause MODY4 and increase type 2 diabetes risk.

Research relevance: Pdx1-Cre drives pancreas-wide recombination in the classic KPC mouse model of PDAC (Pdx1-Cre; LSL-KrasG12D; LSL-Trp53R172H). PDX1 is a key marker in stem-cell differentiation protocols for β-like cells and is re-expressed in some PDAC and neuroendocrine tumours.

attrs.mnemonic: PDX1 starts the pancreas; KPC mice are 'Pdx1-Cre + KRAS + p53' – no PDX1-Cre, no KPC.

items.gloss_md: Homeodomain transcription factor that specifies the pancreatic endoderm and maintains β-cell function by activating the insulin gene.
items.body_md:
ParaHox-family homeodomain protein (283 amino acids) with an N-terminal transactivation domain; binds A/T-rich elements (A boxes) in the insulin promoter together with NEUROD1/E47 and MAFA, recruiting coactivators p300 and SET7/9.

Expression pattern: all pancreatic progenitors (with PTF1A, SOX9, NKX6-1), later high in β cells, low in acinar and ductal cells. Glucose and GLP-1 signalling increase PDX1 activity; glucotoxicity and oxidative stress reduce it, contributing to β-cell dedifferentiation in type 2 diabetes.

Encoded by *PDX1*.

PDX1 is also a reprogramming factor: together with NGN3 and MAFA it converted pancreatic acinar cells into insulin-producing β-like cells in adult mice (Zhou, Melton and colleagues, 2008).

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding PTF1A, the bHLH transcription factor that specifies and maintains acinar cell identity.
items.body_md:
Pancreas associated transcription factor 1a. Aliases p48, PTF1-p48, bHLHa29. Located on 10p12.2.

Encodes PTF1A, which with an E protein and RBPJ (early) or RBPJL (in mature acinar cells) forms the trimeric PTF1 complex driving digestive enzyme genes; it is also needed for GABAergic neurons of cerebellum and spinal cord.

Disease relevance: coding loss-of-function mutations cause pancreatic and cerebellar agenesis; deletions or variants of a distal enhancer cause isolated pancreatic agenesis (identified by genome sequencing, Weedon et al., 2014).

Research relevance: Ptf1a-Cre (p48-Cre) is the second classic driver for PDAC mouse models (KC mice); during acinar-to-ductal metaplasia induced by KRAS and inflammation, PTF1A is lost, and maintaining it suppresses tumorigenesis in mice.

items.gloss_md: bHLH transcription factor of the PTF1 complex that drives acinar cell development and digestive enzyme expression.
items.body_md:
Class B basic helix-loop-helix protein that heterodimerises with E proteins (E12/E47) and binds RBPJL to form PTF1-L, which binds bipartite E-box/TC-box elements in promoters of *CPA1*, *CELA*, *PRSS1*, *CTRB* and other acinar genes and of *RBPJL* itself (feed-forward loop).

Together with NR5A2, GATA4 and MIST1 (BHLHA15) it maintains the differentiated acinar state; loss of these factors promotes acinar-to-ductal metaplasia, a precursor of PanIN and PDAC in mouse models.

Encoded by *PTF1A*.

Ptf1a-Cre is widely used to target pancreatic lineages in mouse models, and PTF1A is a standard acinar-cell marker in single-cell atlases of the human pancreas.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding mucin 1, a transmembrane mucin overexpressed and underglycosylated in PDAC; carrier of the CA15-3 and KL-6 epitopes.
items.body_md:
Mucin 1, cell surface associated. Aliases EMA (epithelial membrane antigen), CD227, PEM, episialin. Located on 1q22.

Encodes MUC1, expressed apically on glandular epithelia. Its extracellular domain contains a variable number of 20-amino-acid tandem repeats.

Disease relevance: frameshifts in the VNTR cause autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD-MUC1), notoriously hard to detect by standard sequencing.

Clinical relevance: serum CA15-3 (breast cancer) and KL-6 (interstitial lung disease) measure MUC1 epitopes; EMA IHC marks carcinomas, plasma cells and meningiomas. In the pancreas, MUC1 is expressed in PDAC and in the aggressive pancreatobiliary-type IPMN, whereas gastric-type IPMN are MUC5AC+ and intestinal-type MUC2+/CDX2+. Underglycosylated tumour MUC1 is a target of vaccines and CAR T cells.

items.gloss_md: Heavily O-glycosylated transmembrane mucin of glandular epithelia; overexpressed in adenocarcinomas and measured in serum as CA15-3 or KL-6.
items.body_md:
Heterodimer formed by autocleavage in the SEA domain: a large extracellular subunit with 20–120 glycosylated tandem repeats, non-covalently attached to a transmembrane subunit with a cytoplasmic tail that interacts with β-catenin, EGFR and other signalling proteins.

In cancer, MUC1 loses apical polarity, is overexpressed and carries truncated O-glycans (Tn, sialyl-Tn, T antigens), which expose peptide epitopes (tumour-associated MUC1) and promote immune evasion via Siglecs.

Encoded by *MUC1*. Markers: CA15-3, CA27.29 (breast cancer monitoring), KL-6 (interstitial lung disease activity); EMA in IHC.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding mesothelin, a GPI-anchored protein overexpressed in PDAC, mesothelioma and ovarian cancer and an immunotherapy target.
items.body_md:
Mesothelin, located on 16p13.3.

Encodes a 71 kDa precursor cleaved by furin into megakaryocyte-potentiating factor (MPF, secreted) and membrane-bound mesothelin. Normal expression is restricted to mesothelial cells of pleura, peritoneum and pericardium and some epithelia (trachea, ovary surface, tonsil), and mesothelin-knockout mice are normal.

Clinical relevance: overexpressed in most PDACs (including precursor lesions from high-grade PanIN), epithelioid mesotheliomas, ovarian, lung and gastric carcinomas; IHC helps distinguish PDAC from reactive ducts. Soluble mesothelin-related peptide (SMRP) is a serum marker for mesothelioma. Because of its restricted normal expression it is a popular target: antibody–drug conjugates (anetumab ravtansine), immunotoxins, vaccines and mesothelin-directed CAR T cells, so far with limited efficacy in solid tumours.

items.gloss_md: GPI-anchored glycoprotein of mesothelium overexpressed in PDAC and mesothelioma; binds CA-125/MUC16 and is an immunotherapy target.
items.body_md:
About 40 kDa membrane protein built from superhelical ARM-type repeats, anchored by GPI and shed by ADAM17 to give soluble forms. Its best-known interaction is binding to MUC16 (CA-125), proposed to promote peritoneal implantation of ovarian and pancreatic cancer cells.

In PDAC, mesothelin is expressed by tumour cells but not by normal pancreatic ducts or chronic pancreatitis, supporting diagnosis in difficult biopsies. Tumour-specific expression with limited normal tissue distribution made it one of the most targeted antigens for cellular immunotherapy; obstacles include shedding of the antigen (sink effect), the dense PDAC stroma and immunosuppressive microenvironment.

Encoded by *MSLN*.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding claudin 18; its gastric isoform CLDN18.2 is the target of zolbetuximab and is expressed in many PDACs.
items.body_md:
Claudin 18, located on 3q22.3.

Encodes two isoforms from alternative first exons: CLDN18.1 (lung alveolar epithelium) and CLDN18.2 (differentiated gastric mucosa only). In malignant transformation the tight junctions are disrupted and CLDN18.2 epitopes become accessible on the cell surface.

Disease relevance: CLDN18.2 is expressed in a large fraction of gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinomas and in a majority of PDACs (often retained in metastases), as well as in mucinous lung and biliary tumours. CLDN18–ARHGAP26/6 fusions occur in diffuse-type gastric cancer.

Clinical relevance: zolbetuximab (Vyloy), an anti-CLDN18.2 IgG1 antibody, was approved in 2024 (EU and US) with chemotherapy for HER2-negative, CLDN18.2-positive advanced gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma (positivity: ≥ 75 % of tumour cells with moderate-to-strong membranous staining, VENTANA 43-14A assay); CLDN18.2 antibodies, ADCs, bispecifics and CAR T cells are being tested in PDAC.

items.gloss_md: Gastric-specific tight-junction isoform of claudin 18 that becomes exposed on gastric and pancreatic cancer cells; target of zolbetuximab.
items.body_md:
Four-transmembrane-domain tight-junction protein with two extracellular loops; it seals the paracellular space of gastric mucosa against acid and regulates H⁺ permeability. The first extracellular loop differs from CLDN18.1 by a few residues, allowing isoform-specific antibodies.

Mechanism of zolbetuximab: binds CLDN18.2 on tumour cells and kills through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement-dependent cytotoxicity; nausea and vomiting are the typical side effects (targeting of normal gastric mucosa). Assessment uses IHC (membranous staining intensity and percentage).

Encoded by *CLDN18*.

Because normal CLDN18.2 is hidden within tight junctions of the gastric mucosa, tumour-selective accessibility rather than tumour-specific expression creates the therapeutic window.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding the transcription factor GATA6, the key marker of the classical PDAC subtype; its loss defines basal-like tumours.
items.body_md:
GATA binding protein 6, located on 18q11.2.

Encodes GATA6, a zinc-finger transcription factor of endodermal and cardiac development, required for pancreas formation and acinar differentiation.

Disease relevance: heterozygous GATA6 mutations are the most common cause of pancreatic agenesis (often with congenital heart defects and neonatal diabetes), with variable expressivity.

PDAC subtypes: transcriptomic classifications (Collisson 2011, Moffitt 2015, Bailey 2016) converge on two main tumour-cell states – classical/pancreatic progenitor (GATA6 high, HNF1A, TFF1, CLDN18) and basal-like/squamous (GATA6 low; KRT5, KRT17, S100A2, ΔNp63 programmes). GATA6 is the best single surrogate: low GATA6 identifies basal-like tumours with poorer survival and poor response to modified FOLFIRINOX in the COMPASS trial. GATA6 is amplified in a subset of PDAC.

attrs.mnemonic: GATA6 high = 'classical and calmer' PDAC; GATA6 low = basal-like, squamous, chemo-resistant.

items.gloss_md: Endodermal zinc-finger transcription factor; high nuclear GATA6 marks the classical PDAC subtype with better prognosis and chemotherapy response.
items.body_md:
Member of the GATA family (GATA4/5/6 endodermal and cardiac; GATA1–3 haematopoietic) with two zinc fingers binding (A/T)GATA(A/G) motifs. In the pancreas it maintains endodermal/epithelial differentiation and represses basal-like and EMT programmes; GATA6 loss is permissive for the basal-like state and metastatic dissemination.

Measurement: RNA in situ hybridisation or IHC on biopsies, enabling subtype stratification in clinical trials (e.g. selecting basal-like tumours for alternative regimens). Tumour heterogeneity means classical and basal-like cells can coexist in the same tumour, and subtype can shift under therapy.

Encoded by *GATA6*.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding chromogranin A, the secretory granule protein used as the main IHC and serum marker of neuroendocrine neoplasms.
items.body_md:
Chromogranin A, located on 14q32.12.

Encodes chromogranin A, the most abundant granin protein of dense-core secretory granules in neuroendocrine cells (islet cells, enterochromaffin and ECL cells, adrenal medulla, pituitary, parathyroid). It is processed into bioactive peptides: vasostatins, pancreastatin (inhibits insulin secretion), catestatin (inhibits catecholamine release) and others.

Clinical relevance: IHC marker (with synaptophysin and INSM1) of well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours, including pancreatic NETs, and of neuroendocrine carcinomas (weaker, more variable in poorly differentiated tumours). Serum chromogranin A is used for follow-up of NETs, with important false-positive elevations from proton pump inhibitors, chronic atrophic gastritis, renal failure, heart failure, liver cirrhosis and inflammatory bowel disease.

items.gloss_md: Acidic granule protein of neuroendocrine cells that is the standard IHC and serum marker of neuroendocrine tumours.
items.body_md:
About 49 kDa (migrating at about 70 kDa) acidic, calcium-binding protein that helps sort and condense hormones into dense-core granules; secreted with the hormones and cleaved by prohormone convertases into peptides with regulatory functions.

Serum CgA correlates with tumour burden in well-differentiated NETs and helps monitor treatment; it should be measured off PPIs (which cause ECL-cell hyperplasia and high CgA), and values are raised in renal and liver failure.

Encoded by *CHGA*. In pancreatic NET pathology, grading uses Ki-67 and mitoses (WHO 2019: G1 < 3 %, G2 3–20 %, G3 > 20 %), while chromogranin A and synaptophysin confirm neuroendocrine differentiation.

attrs.mnemonic: Neuroendocrine IHC trio: chromogranin A, synaptophysin, INSM1 – and a high serum CgA in a patient on a PPI means nothing.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding TOX, the HMG-box transcription factor that establishes the epigenetic programme of exhausted T cells.
items.body_md:
Thymocyte selection associated high mobility group box, alias TOX1. Located on 8q12.1.

Encodes TOX, a nuclear HMG-box DNA-binding protein first described for thymocyte positive selection and CD4+ T-cell lineage development; it is also required for NK cells, innate lymphoid cells and lymph-node organogenesis.

Exhaustion: in 2019 several groups showed that persistent TCR stimulation (via calcineurin–NFAT) induces high TOX expression, which is necessary for the exhausted CD8+ T-cell state in chronic infection and cancer; TOX deletion abolishes the exhaustion programme but the cells then die, so TOX also protects them from overstimulation.

Clinical relevance: TOX is a core gene of exhaustion signatures (with PDCD1, HAVCR2, ENTPD1, LAG3, CXCL13) in scRNA-seq of tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes and is studied as a target for improving CAR T-cell persistence. Precursor-exhausted T cells (TCF-1+ PD-1+ TOX+) proliferate after PD-1 blockade, whereas terminally exhausted cells (TIM-3+ CD39+ TOX high) do not.

attrs.full_name: thymocyte selection associated high mobility group box

items.gloss_md: HMG-box transcription factor that locks chronically stimulated CD8+ T cells into the exhausted state.
items.body_md:
Nuclear protein with a single high-mobility-group (HMG) box that binds DNA in a sequence-independent way and remodels chromatin; it acts with partners such as the HBO1 histone acetyltransferase complex.

In chronic antigen exposure, NFAT (without AP-1 partners) induces TOX, which opens exhaustion-specific chromatin regions and sustains expression of inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIM-3, CD39) while limiting effector cytokine production. The exhausted epigenetic state is only partly reversible by PD-1 blockade.

Encoded by *TOX*. TOX expression is also high in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, where it is used as a diagnostic marker.

attrs.mnemonic: TOX = 'toxic' long-term antigen exposure makes T cells tired: chronic stimulation → NFAT → TOX → exhaustion.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD39, the ectonucleotidase that degrades extracellular ATP and starts adenosine-mediated immunosuppression.
items.body_md:
Ectonucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolase 1. Aliases CD39, NTPDase1. Located on 10q24.1.

Encodes CD39, expressed on Tregs, B cells, monocytes, endothelial cells, Kupffer cells and on chronically activated, tumour-reactive CD8+ T cells.

Function: hydrolyses pro-inflammatory extracellular ATP (a danger signal released from dying cells) and ADP to AMP, which CD73 converts to immunosuppressive adenosine; on endothelium it limits platelet activation (ADP degradation).

Clinical relevance: CD39+CD103+ CD8+ tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes are enriched for tumour-reactive clones; CD39 is a marker of exhausted T cells. Anti-CD39 antibodies are in early clinical trials. In transplantation, CD39 on Tregs and endothelium protects against ischaemia–reperfusion injury and rejection in experimental models.

items.gloss_md: Cell-surface ectoenzyme that hydrolyses ATP and ADP to AMP, the first step of the immunosuppressive adenosine pathway.
items.body_md:
Membrane glycoprotein with two transmembrane helices and a large extracellular catalytic domain containing apyrase conserved regions; requires Ca²⁺ or Mg²⁺.

Adenosine pathway: ATP (pro-inflammatory, via P2X7 on immune cells) → ADP → AMP by CD39, then AMP → adenosine by CD73; adenosine signals through A2A and A2B receptors (cAMP), suppressing T-cell and NK-cell effector function and promoting Tregs and M2-like macrophages. Hypoxia (HIF-1α) induces the pathway in tumours.

Encoded by *ENTPD1*. Marker of Tregs (with FOXP3), terminally exhausted and tumour-reactive CD8+ T cells.

attrs.mnemonic: ATP → (CD39) → AMP → (CD73) → adenosine: '39 then 73, from danger to calm'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CD73, the ecto-5'-nucleotidase that produces extracellular adenosine; loss causes arterial calcification.
items.body_md:
5'-nucleotidase ecto. Aliases CD73, eN, NT5. Located on 6q14.3.

Encodes CD73, a GPI-anchored enzyme on endothelium, epithelia, fibroblasts, Tregs, B and T cell subsets, mesenchymal stromal cells and many tumour cells (high in PDAC, triple-negative breast cancer and others, where it correlates with poor prognosis).

Disease relevance: biallelic loss-of-function causes arterial calcification due to deficiency of CD73 (ACDC), with calcification of lower-limb arteries and joint capsules, described in 2011.

Clinical relevance: CD73 is a defining marker of mesenchymal stromal cells (with CD90, CD105). Anti-CD73 antibodies (oleclumab and others) and small-molecule inhibitors (quemliclustat, tested in PDAC) are investigational immunotherapies, typically combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade and chemotherapy; A2A receptor antagonists target the same pathway downstream.

items.gloss_md: GPI-anchored ectoenzyme that converts AMP into adenosine, the rate-limiting step of extracellular adenosine production.
items.body_md:
Homodimeric zinc-dependent metallophosphoesterase anchored by GPI; it can be shed as soluble CD73 by phospholipases. Its product adenosine suppresses T-cell, NK-cell and dendritic-cell function via A2A receptors, promotes angiogenesis and metastasis, and protects tissues from inflammation and hypoxia (e.g. endothelial barrier function).

In arteries, CD73-derived adenosine suppresses tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase; its loss raises ALP activity and drives ectopic calcification.

Encoded by *NT5E*. A therapeutic target in immuno-oncology, also a marker of mesenchymal stromal cells and of naive and memory lymphocyte subsets.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CXCL9 (MIG), an interferon-γ-induced chemokine that recruits CXCR3+ T cells into tissues and tumours.
items.body_md:
C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 9. Previous names MIG (monokine induced by gamma interferon), CMK, Humig. Located on 4q21.1 next to *CXCL10* and *CXCL11*.

Encodes CXCL9, produced by macrophages, dendritic cells, endothelial and stromal cells strictly in response to IFN-γ (via STAT1 and IRF1), unlike CXCL10, which is also induced by type I interferons.

Clinical relevance: a core gene of 'T-cell-inflamed' and IFN-γ signatures predicting response to checkpoint blockade; CXCL9-expressing macrophages (versus SPP1+ macrophages) define a favourable tumour macrophage polarity. Serum CXCL9 is a specific readout of IFN-γ activity used in haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and macrophage activation syndrome (monitoring emapalumab therapy) and is raised in kidney and liver allograft rejection.

items.gloss_md: IFN-γ-induced chemokine that attracts CXCR3+ Th1 cells, CD8+ T cells and NK cells.
items.body_md:
ELR-negative CXC chemokine (angiostatic) that binds CXCR3, a GPCR on activated Th1 and CD8+ T cells, NK cells and some B cells; CXCR3 also binds CXCL10 and CXCL11. Gradients of CXCL9 on endothelium and in tissue direct effector T cells to sites of IFN-γ activity, forming a positive feedback loop (T cells make IFN-γ → more CXCL9).

Tumours that silence CXCL9/10 (epigenetically, or through β-catenin or loss of IFN signalling) are 'cold' and resist checkpoint blockade.

Encoded by *CXCL9*. Serum CXCL9 correlates with disease activity in HLH and macrophage activation syndrome and with T-cell-mediated rejection.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CXCL10 (IP-10), an interferon-induced chemokine and biomarker of Th1 inflammation and transplant rejection.
items.body_md:
C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 10. Previous name IP-10 (interferon gamma-induced protein 10 kDa), alias INP10, crg-2 (mouse). Located on 4q21.1 next to *CXCL9* and *CXCL11*.

Encodes CXCL10, produced by monocytes, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, keratinocytes and hepatocytes in response to IFN-γ, type I interferons and TLR ligands.

Clinical relevance: urinary CXCL10 (often normalised to creatinine) is one of the best-studied non-invasive biomarkers of kidney allograft inflammation (T-cell-mediated and antibody-mediated rejection and BK polyomavirus nephropathy); serum IP-10 rises in hepatitis C, tuberculosis (IP-10 release assays), COVID-19 and autoimmune thyroiditis. Baseline IP-10 predicted non-response to interferon-based HCV therapy. CXCL10 is a core gene of IFN-γ signatures in tumours and in molecular rejection classifiers.

items.gloss_md: Interferon-induced CXCR3 ligand that recruits Th1, CD8+ T and NK cells; a serum and urine biomarker of interferon-driven inflammation.
items.body_md:
ELR-negative CXC chemokine (77 amino acids, about 10 kDa) binding CXCR3 (CXCR3-A mediates chemotaxis; CXCR3-B is angiostatic on endothelium). Induced through STAT1 (both type I and type II interferon response elements in its promoter) and NF-κB.

Regulation: dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4/CD26) cleaves two N-terminal amino acids, converting CXCL10 into a CXCR3 antagonist – the high levels of 'antagonist IP-10' in chronic HCV may help explain impaired T-cell recruitment.

Encoded by *CXCL10*. Biomarker use: kidney transplant monitoring (urinary CXCL10), tuberculosis diagnostics, viral and autoimmune disease activity.

attrs.mnemonic: IP-10 = 'Interferon Protein, 10 kDa': where interferon is, IP-10 calls the T cells – even into the urine of a rejecting kidney.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding CCL2 (MCP-1), the main chemokine recruiting CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes into injured liver and tumours.
items.body_md:
C-C motif chemokine ligand 2. Previous names MCP-1 (monocyte chemoattractant protein 1), MCAF, SCYA2. Located on 17q12 in the CC chemokine cluster.

Encodes CCL2, produced by macrophages, endothelium, fibroblasts, hepatic stellate cells, hepatocytes and many tumour cells in response to IL-1, TNF, TLR ligands and oxidised lipids.

Clinical relevance: in liver injury, CCL2 from Kupffer and stellate cells recruits CCR2+ monocytes that become monocyte-derived macrophages driving inflammation and fibrosis; the CCR2/CCR5 antagonist cenicriviroc reduced fibrosis in phase 2 but failed in the phase 3 AURORA trial in MASH. In PDAC, CCL2 recruits tumour-associated macrophages and is associated with poor survival; a CCR2 inhibitor was combined with FOLFIRINOX in early trials. CCL2 also mediates monocyte recruitment in atherosclerosis and allograft inflammation.

items.gloss_md: CC chemokine that recruits CCR2+ classical monocytes from the bone marrow and blood into inflamed tissues and tumours.
items.body_md:
76-amino-acid CC chemokine that binds CCR2 (high affinity) on classical monocytes (CD14++CD16−; Ly6C-high in mice), memory T cells, NK cells and basophils; CCR2 signalling is required for monocyte egress from bone marrow and their entry into tissues.

Functions: monocyte recruitment in infection, sterile injury (liver, kidney, myocardium), atherosclerosis, tumours (tumour-associated macrophages and metastasis-associated macrophages) and pain. Serum MCP-1 rises in many inflammatory conditions and in MASH and alcohol-related hepatitis.

Encoded by *CCL2*. Therapeutic antagonism (CCR2 inhibitors, cenicriviroc) has been tested in MASH, PDAC and diabetic nephropathy, without approval so far.

attrs.mnemonic: MCP-1 = Monocyte Chemoattractant Protein 1: CCL2 calls classical monocytes via CCR2 – '2 calls 2'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding STAT1, the transcription factor mediating responses to all interferons; loss and gain of function cause distinct immunodeficiencies.
items.body_md:
Signal transducer and activator of transcription 1, located on 2q32.2 next to *STAT4*.

Encodes STAT1, activated by JAK phosphorylation at Tyr701 downstream of type I (IFN-α/β), type II (IFN-γ) and type III (IFN-λ) interferon receptors and IL-27.

Disease relevance (inborn errors of immunity, Casanova and others): complete autosomal recessive STAT1 deficiency causes lethal mycobacterial and viral infections; partial or dominant-negative loss causes Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease; heterozygous gain-of-function mutations (2011) cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (impaired Th17 responses), autoimmunity, aneurysms and are treatable with JAK inhibitors.

Clinical relevance: STAT1 is part of interferon-response signatures in tumours, rejection biopsies and autoimmunity; loss of JAK–STAT1 signalling in tumours causes resistance to IFN-γ and checkpoint blockade. Ruxolitinib and other JAK inhibitors block STAT1 activation.

attrs.full_name: signal transducer and activator of transcription 1

items.gloss_md: Latent cytoplasmic transcription factor activated by JAK kinases downstream of interferon receptors; drives interferon-stimulated gene expression.
items.body_md:
SH2-domain-containing transcription factor (isoforms STAT1α, 91 kDa, and the truncated STAT1β). Phosphorylation at Tyr701 leads to dimerisation via reciprocal SH2–phosphotyrosine interactions; Ser727 phosphorylation increases transcriptional activity.

Complexes: IFN-γ → STAT1 homodimer (gamma-activated factor, GAF) → GAS elements (e.g. IRF1, CXCL9, CIITA → MHC class II); type I and III IFN → STAT1–STAT2–IRF9 (ISGF3) → ISRE elements (MX1, OAS1, ISG15, IFIT genes). Inhibitors: SOCS1, PIAS1, phosphatases (TC-PTP, SHP-2).

Encoded by *STAT1*. Phospho-STAT1 by flow cytometry (after IFN stimulation) is used to diagnose STAT1 loss- and gain-of-function disorders.

aliases: signal transducer and activator of transcription 1
attrs.mnemonic: STAT1 = the 'interferon STAT'; STAT3 = the 'IL-6/IL-10 STAT'; STAT5 = the 'IL-2 STAT'.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding IRF1, the IFN-γ-induced transcription factor that amplifies interferon responses, including PD-L1 and MHC expression.
items.body_md:
Interferon regulatory factor 1, located on 5q31.1 in the cytokine cluster (near *IL3*, *IL4*, *IL5*, *IL13*).

Encodes IRF1, the first member of the IRF family, identified in 1988 by Tadatsugu Taniguchi's group as a factor binding the IFN-β gene promoter. It is a primary STAT1 target gene after IFN-γ stimulation and induces secondary interferon-response genes.

Disease relevance: in 2023 autosomal recessive complete IRF1 deficiency was described in children with Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease and severe viral disease, confirming its role in IFN-γ immunity. IRF1 has tumour-suppressive properties (deletion or loss of expression in some leukaemias and cancers).

Clinical relevance: IRF1 is required for IFN-γ-induced PD-L1 expression (via an IRF1-binding site in the CD274 promoter) and is a component of interferon signatures used in immuno-oncology and transplant molecular diagnostics.

items.gloss_md: Interferon regulatory transcription factor induced by IFN-γ via STAT1 that activates genes for antigen presentation, PD-L1, IL-12 and antimicrobial defence.
items.body_md:
Transcription factor with an N-terminal tryptophan-pentad DNA-binding domain recognising IRF-element/ISRE sequences. It is short-lived (half-life about 30 minutes) and constitutively expressed at low level, but strongly induced by IFN-γ, TNF and TLR signalling.

Targets: CD274 (PD-L1), MHC class I and immunoproteasome genes, TAP1, CIITA (with STAT1), IL12B and IL15, NOS2, guanylate-binding proteins, caspase-1 and gasdermin D (pyroptosis), and the IFN-β promoter.

Encoded by *IRF1*. Mediates much of IFN-γ's antimycobacterial macrophage programme.

Loss of IRF1 in tumour cells weakens interferon-induced antigen presentation and PD-L1 expression and can contribute to resistance to checkpoint blockade.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding Toll-like receptor 4, the receptor for bacterial lipopolysaccharide.
items.body_md:
Toll like receptor 4, alias CD284, hToll. Located on 9q33.1.

Encodes TLR4, expressed on monocytes, macrophages (including Kupffer cells), dendritic cells, neutrophils, endothelium, hepatic stellate cells and hepatocytes.

Discovery: in 1998 Bruce Beutler's group positionally cloned the Lps locus of LPS-resistant C3H/HeJ and C57BL/10ScCr mice and found Tlr4 mutations, identifying the long-sought LPS receptor; Beutler and Jules Hoffmann (Toll in Drosophila immunity) shared the 2011 Nobel Prize with Ralph Steinman.

Liver relevance: gut-derived LPS reaching the liver through the portal vein (increased in cirrhosis, alcohol use and MASH due to dysbiosis and barrier failure) activates TLR4 on Kupffer cells and stellate cells; stellate-cell TLR4 downregulates the TGF-β pseudoreceptor BAMBI, sensitising cells to TGF-β and promoting fibrosis. Variants D299G and T399I modestly reduce responsiveness and have been associated with lower fibrosis risk in hepatitis C. TLR4 antagonism (eritoran) failed in sepsis.

items.gloss_md: Pattern-recognition receptor that senses bacterial lipopolysaccharide with MD-2 and signals through MyD88 and TRIF to induce inflammatory cytokines and type I interferon.
items.body_md:
Type I transmembrane receptor with an extracellular leucine-rich-repeat ectodomain and a cytoplasmic TIR domain. The lipid A part of LPS is delivered by LBP and CD14 to MD-2, which binds TLR4 and triggers dimerisation of two TLR4–MD-2 complexes.

Two signalling arms: at the plasma membrane TIRAP–MyD88 → IRAK4/IRAK1 → TRAF6 → NF-κB and MAPK (TNF, IL-6, IL-1β pro-forms); after CD14-dependent endocytosis TRAM–TRIF → TBK1 → IRF3 → IFN-β. TLR4 is the only TLR using both adaptors. Also senses endogenous danger signals (HMGB1, oxidised phospholipids, saturated fatty acids – debated) and the monophosphoryl lipid A adjuvant in some vaccines (e.g. AS04).

Encoded by *TLR4*. Excessive TLR4 signalling contributes to septic shock and to inflammation in cirrhosis (systemic inflammation hypothesis of decompensation).

attrs.mnemonic: TLR4 = the LPS receptor and the only TLR that uses both adaptors, MyD88 and TRIF.
attrs.anecdote: 'Toll' means 'great!' in German: Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard reportedly exclaimed 'Das ist ja toll!' on seeing the Drosophila mutant embryos, and the name stuck for the whole receptor family.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding cGAS, the cytosolic DNA sensor that produces cGAMP to activate STING.
items.body_md:
Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase. Previous symbol MB21D1, alias C6orf150. Located on 6q13.

Encodes cGAS, discovered in 2013 by Zhijian (James) Chen's laboratory as the enzyme that synthesises the second messenger 2'3'-cGAMP upon binding cytosolic double-stranded DNA.

Function: detects DNA from viruses, bacteria, damaged mitochondria (mtDNA release), micronuclei and ruptured nuclei in chromosomally unstable cells, and retroelement cDNA; most cGAS is tethered to chromatin by nucleosomes, which keeps it inactive.

Disease relevance: cGAS–STING activation by self-DNA drives type I interferonopathies when DNA-degrading nucleases fail (TREX1 – Aicardi–Goutières syndrome, DNASE2), contributes to senescence-associated inflammation, and to liver inflammation in alcohol-related and metabolic liver disease and ischaemia–reperfusion injury in experimental models. In cancer, cGAS–STING links chromosomal instability and radiotherapy to anti-tumour immunity (or to chronic inflammation and metastasis).

items.gloss_md: Cytosolic DNA sensor enzyme that synthesises the cyclic dinucleotide 2'3'-cGAMP, which activates STING and type I interferon production.
items.body_md:
Nucleotidyltransferase of the Mab21 family with a disordered, positively charged N-terminus and a catalytic domain. Binding of dsDNA (length-dependent, sequence-independent; longer DNA forms ladder-like condensates) causes a conformational change that allows it to convert ATP and GTP into 2'3'-cGAMP, with an unusual 2'-5' and 3'-5' phosphodiester pair.

cGAMP binds STING in the same cell and can pass to neighbouring cells through gap junctions or transporters (e.g. SLC19A1), spreading the alarm; the ectonuclease ENPP1 degrades extracellular cGAMP.

Encoded by *CGAS*. Inhibitors are developed for interferonopathies and autoimmune diseases.

attrs.mnemonic: cGAS 'gasps' when it smells DNA in the cytosol: DNA → cGAS → cGAMP → STING → TBK1 → IRF3 → interferon.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding STING, the ER adaptor activated by cGAMP that induces type I interferon; gain-of-function causes SAVI.
items.body_md:
Stimulator of interferon response cGAMP interactor 1. Previous symbol TMEM173; aliases STING, MITA, ERIS, MPYS, NET23. Located on 5q31.2.

Encodes STING, an ER membrane adaptor identified in 2008 by several groups (Ishikawa and Barber named it STING) as an essential mediator of cytosolic DNA-induced interferon responses; in 2013 2'3'-cGAMP from cGAS was identified as its endogenous ligand. It also senses bacterial cyclic dinucleotides directly.

Disease relevance: heterozygous gain-of-function mutations cause STING-associated vasculopathy with onset in infancy (SAVI, 2014): skin vasculopathy, interstitial lung disease and systemic inflammation, partly responsive to JAK inhibitors. Common human STING alleles (e.g. HAQ) differ in responsiveness.

Clinical relevance: STING agonists (e.g. ADU-S100, diABZI analogues) were developed as cancer immunotherapy but have shown limited efficacy so far; STING inhibitors are explored for interferonopathies and MASH, where hepatocyte and macrophage STING promotes inflammation in mouse models.

attrs.full_name: stimulator of interferon response cGAMP interactor 1
attrs.anecdote: The mouse STING agonist DMXAA (vadimezan) looked impressive against mouse tumours but failed in a phase 3 lung cancer trial; only later was it found that DMXAA binds mouse STING but not human STING.

items.gloss_md: ER-resident adaptor that binds cGAMP and activates TBK1–IRF3 and NF-κB to induce type I interferon and inflammatory cytokines.
items.body_md:
Homodimeric protein with four N-terminal transmembrane helices, a cytosolic ligand-binding domain and a C-terminal tail (CTT). cGAMP binding closes a 'lid' over the binding pocket, triggers oligomerisation and COPII-dependent trafficking from the ER to the ER–Golgi intermediate compartment and Golgi, where palmitoylation is required. The CTT then recruits and activates TBK1, which phosphorylates STING (pLxIS motif) to recruit IRF3; IRF3 dimers enter the nucleus and induce IFN-β. STING also activates NF-κB, non-canonical autophagy (LC3 lipidation) and, when overactivated, cell death; it is finally degraded in lysosomes.

Encoded by *STING1*. Pathway inhibitors (e.g. H-151 in mice) and agonists are under investigation; the ancestral function of STING is probably autophagy induction.

items.gloss_md: Gene encoding NLRP3 (cryopyrin), the sensor of the canonical inflammasome; gain-of-function causes cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.
items.body_md:
NLR family pyrin domain containing 3. Previous symbols CIAS1, NALP3; alias cryopyrin. Located on 1q44.

Encodes NLRP3, expressed mainly in monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils and dendritic cells; expression requires a priming signal (TLR or TNF via NF-κB).

Disease relevance: in 2001 Hal Hoffman and colleagues identified heterozygous gain-of-function mutations (exon 3, NACHT domain) as the cause of familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome and Muckle–Wells syndrome; the spectrum including neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (NOMID/CINCA) is now called cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), effectively treated with IL-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab, rilonacept).

Clinical relevance: NLRP3 is activated by monosodium urate crystals (gout), cholesterol crystals (atherosclerosis), amyloid, silica and asbestos; in the liver it contributes to inflammation and fibrosis in MASH and alcohol-related hepatitis in mouse models. Several direct NLRP3 inhibitors (e.g. dapansutrile and others) are in clinical trials; the prototype MCC950 caused liver toxicity in an early trial.

attrs.anecdote: Cryopyrin got its name from familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome: carriers develop fever, rash and joint pain after exposure to cold – 'cryo' for cold, 'pyrin' for its pyrin domain and fever.

items.gloss_md: Cytosolic NOD-like receptor that assembles the NLRP3 inflammasome with ASC and caspase-1, releasing IL-1β and IL-18 and triggering pyroptosis.
items.body_md:
Tripartite protein: N-terminal pyrin domain (PYD), central NACHT nucleotide-binding and oligomerisation domain (ATPase), C-terminal leucine-rich repeats. Inactive NLRP3 forms cage-like oligomers on membranes.

Two-signal activation: priming (NF-κB induces NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β) and activation by diverse stimuli that converge on potassium efflux (extracellular ATP via P2X7, the toxin nigericin, crystals and particulates with lysosomal rupture, mitochondrial dysfunction). NEK7 binding allows oligomerisation; NLRP3 PYDs nucleate ASC (PYCARD) filaments ('specks'), which recruit and activate caspase-1. Caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β, pro-IL-18 and gasdermin D; GSDMD pores release the cytokines and cause pyroptotic cell death.

Encoded by *NLRP3*. ASC specks released from dying cells can propagate inflammation; inflammasome readouts include IL-1β, IL-18 and caspase-1 activity.

attrs.mnemonic: Inflammasome = 'two keys': signal 1 primes (NF-κB), signal 2 activates (K⁺ efflux) – then caspase-1 cuts IL-1β, IL-18 and gasdermin D.
